# LINEAR ALGEBRA AND MATRIX THEORY
**Course Code:** MATH 2210 | **Credits:** 4 | **Quarter:** Fall 2024

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

- Lecture: MWF 9:00-9:50 AM, Lecture Hall B-205  
- Lab Section: Thursday 1:00-2:50 PM, Computer Lab Math-118  

**Course Website:** Available through university learning management system

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra and matrix theory, fundamental mathematical tools essential for advanced mathematics, engineering, computer science, economics, and data science. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and matrix decompositions through both theoretical analysis and computational applications. The course emphasizes developing mathematical reasoning skills while building practical competency in solving systems of linear equations, performing matrix operations, and understanding geometric interpretations of linear algebraic concepts. 

Students will work with real-world applications including computer graphics transformations, principal component analysis, least squares regression, and network analysis. Through a combination of rigorous proofs, computational exercises, and applied projects, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for advanced coursework in pure and applied mathematics. The course integrates technology through computational software like MATLAB or Python to visualize concepts and solve complex problems.

**Target Audience:** Undergraduate students in mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, or economics who have completed introductory calculus and are preparing for advanced coursework requiring linear algebra.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Analyze vector spaces and linear transformations to solve real-world problems in computer graphics, data compression, and optimization
• Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors through both hand calculation and computational software like MATLAB or Python
• Construct mathematical proofs by applying fundamental theorems of linear algebra to verify properties of matrices and linear transformations
• Model practical applications using matrix decomposition techniques including LU factorization, QR decomposition, and singular value decomposition

---

## PREREQUISITES

- Completion of Calculus II (multivariable calculus) with a grade of C or better
- Introduction to Mathematical Proofs or equivalent proof-writing experience
- Students should be comfortable with algebraic manipulation, basic trigonometry, and have exposure to formal mathematical reasoning and notation

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Textbook:** Lay, D.C., Lay, S.R., & McDonald, J.J. (2021). *Linear Algebra and Its Applications*, 6th Edition. Pearson.

**Software:** 
- MATLAB (free student license available) or Python with NumPy/SciPy libraries
- Graphing calculator (TI-84 Plus or equivalent)

**Supplementary Materials:**
- Course packet with additional exercises (available at campus bookstore)
- Online homework system access code (bundled with textbook)

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1: Linear Systems and Matrix Operations**
*Topics:* Introduction to linear systems, augmented matrices, Gaussian elimination, elementary row operations, row echelon form
- **Monday:** Course introduction and linear systems fundamentals
- **Wednesday:** Matrix operations and augmented matrices
- **Thursday Lab:** Computational introduction to MATLAB/Python for matrix operations
- **Friday:** Gaussian elimination and back-substitution methods

### **Week 2: Matrix Operations and Properties**
*Topics:* Matrix arithmetic, matrix multiplication, inverse matrices, determinants
- **Activity:** Shopping Cart Budget Challenge (50 min) - Apply systematic calculation methods
- **Assessment:** Problem Set 1 Due (Friday)

### **Week 3: Determinants and Matrix Inverses**
*Topics:* Properties of determinants, cofactor expansion, inverse matrix calculations, applications to solving systems
- **Thursday Lab:** Computing determinants and inverses using technology

### **Week 4: Vector Spaces and Subspaces**
*Topics:* Vector spaces, subspaces, spanning sets, linear independence
- **Activity:** Design Your Dream School Project (190 min, split over multiple sessions) - Apply systems of linear equations to real-world constraints
- **Assessment:** Midterm Exam 1 (Friday, 100 points)

### **Week 5: Basis and Dimension**
*Topics:* Basis for vector spaces, dimension, coordinate systems, change of basis
- **Thursday Lab:** Visualizing vector spaces and geometric interpretations

### **Week 6: Linear Transformations**
*Topics:* Linear transformations, matrix representations, kernel and range
- **Activity:** Personal Budget Planning (45 min) - Apply systematic mathematical procedures

### **Week 7: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors**
*Topics:* Characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues, eigenvectors, diagonalization
- **Thursday Lab:** Computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors with software
- **Assessment:** Mathematical Modeling Project Assigned (100 points, due Week 9)

### **Week 8: Applications of Eigenvalues**
*Topics:* Diagonalization, similarity transformations, applications to dynamical systems
- **Assessment:** Problem Set 2 Due (Monday)

### **Week 9: Orthogonality and Least Squares**
*Topics:* Inner products, orthogonal sets, orthogonal projections, least squares solutions
- **Thursday Lab:** Least squares regression analysis with real data
- **Assessment:** Mathematical Modeling Project Due (Friday, 100 points)

### **Week 10: Matrix Decompositions and Final Applications**
*Topics:* QR decomposition, singular value decomposition, principal component analysis
- **Activity:** Design and Present Mathematical Community Model (115 min) - Integrate multiple linear algebra concepts
- **Assessment:** Comprehensive Final Exam (Finals Week, 100 points)

---

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

| Assessment Type | Description | Points | Weight |
|-----------------|-------------|---------|---------|
| **Problem Sets (2)** | Weekly homework assignments | 50 each | 25% |
| **Lab Reports** | Weekly computational lab assignments | 100 total | 25% |
| **Midterm Exam** | In-class examination covering Weeks 1-4 | 100 | 20% |
| **Mathematical Modeling Project** | Real-world optimization problem analysis | 100 | 15% |
| **Final Exam** | Comprehensive final examination | 100 | 15% |
| **Total** |  | **400** | **100%** |

### **Grading Scale:**
- A: 93-100% | A-: 90-92%
- B+: 87-89% | B: 83-86% | B-: 80-82%
- C+: 77-79% | C: 73-76% | C-: 70-72%
- D+: 67-69% | D: 63-66% | D-: 60-62%
- F: Below 60%

---

## COURSE POLICIES

### **Attendance Policy**
Regular attendance is essential for success in this course. Students are expected to attend all lectures and lab sessions. More than three unexcused absences may result in a reduction of the final grade. Students must notify the instructor in advance of any anticipated absence.

### **Late Work Policy**
Problem sets submitted late will receive a 10% penalty per day. Lab reports must be submitted by the end of the lab session unless prior arrangements are made. No late work will be accepted after solutions have been distributed.

### **Makeup Policy**
Makeup exams will only be given for documented emergencies or university-sanctioned absences with advance notice when possible. Alternative arrangements must be made within one week of the missed exam.

### **Academic Integrity**
All work submitted must be your own. Collaboration on homework is encouraged, but each student must write up solutions independently. Any form of cheating or plagiarism will result in course failure and disciplinary action. Use of unauthorized materials during exams is strictly prohibited.

### **Technology Policy**
Graphing calculators are permitted on homework and specified exam problems. Cell phones must be turned off during class. Laptop computers are allowed for note-taking but must be used appropriately.

### **Accommodations**
Students with documented disabilities who may need accommodations should schedule an appointment with the instructor as soon as possible. All discussions will remain confidential. Students should contact the Office of Disability Services to verify their eligibility for reasonable accommodations.

---

## ADDITIONAL RESOURCES

### **Tutoring Support**
- Math Help Center: Monday-Friday 10:00 AM - 4:00 PM, Mathematics Building Lobby
- Online tutoring available through university student success center
- Study groups encouraged - contact instructor for coordination

### **Communication**
- Check university email daily for course announcements
- Use office hours for individual help - no appointment necessary
- Course website contains all materials, grades, and announcements

### **Success Strategies**
- Complete practice problems beyond assigned homework
- Form study groups with classmates
- Attend lab sessions prepared with questions
- Seek help early if concepts are unclear

# MATH 2120: LINEAR ALGEBRA WITH APPLICATIONS

**Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Schedule:**  
- - **Lab Session:** Wednesday 2:00-3:50 PM, Computer Lab MAC 115

**Course Website:** Available through university learning management system

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical applications across multiple disciplines. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and orthogonality. The course bridges abstract mathematical concepts with real-world applications in computer science, engineering, physics, economics, and data science. Through computational exercises using MATLAB or Python, students will solve systems of linear equations, perform matrix decompositions, and analyze linear models. Topics include Gaussian elimination, determinants, basis and dimension, diagonalization, and least squares approximation. Students will develop critical thinking skills through proof-writing exercises and gain practical experience through projects involving data analysis, computer graphics transformations, and optimization problems. This course serves as essential preparation for advanced mathematics courses including differential equations, numerical analysis, and abstract algebra, while also providing foundational knowledge for machine learning, quantum mechanics, and econometrics. By the end of the semester, students will possess both the theoretical understanding and computational skills necessary to apply linear algebra concepts in their chosen field of study.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Students will analyze systems of linear equations to solve real-world problems in engineering, economics, and computer science using matrix methods and Gaussian elimination

• Students will compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors through hand calculations and computational software to understand dynamic systems and data dimensionality reduction

• Students will construct mathematical proofs by applying fundamental theorems of linear algebra including the rank-nullity theorem and spectral theorem

• Students will implement matrix operations and decompositions using MATLAB or Python to process datasets and perform numerical computations in scientific applications

---

## TARGET AUDIENCE & PREREQUISITES

**Target Audience:** Second or third-year undergraduate students majoring in mathematics, computer science, engineering, physics, or economics who seek to develop advanced mathematical reasoning skills and computational proficiency. **Prerequisites:** Completion of Calculus I and II (MATH 1251 and 1252) with grades of C or better, and either Discrete Mathematics (MATH 2300) or Introduction to Mathematical Reasoning (MATH 2200). # Advanced Topics in Functional Analysis and Operator Theory
**Mathematics 8950 | Spring 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## Course Description

This advanced graduate course explores the theoretical foundations and applications of functional analysis with emphasis on operator theory in infinite-dimensional spaces. Students will investigate the spectral theory of linear operators, compact and bounded operators on Banach and Hilbert spaces, and their applications to partial differential equations and quantum mechanics. The course covers advanced topics including the theory of C*-algebras, unbounded operators, and semigroup theory. Through rigorous proof-based assignments and research projects, students will develop expertise in abstract mathematical reasoning while connecting theoretical concepts to applications in mathematical physics, signal processing, and numerical analysis. This course is essential for students pursuing research in pure mathematics, mathematical physics, or applied mathematics areas requiring sophisticated analytical tools. Students will engage with current research literature and complete an independent project investigating recent developments in operator theory or its applications to emerging fields such as quantum information theory or machine learning.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Analyze spectral properties of bounded and unbounded operators to solve problems in quantum mechanics and partial differential equations  
• Construct rigorous proofs of fundamental theorems in functional analysis through systematic application of topological and algebraic methods  
• Evaluate the structure and properties of C*-algebras and von Neumann algebras by investigating their representation theory and classification schemes  
• Synthesize operator theory techniques using computational tools such as MATLAB or Python to model infinite-dimensional dynamical systems  

---

## Target Audience & Prerequisites

**Target Audience:** Second or third-year PhD students in mathematics, mathematical physics, or related fields who have completed core graduate sequences and are preparing for doctoral research. Ideal for students interested in pure mathematics research areas including functional analysis, operator algebras, or mathematical physics, as well as those pursuing applied research requiring advanced analytical techniques.

**Prerequisites:** Completion of graduate-level real analysis (measure theory, Lebesgue integration), complex analysis, and introductory functional analysis covering normed spaces, Banach and Hilbert spaces, and basic operator theory. Strong background in linear algebra and topology required. Prior exposure to partial differential equations and mathematical physics recommended but not mandatory.

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations and Spectral Theory Review
**Module Focus:** Review of Banach and Hilbert spaces, bounded linear operators  
**Key Concepts:** Operator norms, adjoint operators, compact operators  
**Activities:** Problem set on spectral radius calculations  

### Week 2: Spectral Theory of Bounded Operators
**Module Focus:** Spectrum, resolvent, spectral radius theorem  
**Key Concepts:** Point spectrum, continuous spectrum, residual spectrum  
**Assessment:** Real-World Problem Solving Discussion (100 points)  

### Week 3: Compact Operators and Fredholm Theory
**Module Focus:** Properties of compact operators, Fredholm alternative  
**Key Concepts:** Riesz-Schauder theory, index theory  
**Activities:** Optimization of Urban Water Distribution Networks (120 minutes)  

### Week 4: Self-Adjoint Operators and Spectral Theorem
**Module Focus:** Spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators  
**Key Concepts:** Eigenvalue decomposition, spectral measures  
**Activities:** Design and Construct Dynamic Optimization System (Week 1 of 5)  

### Week 5: Unbounded Operators - Fundamentals
**Module Focus:** Closed operators, domains, extensions  
**Key Concepts:** Graph topology, closable operators, self-adjoint extensions  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 2)  

### Week 6: Unbounded Self-Adjoint Operators
**Module Focus:** Spectral theorem for unbounded self-adjoint operators  
**Key Concepts:** Spectral families, Stone's theorem  
**Assessment:** Advanced Calculus and Linear Algebra Integration Exam (100 points)  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 3)  

### Week 7: Applications to Quantum Mechanics
**Module Focus:** Quantum mechanical operators, momentum and position  
**Key Concepts:** Heisenberg uncertainty principle, canonical commutation relations  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 4)  

### Week 8: Introduction to C*-Algebras
**Module Focus:** Definition, examples, basic properties  
**Key Concepts:** Involution, C*-identity, Gelfand-Naimark theorem  
**Assessment:** Statistical Analysis Laboratory Report Due (100 points)  
**Activities:** Dynamic Optimization System (Week 5 - Final presentations)  

### Week 9: Representation Theory of C*-Algebras
**Module Focus:** *-representations, irreducible representations  
**Key Concepts:** GNS construction, pure states  
**Activities:** Optimization of Urban Traffic Flow (130 minutes)  

### Week 10: Von Neumann Algebras
**Module Focus:** Weak and strong operator topologies, double commutant theorem  
**Key Concepts:** Type classification, factors  
**Activities:** Design Mathematical Urban Planning Model (105 minutes)  

### Week 11: Semigroup Theory - Fundamentals
**Module Focus:** One-parameter semigroups, generators  
**Key Concepts:** Hille-Yosida theorem, contraction semigroups  

### Week 12: Applications of Semigroup Theory
**Module Focus:** Evolution equations, heat equation, wave equation  
**Key Concepts:** Analytic semigroups, interpolation spaces  
**Activities:** Predictive Financial Model Construction (4.5 hours)  

### Week 13: Advanced Topics - Quantum Information Theory
**Module Focus:** Quantum channels, completely positive maps  
**Key Concepts:** Stinespring dilation, Kraus representation  

### Week 14: Research Project Presentations I
**Student presentations of independent research projectsAssessment:** Real-World Mathematics Portfolio Due (100 points)  

### Week 15: Research Project Presentations II  
**Student presentations continuedAssessment:** Personal Budget Planning Project Due (100 points)  

### Finals Week: Final Project Reports Due
**Comprehensive written reports on independent research projects**

---

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage | Description |
|----------------|--------|------------|-------------|
| Homework Sets (6) | 300 | 30% | Bi-weekly problem sets emphasizing proof techniques and computational applications |
| Midterm Exam | 100 | 10% | Advanced Calculus and Linear Algebra Integration Exam |
| Laboratory Report | 100 | 10% | Statistical Analysis of Real-World Data |
| Class Participation | 100 | 10% | Discussion forums, peer review, presentation feedback |

# Linear Algebra and Matrix Theory
**MATH 230 | 4 Credits | [Semester/Quarter]**

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra, focusing on vector spaces, linear transformations, and matrix theory with applications across science, engineering, and data science. Students will explore fundamental concepts including systems of linear equations, matrix operations, determinants, eigenvalues, and eigenvectors. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and computational proficiency, preparing students to apply linear algebraic methods to real-world problems in computer graphics, machine learning, optimization, and engineering systems. 

Through a combination of rigorous proofs, computational exercises, and practical applications, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for advanced coursework in mathematics, statistics, computer science, and related fields. The course integrates technology tools including MATLAB or Python for matrix computations and visualization. Topics covered include Gaussian elimination, vector spaces and subspaces, linear independence and basis, orthogonality and least squares, diagonalization, and singular value decomposition. Students will complete projects that demonstrate the power of linear algebra in modeling and solving contemporary problems in data analysis, image processing, and scientific computing.

**Target Audience:** Second or third-year undergraduate students majoring in mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, or statistics who seek to build foundational skills in linear algebra for advanced coursework and career applications in technical fields requiring quantitative analysis.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Solve systems of linear equations and analyze their solutions to model real-world scenarios in engineering and economics  
• Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors through both analytical methods and computational software like MATLAB or Python  
• Construct mathematical proofs by applying fundamental theorems of linear algebra including the rank-nullity theorem and spectral theorem  
• Implement matrix decomposition techniques using programming environments to analyze large datasets and perform dimensionality reduction  

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Systems of Linear Equations and Matrix Operations
**Module:** Linear Systems and Matrix Operations  
*Topics: Matrix notation, elementary row operations, Gaussian elimination*

- **Monday:** Introduction to linear systems and augmented matrices
- **Wednesday:** Elementary row operations and row echelon form  
- **Friday:** Matrix operations: addition, multiplication, and transpose
- 
**Activity:** Budget Planning for a Class Pizza Party (45 min) - Apply arithmetic operations to real-world budgeting

### Week 2: Solving Linear Systems
**Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Applications  
*Topics: Gaussian elimination, solution classification, parametric solutions*

- **Monday:** Gauss-Jordan elimination and reduced row echelon form
- **Wednesday:** Consistent, inconsistent, and dependent systems
- **Friday:** Parametric representations of solution sets
- 
**Assessment:** Mathematical Problem-Solving Strategies Discussion (100 pts) - Real-world applications of linear systems

### Week 3: Matrix Algebra and Invertibility  
**Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Real-World Applications  
*Topics: Matrix multiplication, inverses, determinants*

- **Monday:** Properties of matrix multiplication
- **Wednesday:** Matrix inverses and the inverse algorithm
- **Friday:** Introduction to determinants
- 
**Activity:** Multi-Variable Optimization for Real-World Business Problems (110 min) - Apply linear algebra to business scenarios

### Week 4: Determinants and Cramer's Rule
*Topics: Determinant properties, cofactor expansion, applications*

- **Monday:** Determinant calculation methods
- **Wednesday:** Properties of determinants
- **Friday:** Cramer's rule and applications
- 
**Assessment:** Advanced Calculus Problem Solving Quiz (100 pts) - Problem-solving with matrix methods

### Week 5: Vector Spaces and Subspaces
*Topics: Vector space axioms, subspaces, span*

- **Monday:** Introduction to vector spaces
- **Wednesday:** Subspaces and the subspace test
- **Friday:** Span and linear combinations
- 
**Activity:** Design Your Dream City: Scale Model with Mathematical Constraints (120 min) - Apply geometric principles and linear relationships

### Week 6: Linear Independence and Basis
*Topics: Linear independence, basis, dimension*

- **Monday:** Linear independence and dependence
- **Wednesday:** Basis for vector spaces
- **Friday:** Dimension and the dimension theorem
- 
### Week 7: Linear Transformations
*Topics: Matrix transformations, kernel, range*

- **Monday:** Linear transformations and their matrices
- **Wednesday:** Kernel (null space) and range (column space)
- **Friday:** The rank-nullity theorem
- 
**Activity:** Design and Validate Mathematical Model for Urban Traffic Flow (240 min) - Create comprehensive linear algebra applications

### Week 8: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
*Topics: Characteristic equation, eigenspaces, diagonalization*

- **Monday:** Introduction to eigenvalues and eigenvectors
- **Wednesday:** The characteristic equation
- **Friday:** Eigenspaces and geometric multiplicity
- 
**Assessment:** Mathematical Patterns Lab Report (100 pts) - Exploring eigenvalue applications in real systems

### Week 9: Diagonalization and Applications
*Topics: Diagonalizable matrices, applications to differential equations*

- **Monday:** Diagonalization process
- **Wednesday:** Applications to systems of differential equations
- **Friday:** Symmetric matrices and orthogonal diagonalization
- 
### Week 10: Orthogonality and Least Squares
*Topics: Orthogonal vectors, projections, least squares approximation*

- **Monday:** Orthogonal and orthonormal sets
- **Wednesday:** Orthogonal projections
- **Friday:** Least squares solutions
- 
**Activity:** Design Optimal Solar Panel Arrays Using Mathematical Optimization (100 min) - Apply orthogonal projections to engineering problems

**Assessment:** Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation (100 pts) - Modern applications of linear algebra

| Homework & Lab Assignments | 300 | 30% | Weekly computational and theoretical problems |
| Quizzes | 200 | 20% | In-class assessments of key concepts |
| Discussion Participation | 100 | 10% | Collaborative problem-solving activities |
| Lab Report | 100 | 10% | Mathematical patterns investigation |

### Make-up Policy
Make-up exams and quizzes will only be given for documented emergencies or university-approved absences. Students must contact the instructor within 24 hours of the missed assessment to arrange a make-up.

### Accommodations
Students with documented disabilities should contact the Office of Disability Services to arrange reasonable accommodations. Please notify the instructor within the first two weeks of class to ensure proper accommodations can be implemented.

### Communication
The best way to reach the instructor is via email. Please include "MATH 230" in the subject line. Expect a response within 24 hours during weekdays. For urgent matters, attend office hours or schedule an appointment.

# Linear Algebra and Its Applications
**MATH 3310 | 3 Credit Hours | Spring 2024**

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to linear algebra with emphasis on both theoretical foundations and practical applications across multiple disciplines. Students will explore vector spaces, linear transformations, matrix operations, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and systems of linear equations. The course bridges abstract mathematical concepts with real-world applications in computer science, engineering, economics, and data science. Through a combination of rigorous proofs and computational problem-solving, students develop critical thinking skills essential for advanced mathematics and quantitative fields. Topics include Gaussian elimination, determinants, orthogonality, diagonalization, and least squares approximation. Students will use mathematical software to visualize concepts and solve complex problems, preparing them for advanced coursework in differential equations, numerical analysis, optimization, and machine learning. The course emphasizes both hand calculations and computational approaches, ensuring students understand underlying principles while gaining practical skills for modern applications.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Analyze** vector spaces and linear transformations to model real-world phenomena in engineering and computer graphics applications  
• **Solve** systems of linear equations and optimization problems through matrix operations and computational software like MATLAB or Python  
• **Evaluate** eigenvalues and eigenvectors by applying diagonalization techniques to problems in data analysis and dynamical systems  
• **Construct** mathematical proofs and verify linear algebra concepts using both analytical methods and computer algebra systems  

## Target Audience

This course is designed for second or third-year undergraduate students majoring in mathematics, engineering, computer science, physics, or economics who seek to develop strong analytical and computational skills. Ideal for students planning to pursue advanced coursework in applied mathematics, data science, machine learning, or graduate studies in STEM fields.

---

## Weekly Schedule

### **Week 1-2: Foundations of Linear SystemsModule:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Real-World Applications

**Key Concepts:**
- Augmented matrix representation and systematic solution methods
- Row operations and Gaussian elimination procedures  
- Matrix inverse method for solving systems (Ax = b format)

**Activities:**
- *Optimizing Manufacturing Production Using Linear Programming* (Week 2, 70 min)

### **Week 3-4: Matrix Operations and PropertiesModule:** Linear Systems and Matrix Operations (Extended)

**Key Concepts:**
- Matrix arithmetic: addition, subtraction, scalar multiplication
- Matrix multiplication and properties of matrix operations
- Determinants and their applications to system solvability

**Activities:**
- *Multi-Step Optimization: Designing a Community Solar Farm Layout* (Week 4, 120 min)

**Assessment:**
- **Quiz 1:** Basic matrix operations and Gaussian elimination (Week 4, 25 points)

### **Week 5-6: Vector Spaces and Linear IndependenceKey Concepts:**
- Definition and properties of vector spaces
- Linear combinations, span, and linear independence
- Basis and dimension of vector spaces

**Activities:**
- *Design a Mathematical Model for a Community Garden Water Distribution System* (Week 6, 85 min)

### **Week 7-8: Linear TransformationsKey Concepts:**
- Definition and properties of linear transformations
- Matrix representation of linear transformations
- Kernel (null space) and image (column space) of transformations

**Assessment:**
- **Midterm Exam** (Week 8, 100 points)

### **Week 9-10: Eigenvalues and EigenvectorsKey Concepts:**
- Characteristic polynomial and eigenvalue computation
- Finding eigenvectors and eigenspaces
- Geometric and algebraic multiplicity

**Activities:**
- *Optimizing Solar Panel Array Configuration Using Linear Programming* (Week 10, 110 min)

### **Week 11-12: Diagonalization and ApplicationsKey Concepts:**
- Conditions for diagonalizability
- Similarity transformations and change of basis
- Applications to dynamical systems and differential equations

**Assessment:**
- **Community Statistics Analysis Project** due (Week 12, 100 points)

### **Week 13-14: Orthogonality and Least SquaresKey Concepts:**
- Inner products, orthogonal and orthonormal sets
- Gram-Schmidt process and QR factorization
- Least squares approximation and applications

**Activities:**
- *Design and Build a Community Garden Budget Optimization Model* (Week 14, 130 min)

### **Week 15: Advanced Topics and ReviewKey Concepts:**
- Applications to data science and machine learning
- Principal component analysis (PCA) introduction
- Course review and synthesis

**Assessment:**
- **Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio** due (Week 15, 100 points)

### **Week 16: Final Examinations**
- **Comprehensive Final Exam** (100 points)

---

## Assessment Plan

### Grade Distribution

|----------------|--------|------------|
| Quizzes (4 × 25 pts) | 100 | 20% |

| Final Exam | 100 | 20% |

### Assessment Descriptions

**Quizzes:** Four 25-point quizzes will assess understanding of key concepts and computational skills. Lowest quiz score may be dropped.

**Examinations:** The midterm and final exams will test both theoretical understanding and problem-solving abilities, including proofs and applications.

**Community Statistics Analysis Project:** Students will conduct a comprehensive statistical investigation of a real-world community issue, integrating data collection, analysis, and mathematical communication skills.

**Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio:** A comprehensive portfolio demonstrating mastery of linear algebra concepts through four distinct real-world modeling projects, showcasing different mathematical applications with complete documentation of problem-solving processes and critical analysis.

# ADVANCED TOPICS IN ALGEBRAIC TOPOLOGY
**MATH 8XX • Quarter System • 4 Credits**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Schedule:** [Days] [Time] in [Room]  
**Final Exam:** [Date and Time] in [Room]  

**Course Website:** [LMS/Website URL]  
**Prerequisites:** Completion of undergraduate real analysis, abstract algebra, and point-set topology. Graduate-level algebraic topology covering fundamental groups, covering spaces, homology theory, and cohomology theory. Familiarity with category theory and basic homological algebra including exact sequences, chain complexes, and derived functors. Mathematical maturity equivalent to passing graduate qualifying examinations in analysis and algebra.

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This graduate-level course explores advanced concepts in algebraic topology, focusing on spectral sequences, characteristic classes, and modern computational methods. Students will develop expertise in homological algebra techniques applied to topological problems, including the construction and application of Serre and Eilenberg-Moore spectral sequences. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications in geometric topology, differential geometry, and mathematical physics. Students will engage with current research literature and learn to apply sophisticated topological invariants to classify spaces and maps. Topics include fiber bundles, vector bundles, Chern classes, Stiefel-Whitney classes, and cobordism theory. The curriculum integrates traditional proof-based approaches with modern computational topology tools, preparing students for research in pure mathematics, theoretical physics, or data science applications. Through rigorous problem-solving and independent research projects, students will develop the mathematical maturity necessary for doctoral research or advanced positions in academia and industry.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Construct and analyze spectral sequences** to compute homology and cohomology groups of complex topological spaces in algebraic topology research contexts
• **Evaluate characteristic classes** of vector bundles through explicit calculations using Chern-Weil theory and cohomological methods
• **Prove fundamental theorems** in fiber bundle theory by applying advanced techniques from homological algebra and differential geometry
• **Implement computational topology algorithms** using Python and SageMath to verify theoretical results and explore conjectures in modern research problems

## TARGET AUDIENCE

Graduate students in mathematics, mathematical physics, or related fields who have completed foundational courses in algebraic topology and seek advanced research preparation. Intended for students pursuing doctoral degrees with research interests in topology, geometry, or theoretical physics, as well as advanced master's students planning academic or industry careers requiring sophisticated mathematical modeling and abstract reasoning skills.

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

### Software & Technology
- Python 3.8+ with SageMath environment
- Access to university computing cluster for intensive calculations
- LaTeX distribution for mathematical typesetting
- Course website access for supplementary materials and research papers

### Additional Materials
- Scientific calculator
- Access to mathematics library databases for current research literature

---

- Mathematical Proof Techniques and Applications Discussion Forum (launch)
**Readings:** Hatcher Ch. 1, Weibel Ch. 5

### Week 2: Serre Spectral Sequence - Construction
**Topics:** Fibrations, filtrations, construction of Serre spectral sequence
**Activities:**
- Optimization of Manufacturing Production Lines Using Calculus (adapted for topological filtrations)
**Readings:** Hatcher Ch. 2.1-2.3

### Week 3: Serre Spectral Sequence - Applications
**Topics:** Computing homology of fiber bundles, sphere bundles
**Activities:**
- Design and Construct a Mathematical Model for Optimizing Urban Traffic Flow Using Differential Equations and Network Theory (adapted for bundle computations)
**Assessment:** Mathematical Proof Techniques Discussion Forum due
**Readings:** Hatcher Ch. 2.4-2.6

### Week 4: Introduction to Characteristic Classes
**Topics:** Vector bundles, principal bundles, classifying spaces
**Activities:**
- Applying Optimization Techniques to Design a Cost-Efficient Packaging System (adapted for bundle optimization)
**Assessment:** Problem Set 1 due (Spectral sequences)
**Readings:** Milnor-Stasheff Ch. 1-3

### Week 5: Chern Classes
**Topics:** Construction via Chern-Weil theory, computational methods
**Activities:**

**Readings:** Milnor-Stasheff Ch. 14-16

### Week 6: Stiefel-Whitney Classes
**Topics:** Characteristic classes for real bundles, Steenrod operations
**Activities:**

**Assessment:** Midterm Examination
**Readings:** Milnor-Stasheff Ch. 4-7

### Week 7: Eilenberg-Moore Spectral Sequence
**Topics:** Construction, comparison with Serre spectral sequence
**Activities:**
- Optimization in Manufacturing: Applying Calculus to Minimize Production Costs (adapted for spectral sequence convergence optimization)
**Assessment:** Statistical Analysis Lab Report due
**Readings:** Current research papers (provided)

### Week 8: Computational Topology Methods
**Topics:** Python/SageMath implementation of topological computations
**Activities:**
- Design a City Transportation System Using Linear Programming (adapted for CW complex optimization)
**Assessment:** Problem Set 2 due (Characteristic classes)
**Readings:** SageMath documentation, selected papers

### Week 9: Cobordism Theory
**Topics:** Thom spectra, bordism groups, relationship to characteristic classes
**Activities:**
- Advanced Mathematical Modeling Portfolio: Real-World Applications (launch)

### Week 10: Research Applications and Current Topics

**Assessment:** Final Examination

# Database Systems and Design
**Spring 2024 Semester**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Course Title:** Database Systems and Design  
**Course Code:** CS 350  
**Credits:** 3 credit hours  
**Prerequisites:** CS 201 Data Structures and Algorithms (C+ or better), CS 205 Object-Oriented Programming, MATH 210 Discrete Mathematics  

**Class Schedule:**  
- - 
**Teaching Assistant:** Michael Chen ()  
**TA Office Hours:** Monday/Wednesday 3:00-5:00 PM (ENG 102)

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of database management systems, covering both theoretical foundations and practical implementation skills. Students will explore relational database design principles, normalization theory, SQL programming, and transaction management while gaining hands-on experience with modern database technologies. The curriculum emphasizes real-world applications through the design and implementation of complete database solutions for various business scenarios. Students will learn to analyze data requirements, create efficient database schemas, optimize query performance, and ensure data integrity and security. Special attention is given to emerging trends including NoSQL databases, cloud database services, and big data considerations. Upon completion, students will possess the technical expertise to design, implement, and maintain robust database systems that meet enterprise-level requirements. This course serves as essential preparation for careers in software development, data analysis, system administration, and database administration, while also providing foundational knowledge for advanced studies in data science and information systems management.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Students will design normalized relational database schemas to solve complex business data storage requirements using entity-relationship modeling and normalization techniques**
2. **Students will implement advanced SQL queries and stored procedures through hands-on practice with MySQL and PostgreSQL database management systems**
3. **Students will analyze database performance bottlenecks by examining query execution plans and implementing appropriate indexing strategies**
4. **Students will develop secure database applications using modern programming frameworks including Python Django ORM and Node.js Sequelize**

---

## TARGET AUDIENCE & PREREQUISITES

**Target Audience:** Third or fourth-year Computer Science majors with solid programming foundation who are preparing for careers in software development, data engineering, or system architecture. Ideal for students interested in backend development, full-stack engineering, or those planning to pursue graduate studies in data science or information systems.

**Prerequisites:** Completion of CS 201 Data Structures and Algorithms with grade of C+ or better, CS 205 Object-Oriented Programming, and MATH 210 Discrete Mathematics. Students must demonstrate proficiency in at least one programming language (preferably Python or Java) and have basic understanding of software development lifecycle concepts.

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Required Textbooks:**
- Silberschatz, A., Galvin, P.B., & Gagne, G. *Database System Concepts* (7th Edition). McGraw-Hill Education, 2019. ISBN: 978-0078022159
- Elmasri, R. & Navathe, S.B. *Fundamentals of Database Systems* (7th Edition). Pearson, 2015. ISBN: 978-0133970777

**Software Requirements:**
- MySQL Community Server 8.0+
- PostgreSQL 13+
- MySQL Workbench
- pgAdmin 4
- Python 3.8+ with Django framework
- Node.js 16+ with Sequelize ORM
- Visual Studio Code or similar IDE

**Hardware Requirements:**
- Laptop with minimum 8GB RAM
- 50GB available disk space for database installations

**Online Resources:**
- Course management system access (Canvas)
- GitHub account for project submissions
- AWS Academy access (provided)

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1: Introduction and Foundations** (January 16-19)
**Topic:** Database Fundamentals and ER Modeling  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 1-2  
**Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flashcard Recall Challenge (35 min) - *Building foundation for data representation*
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 2: Relational Model and Normalization** (January 23-26)
**Topic:** Relational Algebra and Database Design  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 3-4  
**Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge (40 min) - *Reinforcing binary concepts for indexing*
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 3: SQL Fundamentals** (January 30 - February 2)
**Topic:** Basic SQL Queries and DDL  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 5-6  
**Activities:**
- Introduction to Programming Concepts and Python Basics Quiz
**Deliverables:Quiz 1: Database Fundamentals** (100 points) - *Due February 2*

### **Week 4: Advanced SQL** (February 6-9)
**Topic:** Complex Queries, Joins, and Subqueries  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 7  
**Activities:**
- Analyzing Database Query Performance: Execution Plan Investigation (75 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 5: Hash Tables and Database Indexing** (February 13-16)
**Topic:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Reading:** Elmasri Ch. 17  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function: Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across available slots
- Collision Resolution: Strategies to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
- Load Factor: Ratio of filled slots to total capacity that determines when to resize the hash table for optimal performance

**Learning Objectives:**
- Students will implement hash tables using separate chaining and open addressing by coding complete data structures in Python with comprehensive test suites
- Students will analyze collision resolution performance through empirical testing of different hash functions against various data sets

**Activities:**
- Advanced Data Structure Method Signature Memorization Challenge (45 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 6: Database Performance and Indexing** (February 20-23)
**Topic:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Reading:** Elmasri Ch. 18  
**Key Concepts:**
- Binary Search Property: Each node's left subtree contains only values less than the node's value, and right subtree contains only values greater
- Tree Traversal Algorithms: Systematic methods (in-order, pre-order, post-order) for visiting every node in a tree exactly once
- Recursive Data Structure: A tree where each subtree is itself a valid binary search tree, enabling elegant recursive solutions

**Learning Objectives:**
- Students will implement a complete Binary Search Tree class by writing recursive insertion, deletion, and search methods in Python or Java
- Students will analyze time and space complexity through calculating Big-O notation for BST operations in best, average, and worst-case scenarios

**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (135 min)
**Deliverables:Discussion 1: Database Architecture Design** (100 points) - *Due February 23*

### **Week 7: Transaction Management** (February 27 - March 2)
**Topic:** ACID Properties and Concurrency Control  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 14-15  
**Activities:**
- Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure Implementation Details Recall (65 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 8: Query Optimization** (March 6-9)
**Topic:** Query Processing and Optimization Strategies  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 12-13  
**Activities:**
- Security Vulnerability Analysis in Real-World Web Application Code (120 min) - *Applied to database security*
**Deliverables:Midterm Exam** (100 points) - *March 9*

### **Week 9: Spring Break** (March 13-16)
*No classes*

### **Week 10: NoSQL and Graph Databases** (March 20-23)
**Topic:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions  
**Reading:** Supplementary materials on Canvas  
**Key Concepts:**
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): Level-order traversal using queues to explore all neighbors before moving deeper
- Depth-First Search (DFS): Deep traversal using stacks/recursion to explore as far as possible before backtracking
- Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy shortest path algorithm for non-negative weighted graphs using priority queues

**Learning Objectives:**
- Students will implement BFS and DFS traversal algorithms by coding complete solutions in Python with time and space complexity analysis
- Students will solve shortest path problems through hands-on implementation of Dijkstra's and Bellman-Ford algorithms on weighted graphs

**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Time Complexity Decomposition (150 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 11: Database Security and Integrity** (March 27-30)
**Topic:** Access Control and Data Protection  
**Reading:** Silberschatz Ch. 9  
**Activities:**
- Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Recall Challenge (75 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 12: Distributed Databases** (April 3-6)
**Topic:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems  
**Reading:** Elmasri Ch. 25  
**Key Concepts:**
- Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from a single source in non-negative weighted graphs
- Bellman-Ford Algorithm: Dynamic programming technique that detects negative cycles while computing shortest paths from a single source
- Floyd-Warshall Algorithm: All-pairs shortest path algorithm using dynamic programming with O(V³) time complexity

**Learning Objectives:**
- Students will implement Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, and Floyd-Warshall algorithms by writing complete, tested code solutions in Python
- Students will analyze algorithm complexity and correctness through mathematical proofs and empirical testing with various graph structures

**Activities:**
- Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage (150 min)
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 13: Cloud Databases and Scaling** (April 10-13)
**Topic:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation  
**Reading:** AWS Database Services Documentation  
**Key Concepts:**
- Big O Notation - Upper bound representation of algorithm growth rate in worst-case scenarios
- Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required as input size increases
- Space Complexity - Analysis of memory usage growth relative to input size

**Learning Objectives:**
- Students will calculate time and space complexity for given algorithms by applying Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta notation rules
- Students will compare algorithm efficiency through systematic complexity analysis of sorting and searching algorithms

**Activities:**
- Analyzing Distributed System Failure Patterns Through Multi-Layered Architecture Decomposition (135 min)
**Deliverables:Lab Report: Database Implementation Project** (100 points) - *Due April 13*

### **Week 14: Data Warehousing and Analytics** (April 17-20)
**Topic:** OLAP and Data Mining Fundamentals  
**Reading:** Elmasri Ch. 29  
**Activities:**
- Reverse Engineering and Analyzing Malware Static Analysis Patterns in Compiled Binaries (210 min) - *Applied to database forensics*
**Deliverables:** None

### **Week 15: Final Projects and Review** (April 24-27)
**Topic:** Project Presentations and Course Review  
**Activities:**
- Student project presentations
- Comprehensive review session
**Deliverables:Portfolio: Complete Database Application** (100 points) - *Due April 27*

### **Finals Week** (April 30 - May 4)
**Final Exam:** Comprehensive examination covering all course material  
**Date/Time:** To be announced by Registrar

Students will create a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating fundamental programming concepts through building a personal website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The portfolio will showcase their understanding of web development basics, problem-solving skills, and ability to implement interactive features.
- *Learning Objectives:* Demonstrate proficiency in HTML structure and semantic markup; Apply CSS styling principles including layout, typography, and responsive design

# Database Systems and Design
**Computer Science Department | Fall 2024**

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to database systems, covering both theoretical foundations and practical implementation skills essential for modern software development. Students will explore relational database design principles, normalization techniques, and SQL query optimization while gaining hands-on experience with popular database management systems including MySQL and PostgreSQL. The curriculum emphasizes real-world applications through projects involving database design for web applications, data analysis, and business intelligence scenarios. Students will learn to design efficient database schemas, write complex queries, implement transactions, and understand concurrency control mechanisms. The course also covers emerging topics such as NoSQL databases, distributed systems, and cloud-based database services. By integrating theoretical concepts with practical programming assignments, students develop the critical thinking and technical skills necessary for roles in software engineering, data analysis, and system administration.

**Target Audience:** Third or fourth-year Computer Science undergraduates who have completed core programming courses and are preparing for software development careers, data analysis roles, or graduate studies. Ideal for students interested in backend development, full-stack engineering, or data-intensive applications who need practical database skills for internships and entry-level positions.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Design normalized relational database schemas to solve complex business requirements using entity-relationship modeling and functional dependency analysis  
• Construct advanced SQL queries through hands-on practice with joins, subqueries, window functions, and stored procedures using MySQL and PostgreSQL  
• Evaluate database performance by implementing indexing strategies, query optimization techniques, and transaction management protocols  
• Implement database-driven applications using modern frameworks such as Node.js with Sequelize ORM and Python with SQLAlchemy

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Database Foundations and Hash Table Optimization
**Topics:** Introduction to database systems, data models, hash-based indexing  
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Analysis  
**Activities:**
- Database Normalization Forms Recognition Challenge (75 min)
- Lab: Setting up MySQL and PostgreSQL environments
**Due:** Course survey and environment setup confirmation

### Week 2: Entity-Relationship Modeling and Binary Indexing
**Topics:** ER diagrams, conceptual design, binary tree indexing structures  
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis Through Big O Complexity Comparison (105 min)
- Lab: ER modeling for university database
**Due:** ER Diagram Assignment

### Week 3: Relational Model and Query Complexity
**Topics:** Relational algebra, calculus, SQL fundamentals  
**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (90 min)
- Lab: Basic SQL queries and joins
**Assessment:** Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (100 points)

### Week 4: Advanced SQL and Query Optimization
**Topics:** Complex queries, subqueries, window functions, query plans  
**Activities:**
- Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance (160 min)
- Lab: Advanced SQL practice with large datasets
**Due:** SQL Query Portfolio

### Week 5: Database Design and Normalization Theory
**Topics:** Functional dependencies, normalization forms (1NF-6NF), BCNF  
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation  
**Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flash Card Drill (55 min)
- Lab: Database normalization exercises
**Assessment:** Programming Paradigms Discussion: Database Design Approaches (100 points)

### Week 6: Transaction Management and Concurrency Control
**Topics:** ACID properties, isolation levels, locking protocols  
**Activities:**
- Advanced Concurrency Control Mechanisms Recall Challenge (65 min)
- Lab: Transaction isolation experiments
**Due:** Database Design Project Proposal

### Week 7: Indexing and Physical Database Design
**Topics:** B+ trees, hash indexing, query optimization strategies  
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Activities:**
- Analyzing Time and Space Complexity Trade-offs in Dynamic Programming Solutions (140 min)
- Lab: Index performance analysis
**Due:** Midterm Project Checkpoint

### Week 8: Distributed Databases and NoSQL Systems
**Topics:** Distributed data, CAP theorem, MongoDB, Cassandra  
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems  
**Activities:**
- Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Recall Challenge (75 min)
- Lab: NoSQL database implementation
**Assessment:** Distributed System Architecture Design Presentation (100 points)

### Week 9: Database-Driven Application Development
**Topics:** ORM frameworks, SQLAlchemy, Sequelize, API integration  
**Activities:**
- Binary Number Recognition and Recall Flashcard Challenge (35 min)
- Lab: Building REST API with database backend
**Due:** Application Development Milestone

### Week 10: Final Projects and Industry Applications
**Topics:** Cloud databases, data warehousing, project presentations  
**Activities:**
- Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments (195 min)
- Final project presentations and peer review
**Assessment:** Distributed Database System with Consensus Protocol Implementation (100 points)

---

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage | Description |
|-----------------|--------|------------|-------------|
| **Quizzes** | 100 | 15% | Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz |
| **Discussions** | 100 | 15% | Programming Paradigms Discussion participation |
| **Presentations** | 100 | 20% | Distributed System Architecture Design Presentation |
| **Major Project** | 100 | 25% | Distributed Database System Implementation |
| **Labs & Activities** | 100 | 15% | Weekly lab assignments and in-class activities |
| **Final Exam** | 100 | 10% | Comprehensive written examination |
| **Total** | **600** | **100%** | |

## Important Dates

- **Week 3:** First Quiz - Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis
- **Week 5:** Midterm Project Proposal Due
- **Week 7:** Midterm Project Checkpoint
- **Week 8:** Distributed System Presentations
- **Week 10:** Final Project Due and Presentations
- **Finals Week:** Comprehensive Final Examination

---

*This syllabus is subject to change at the instructor's discretion. Students will be notified of any modifications via email and course announcements.*

**Course Syllabus Version:** 1.0

syllabus_content:
# CS 8803: Advanced Machine Learning Systems: Scalable Algorithms and Distributed Computing

**Department of Computer ScienceGraduate Course • 4 Credit Hours • [Semester/Quarter]**

---

## Course Description

This graduate-level course explores the design, implementation, and optimization of machine learning systems at scale. Students will delve into distributed machine learning algorithms, parallel computing frameworks, and the engineering challenges of deploying ML models in production environments. The curriculum covers advanced topics including federated learning, model parallelism, data parallelism, and real-time inference systems. Students will gain hands-on experience with industry-standard tools such as Apache Spark, TensorFlow Distributed, PyTorch Lightning, and Kubernetes for ML workloads. Through a combination of theoretical foundations and practical projects, students will learn to architect robust, scalable ML pipelines that can handle large datasets and high-throughput requirements. The course emphasizes both algorithmic efficiency and system design principles, preparing students for roles in machine learning engineering, research, and technical leadership at technology companies, research institutions, and startups. By the end of the quarter, students will have developed a comprehensive understanding of how to bridge the gap between machine learning research and production-ready systems.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement distributed machine learning algorithms** to solve real-world problems involving datasets exceeding single-machine memory constraints  
• **Optimize machine learning model training and inference performance** through profiling, benchmarking, and systematic performance analysis using GPU clusters and distributed computing frameworks  
• **Evaluate trade-offs between model accuracy, computational efficiency, and system reliability** by implementing and comparing different parallelization strategies in production-like environments  
• **Architect end-to-end ML deployment pipelines** using containerization, orchestration tools like Kubernetes, and cloud-native services for automated model serving and monitoring  

## Target Audience & Prerequisites

**Target Audience:** Graduate students in Computer Science, Data Science, or related fields with strong programming backgrounds and prior exposure to machine learning concepts. Ideal candidates include those pursuing careers as ML engineers, research scientists, or technical leads who need to understand both algorithmic foundations and systems implementation.

**Prerequisites:**
- Completion of undergraduate-level machine learning course (CS 229 or equivalent)
- Proficiency in Python programming with experience in NumPy/Pandas/Scikit-learn
- Solid understanding of linear algebra and probability theory
- Familiarity with deep learning frameworks (TensorFlow or PyTorch)
- Basic knowledge of computer systems and networking concepts
- Experience with version control (Git) and command-line interfaces

**Recommended:** Prior coursework in algorithms and data structures, databases, and distributed systems.

---

### Software & Platforms
- Python 3.9+, Jupyter Notebooks
- TensorFlow 2.x, PyTorch Lightning
- Apache Spark, Dask
- Docker, Kubernetes
- Google Cloud Platform or AWS (credits provided)
- Git/GitHub for version control

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Scalable ML Systems
**Lectures:** Introduction to distributed ML challenges, system design principles  
**Activities:**
- *Advanced Memory Management Terms and Concepts Recall Challenge* (120 min) - Building foundational vocabulary for systems programming
- *Python Data Types Memory Match Challenge* (60 min) - Reinforcing programming fundamentals

### Week 2: Hash-Based Data Structures for ML Systems  
**Lectures:** Hash tables in distributed systems, consistent hashing, feature hashing  
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Key Concepts:** Hash functions, load factors, collision resolution techniques  
**Activities:**
- Implementation of hash tables with chaining and linear probing collision resolution
- Analysis of collision resolution performance through empirical testing

### Week 3: Graph Algorithms for ML Pipelines
**Lectures:** Graph-based ML algorithms, computational graphs, dependency management  
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions  
**Key Concepts:** Graph traversal, DFS/BFS, shortest path algorithms  
**Activities:**
- *Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Dissecting Sorting Performance* (110 min) - Analyzing algorithmic efficiency
- Implementation of DFS and BFS for ML pipeline optimization

### Week 4: Distributed Training Strategies
**Lectures:** Data parallelism, model parallelism, parameter servers  
**Activities:**
- *Distributed System Bottleneck Analysis* (120 min) - Performance investigation of microservices
**Assessment:** Lab Report 1 - Basic distributed training implementation (20 points)

### Week 5: Advanced Parallelization Techniques
**Lectures:** Federated learning, gradient compression, asynchronous training  
**Activities:**
- *Binary Number System Memorization Challenge* (55 min) - Building computational fundamentals
- *Database Query Performance Analysis* (100 min) - Optimizing data access patterns

### Week 6: Fault Tolerance and System Reliability
**Lectures:** Consensus algorithms, Byzantine fault tolerance, checkpointing  
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding  
**Activities:**
- *Distributed Systems Consensus Algorithm Memory Challenge* (75 min) - Learning Raft, PBFT, Paxos
- *Analyzing Distributed System Fault Tolerance: Netflix Chaos Engineering Case Study* (3.5 hours)

### Week 7: Model Serving and Inference Systems
**Lectures:** Real-time inference, batch processing, streaming ML  
**Activities:**
- *Analyzing Security Vulnerabilities in Multi-Threaded Banking System Code* (105 min) - Understanding concurrency
**Assessment:** Midterm Exam (100 points)

### Week 8: Performance Optimization and Profiling
**Lectures:** GPU optimization, memory management, performance profiling  
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Activities:**
- *Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Challenge* (60 min) - Mastering complexity analysis
- Implementation of efficient data structures for ML applications

### Week 9: Production ML Systems Architecture
**Lectures:** MLOps, CI/CD for ML, monitoring and observability  
**Activities:**
- *Database Performance Analysis: Query Optimization* (110 min) - Optimizing data access
**Assessment:** Lab Report 2 - Distributed system design and implementation (100 points)

### Week 10: Advanced Topics and Project Presentations
**Lectures:** Edge computing, neuromorphic computing, quantum ML  
**Activities:**
- *Deconstructing Algorithm Efficiency: Comparative Analysis* (130 min) - Final performance analysis
**Assessment:** Final Project Presentations and Portfolio (100 points)

---

## Assessment Plan

### Grade Distribution
| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage |
|----------------|--------|------------|
| Lab Reports (2) | 120 | 30% |
| Midterm Exam | 100 | 25% |
| Final Project & Portfolio | 100 | 25% |
| Lab Participation & Activities | 80 | 20% |
| **Total** | **400** | **100%** |

### Assessment Details

**Lab Reports (30%)**
1. **Basic Distributed Training Implementation** (Week 4, 20 points): Implementation and analysis of data-parallel training systems
2. **Distributed System Design and Implementation** (Week 9, 100 points): Building a fault-tolerant microservices architecture with comprehensive analysis

**Midterm Exam (25%)Advanced Algorithms Design and Analysis Comprehensive Exam** (Week 7, 100 points): Demonstration of mastery in algorithmic concepts, complexity analysis, and distributed system design principles

**Final Project & Portfolio (25%)Web Application Development Portfolio** (Week 10, 100 points): Full-stack ML application demonstrating end-to-end system design, implementation, and deployment with comprehensive documentation

**Lab Participation & Activities (20%)**
Weekly hands-on activities, coding exercises, and active participation in lab sessions

---

## Important Dates

- **Week 4:** Lab Report 1 Due (Friday, 5:00 PM)
- **Week 7:** Midterm Exam (Thursday, in class)
- **Week 9:** Lab Report 2 Due (Friday, 5:00 PM)
- **Week 10:** Final Project Presentations (Tuesday & Thursday)
- **Week 10:** Final Portfolio Due (Friday, 11:59 PM)

---

## Additional Resources

### Technical Support
- **University IT Help Desk:** Available 24/7 for technical issues

### Academic Support

# Database Systems and Design
**Fall 2024 Semester**

---

## Course Description

This comprehensive course introduces students to the fundamental concepts, design principles, and implementation techniques of modern database systems. Students will explore relational database theory, entity-relationship modeling, SQL programming, normalization techniques, and database administration practices. The course covers both theoretical foundations and practical applications, including hands-on experience with popular database management systems such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, and MongoDB. Students will learn to design efficient database schemas, write complex queries, optimize database performance, and understand transaction processing and concurrency control. The curriculum also addresses contemporary topics including NoSQL databases, data warehousing concepts, and cloud-based database solutions. Through a combination of lectures, laboratory exercises, and a semester-long project, students will develop the skills necessary to design, implement, and maintain database systems in professional software development environments. This course serves as essential preparation for careers in software engineering, data analysis, system administration, and prepares students for advanced coursework in data science, machine learning, and enterprise software development.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design** normalized relational database schemas to solve real-world data management problems using entity-relationship modeling and normalization principles  
• **Implement** complex database queries and stored procedures through advanced SQL programming techniques including joins, subqueries, and aggregate functions  
• **Analyze** database performance issues by applying indexing strategies, query optimization techniques, and transaction management principles  
• **Develop** database-driven applications using modern programming frameworks such as Python with SQLAlchemy or Java with JDBC connections  

## Target Audience

Second or third-year Computer Science majors who have completed foundational programming courses and are interested in software development, data management, or system design. Ideal for students planning careers in software engineering, web development, data analysis, or those preparing for advanced studies in data science and machine learning.

---

### Online Resources
- Course management system (Canvas) for assignments and announcements
- GitHub Classroom for code submissions
- Supplementary video tutorials and documentation (provided via course website)

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1 (Aug 28-30): Introduction and Database Fundamentals
**Topics:** Course overview, database concepts, data models, database users
**Reading:** Chapter 1-2 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Programming Terminology Memory Card Match (40 min) - Building foundational database vocabulary
**Assignments:** Install required software, complete setup verification quiz

### Week 2 (Sep 4-6): Entity-Relationship Modeling
**Topics:** ER diagrams, entities, attributes, relationships, weak entities
**Reading:** Chapter 7 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flashcard Drill (45 min) - Understanding data representation fundamentals

### Week 3 (Sep 11-13): Relational Model and Normalization
**Topics:** Relational algebra, functional dependencies, normal forms (1NF-3NF)
**Reading:** Chapter 8 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Python Basic Syntax Identification Flash Card Challenge (45 min) - Preparing for database programming
**Assessment:** Quiz 1 - ER Modeling and Relational Concepts (25 points)

### Week 4 (Sep 18-20): SQL Fundamentals
**Topics:** DDL, DML, basic queries, data types
**Reading:** Chapter 3-4 (Beaulieu)
**Activities:**
- Python Variables and Data Types Lab Report (100 points) - Foundation for database connectivity programming

### Week 5 (Sep 25-27): Advanced SQL Queries
**Topics:** Joins, subqueries, aggregate functions, grouping
**Reading:** Chapter 5-8 (Beaulieu)
**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementation Performance (95 min) - Understanding query optimization principles

### Week 6 (Oct 2-4): Database Design and Implementation
**Topics:** Schema design, constraints, triggers, stored procedures
**Reading:** Chapter 5 (Silberschatz)
**Assessment:** Lab Report - Database Design Project Phase 1 (75 points)

### Week 7 (Oct 9-11): Indexing and Query Optimization
**Topics:** B+ trees, hash indexing, query execution plans
**Reading:** Chapter 11-12 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Analyzing Database Query Performance Bottlenecks Through Execution Plan Decomposition (95 min) - Hands-on optimization practice

### Week 8 (Oct 16-18): Hash Tables and Database Indexing
**Topics:** Hash function design, collision resolution, database hash indexes
**Reading:** Supplementary materials on hash-based indexing
**Activities:**
- Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies module - Understanding underlying indexing mechanisms
**Assessment:** Midterm Exam (150 points) - Covers Weeks 1-7

### Week 9 (Oct 23-25): Transaction Processing
**Topics:** ACID properties, concurrency control, locking protocols
**Reading:** Chapter 14-15 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation module - Analyzing transaction processing complexity

### Week 10 (Oct 30-Nov 1): Advanced Transaction Management
**Topics:** Deadlock handling, timestamp ordering, validation
**Reading:** Chapter 16 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- TCP/IP Stack Layer Function Memorization Challenge (55 min) - Understanding network protocols for distributed databases

### Week 11 (Nov 6-8): NoSQL Databases
**Topics:** Document stores, key-value stores, MongoDB introduction
**Reading:** Supplementary NoSQL materials
**Assessment:** Database Design Trade-offs: Relational vs NoSQL Architecture Discussion (100 points)

### Week 12 (Nov 13-15): Database Security and Administration
**Topics:** Authentication, authorization, backup and recovery
**Reading:** Chapter 9-10 (Silberschatz)
**Activities:**
- Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting Multi-Node Database Crash Scenarios (160 min) - Understanding database system reliability

### Week 13 (Nov 20): Data Warehousing and Big Data
**Topics:** OLAP vs OLTP, data warehouse design, ETL processes
**Reading:** Chapter 22 (Silberschatz)
*Note: Thanksgiving Break Nov 22*

### Week 14 (Nov 27-29): Cloud Databases and Modern Trends
**Topics:** Database-as-a-Service, distributed databases, cloud deployment
**Reading:** Supplementary cloud database materials
**Activities:**
- Network Protocol Stack Memory Challenge: OSI Layer Component Recall (45 min) - Understanding network foundations for distributed databases

### Week 15 (Dec 4-6): Project Presentations and Course Review
**Topics:** Student project presentations, course synthesis, career applications
**Assessment:** Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture: Design and Implementation Strategy Presentation (100 points)

### Finals Week (Dec 11-15): Comprehensive Final Assessment
**Assessment:** Advanced Data Structures and Algorithm Design Comprehensive Final Exam (200 points)

---

## Assessment Plan

### Grade Distribution
| Assessment Category | Points | Percentage |
|-------------------|--------|------------|
| Quizzes (3) | 75 | 10% |
| Lab Reports & Activities | 175 | 23% |
| Midterm Exam | 150 | 20% |
| Discussion Participation | 100 | 13% |
| Final Project Presentation | 100 | 13% |
| Comprehensive Final Exam | 200 | 27% |
| **Total** | **750** | **100%** |

### Assessment Details

**Quizzes (75 points total):** Short assessments testing comprehension of recent material, including practical SQL queries and theoretical concepts.

**Lab Reports & Activities (175 points total):** Hands-on programming assignments, database design exercises, and structured learning activities that reinforce lecture concepts.

**Discussion Participation (100 points):** Active engagement in class discussions, online forum contributions, and peer collaboration during group activities.

**Midterm Exam (150 points):** Comprehensive examination covering database design, SQL programming, normalization, and indexing concepts from the first half of the course.

**Final Project Presentation (100 points):** Students will design and present a complete database solution for a real-world scenario, demonstrating integration of course concepts.

**Comprehensive Final Exam (200 points):** Cumulative assessment testing mastery of all course learning objectives, including advanced topics in database administration and modern database technologies.

---

### Late Assignment Policy
- Assignments submitted up to 24 hours late: 10% penalty
- Assignments submitted 24-48 hours late: 25% penalty
- Assignments submitted more than 48 hours late: 50% penalty
- No assignments accepted more than one week after the due date without prior arrangement

### Make-up Policy
Make-up exams and quizzes will only be given in cases of documented emergencies, illness, or university-approved absences. Students must contact the instructor within 24 hours of the missed assessment to arrange make-up opportunities.
