## Instructor Information

## Course Description
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithms essential for efficient programming and software development. Students will explore abstract data types including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation of these structures. Key algorithmic concepts covered include searching, sorting, recursion, dynamic programming, and graph traversal algorithms. Students will analyze time and space complexity using Big O notation to evaluate algorithmic efficiency. Through hands-on programming assignments, students will implement data structures from scratch and apply various algorithms to solve real-world computational problems. The course balances theoretical computer science principles with practical coding skills, preparing students for advanced coursework and technical interviews. Laboratory sessions will reinforce concepts through collaborative problem-solving and code review exercises. By course completion, students will possess the foundational knowledge necessary for system design, software optimization, and advanced algorithm development.

## Learning Objectives
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
• Implement fundamental data structures including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs using appropriate programming languages
• Analyze and compare algorithm efficiency using asymptotic notation and complexity analysis techniques  
• Design and apply appropriate algorithms for searching, sorting, and graph traversal problems in various computational contexts

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation and Analysis Framework
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Topics:** 
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
- **Activities:** 
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Big O Evaluation (100 minutes)
- **Readings:** Chapter 3 (Growth of Functions)
- 
### Week 2: Reinforcement of Analysis Concepts  
**Module:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation (Continued)
- **Topics:**
  - Space complexity analysis
  - Best, worst, and average case scenarios
  - Omega and Theta notation
- **Activities:**
  - Programming Language Syntax Flashcard Memory Challenge (45 minutes)
- **Readings:** Chapter 3 continued
- 
### Week 3-4: Advanced Analysis Applications
**Module:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Breakdown
- **Topics:**
  - Comparative analysis methodologies  
  - Empirical vs theoretical complexity
  - Performance profiling techniques
- **Activities:**
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Complexity Breakdown (90 minutes)
- **Readings:** Chapter 2 (Getting Started - Sorting)
- 
### Week 5-6: Tree Data Structures - Part 1
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Topics:**
  - Binary Search Tree Property - left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
  - Tree Traversals - inorder, preorder, and postorder systematic visiting patterns for processing all nodes
- **Activities:**
  - Python Data Types Memory Card Challenge (40 minutes)
- **Readings:** Chapter 12 (Binary Search Trees)
- 
### Week 7-8: Tree Data Structures - Part 2  
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis (Advanced)
- **Topics:**
  - Binary Search Property - the fundamental ordering rule where left subtree values are less than parent, right subtree values are greater

# Data Structures and Algorithms
**CS 2420 | Fall 2024 | 4 Credit Hours**

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic problem-solving techniques essential for computer science. Students will explore the design, implementation, and analysis of core data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation skills through hands-on programming assignments. Students will learn to analyze algorithm efficiency using Big O notation and master essential algorithmic paradigms such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms. Topics include sorting algorithms (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort), searching techniques, graph traversal algorithms (BFS, DFS), and shortest path algorithms. The course balances mathematical rigor with practical application, preparing students to make informed decisions about data structure selection and algorithm design in real-world software development scenarios. Programming assignments will be completed in Java or C++, reinforcing object-oriented programming concepts while building algorithmic thinking skills. Students will also develop skills in debugging, testing, and optimizing code for performance and memory efficiency.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Implement and analyze fundamental data structures including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs, demonstrating understanding of their time and space complexities
• Design and implement efficient algorithms for sorting, searching, and graph traversal problems using appropriate algorithmic paradigms
• Evaluate algorithm performance using asymptotic analysis and Big O notation to make informed decisions about algorithm selection for specific problems

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction and Asymptotic Analysis
- Introduction to data structures and algorithms
- Big O notation and algorithm analysis
- Review of object-oriented programming concepts
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (90 minutes)

### Week 2: Arrays and Basic Data Structures
- Arrays and dynamic arrays
- Linked lists implementation and analysis
- Stacks and queues
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Recall Challenge (75 minutes)

### Week 3: Recursion and Divide-and-Conquer
- Recursive problem solving
- Divide-and-conquer paradigm
- Recurrence relations

### Week 4: Sorting Algorithms I
- Elementary sorting algorithms (bubble, selection, insertion)
- Merge sort implementation and analysis
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithm Performance (90 minutes)

### Week 5: Sorting Algorithms II
- Quick sort implementation and analysis
- Heap sort and heap data structure
- **Activity:** Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments (195 minutes)

### Week 6: Binary Search Trees
- **Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- Binary Search Tree Property: For any node, all values in left subtree are smaller, all values in right subtree are larger
- Tree Traversals: In-order, pre-order, and post-order recursive traversal algorithms for visiting all nodes
- **Quiz 1:** Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (100 points)

### Week 7: Advanced Tree Structures
- AVL trees and rotations
- Red-black trees
- B-trees introduction

### Week 8: Hash Tables I
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Analysis
- Hash Function: Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute data uniformly across the hash table
- Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing

### Week 9: Hash Tables II
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies
- Hash Function: A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
- Collision Resolution: Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
- **Activity:** Analyzing Cryptographic Hash Function Vulnerabilities Through Collision Attack Simulation (140 minutes)

### Week 10: Priority Queues and Heaps
- Heap data structure implementation
- Priority queue applications
- Heap sort algorithm

### Week 11: Graph Representations and Basic Algorithms
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions
- Graph Representation: Adjacency matrices and adjacency lists for storing graph data structures with trade-offs in memory usage and access time
- Depth-First Search (DFS): Recursive traversal algorithm that explores graph branches completely before backtracking, useful for cycle detection and topological sorting

### Week 12: Graph Traversal Algorithms
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): systematic level-by-level graph exploration using queues to find shortest unweighted paths
- Depth-First Search (DFS): recursive or stack-based graph exploration that goes as deep as possible before backtracking

### Week 13: Shortest Path Algorithms
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- Graph Traversal: Systematic exploration of graph vertices using DFS and BFS strategies
- Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a source vertex to all other vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
- **Quiz 2:** Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (100 points)

### Week 14: Advanced Topics
- Dynamic programming introduction
- Greedy algorithms
- String algorithms

### Week 15: Review and Advanced Applications
- Algorithm design strategies
- Performance optimization techniques
- **Discussion:** Programming Paradigms Discussion: Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming (100 points)

### Week 16: Final Projects and Presentations
- **Project Presentations:** Distributed System Architecture Design Presentation (100 points)
- Final exam review

## Assessment Plan

### Grade Distribution
| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage |
|----------------|--------|------------|
| Programming Assignments (4) | 400 | 40% |
| Quizzes (2) | 200 | 20% |
| Major Project | 100 | 10% |
| Lab Reports | 100 | 10% |
| Discussion Participation | 100 | 10% |
| Final Exam | 100 | 10% |
| **Total** | **1000** | **100%** |

### Specific Assessments

**Programming Assignments (100 points each)**
- Assignment 1: Linked List and Stack Implementation (Week 3)
- Assignment 2: Sorting Algorithm Comparison (Week 6)
- Assignment 3: Binary Search Tree Operations (Week 8)
- Assignment 4: Hash Table with Collision Resolution (Week 10)

**Quizzes (100 points each)**
- Quiz 1: Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (Week 6)
- Quiz 2: Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (Week 13)

**Major Project (100 points)**
- Distributed Database System with Consensus Protocol Implementation (Weeks 14-16)

**Lab Reports (100 points total)**
- Distributed System Design and Implementation: Building a Fault-Tolerant Microservices Architecture

**Discussion Participation (100 points)**
- Programming Paradigms Discussion: Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming

### Late Assignment Policy
- Programming assignments submitted up to 24 hours late: 10% penalty
- Programming assignments submitted 24-48 hours late: 25% penalty
- Programming assignments submitted more than 48 hours late: 50% penalty
- No assignments accepted more than one week late without prior arrangement

### Collaboration Policy
- **Encouraged:** Discussing algorithms and approaches at a high level
- **Allowed:** Helping classmates debug syntax errors
- **Prohibited:** Sharing code, copying solutions, working together on individual assignments

Limited extra credit opportunities may be available, including participation in programming contests or additional algorithm implementation challenges. These will be announced during the semester and are available to all students.

# Data Structures and Algorithms
**Course Code:** CS 2420  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 1410 (Introduction to Programming) or equivalent  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:30-11:20 AM  
**Lab Time:** T 2:00-3:50 PM  
**Semester:** Fall 2024

## Instructor Information

## Course Description
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic techniques essential for computer science. Students will explore linear data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues, followed by hierarchical structures such as trees and heaps. The course covers graph representations and traversal algorithms, along with essential sorting and searching techniques. Emphasis is placed on analyzing time and space complexity using Big O notation to evaluate algorithmic efficiency. Students will implement data structures from scratch and apply algorithmic problem-solving strategies including divide-and-conquer, greedy algorithms, and dynamic programming. Laboratory sessions reinforce theoretical concepts through hands-on programming assignments in Python or Java. Real-world applications demonstrate how these fundamental concepts apply to software development, database systems, and computational problem-solving.

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Implement and Analyze Data Structures:** Students will implement and analyze fundamental data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, and graphs, demonstrating understanding of their properties and appropriate use cases.

2. **Design Efficient Algorithms:** Students will design and implement efficient algorithms for searching, sorting, and graph traversal, while analyzing their time and space complexity using Big O notation.

3. **Apply Problem-Solving Techniques:** Students will apply algorithmic problem-solving techniques including recursion, divide-and-conquer, greedy methods, and dynamic programming to solve computational problems.

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Algorithm Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Topics:** Big O Notation, Time Complexity, Space Complexity
- - **Activity:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Dissecting Sorting Performance (110 min)

### Week 2: Linear Data Structures - Arrays and Linked Lists

### Week 3: Stack and Queue Implementations

### Week 4: Recursion and Divide-and-Conquer
- **Topics:** Recursive algorithms, recurrence relations, master theorem
- - **Reading:** Chapter 4 (Divide-and-Conquer)

### Week 5: Sorting Algorithms I
- **Topics:** Bubble sort, selection sort, insertion sort, merge sort
- - **Reading:** Chapter 2 (Getting Started)

### Week 6: Sorting Algorithms II and Analysis
- **Topics:** Quick sort, heap sort, counting sort, radix sort
- - **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Analysis and Design Quiz (100 points)

### Week 7: Binary Search Trees
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Topics:** BST property, insertion, deletion, traversal methods
- - **Reading:** Chapter 12 (Binary Search Trees)

### Week 8: Balanced Trees and Heaps
- **Topics:** AVL trees, Red-Black trees, binary heaps, priority queues
- - **Reading:** Chapter 6 (Heapsort)

### Week 9: Hash Tables I
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Analysis
- **Topics:** Hash functions, uniform hashing, load factor analysis
- - **Reading:** Chapter 11.1-11.2 (Hash Tables)

### Week 10: Hash Tables II - Collision Resolution
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
- **Topics:** Chaining, open addressing, linear/quadratic probing
- - **Activity:** Advanced Memory Management Terms and Concepts Recall Challenge (120 min)
- **Assessment:** Personal Task Manager Application Project Due (100 points)

### Week 11: Graph Representations and Basic Algorithms
- **Topics:** Adjacency matrix, adjacency list, BFS, DFS
- - **Reading:** Chapter 22.1-22.3 (Graph Algorithms)

### Week 12: Graph Algorithms - Shortest Paths
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
- **Topics:** Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford algorithm
- - **Activity:** Database Query Performance Analysis and Optimization (100 min)
- **Reading:** Chapter 24 (Single-Source Shortest Paths)

### Week 13: Dynamic Programming
- **Topics:** Optimal substructure, memoization, tabulation
- - **Reading:** Chapter 15 (Dynamic Programming)

### Week 14: Greedy Algorithms
- **Topics:** Greedy choice property, activity selection, Huffman coding
- - **Reading:** Chapter 16 (Greedy Algorithms)

### Week 15: Advanced Topics and Review
- **Topics:** String algorithms, NP-completeness introduction
- - **Assessment:** Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture Presentation (100 points)

### Week 16: Final Examinations
- **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithms Design and Analysis Comprehensive Exam (100 points)

| Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture Presentation | 100 | 15% | Week 15 |
| Advanced Algorithms Design and Analysis Comprehensive Exam | 100 | 25% | Finals Week |
| Lab Assignments (10 × 10 points) | 100 | 15% | Weekly |
| Participation and Activities | 100 | 10% | Ongoing |
| **Total** | **600** | **100%** | |

### Late Assignment Policy
- **Programming Assignments:** 10% penalty per day late, up to 3 days. After 3 days, assignments receive a zero.
- **Project:** 15% penalty per day late, up to 2 days. No submissions accepted after 2 days without documented emergency.
- **Presentations:** Must be given on scheduled date. Make-up presentations only for documented emergencies.

### Collaboration Guidelines
- **Encouraged:** Discussing algorithms and approaches at a conceptual level
- **Allowed:** Helping classmates debug general programming issues
- **Prohibited:** Sharing actual code, copying solutions, or submitting work that is not your own

### Accommodations
Students with documented disabilities who may need accommodations should schedule an appointment with the instructor as soon as possible. All discussions will remain confidential. Students with disabilities must contact the Office of Disability Services to verify their eligibility for reasonable accommodations.

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithms essential for computer science and software development. The course emphasizes algorithmic thinking and problem-solving strategies, covering sorting algorithms, searching techniques, recursion, dynamic programming, and graph algorithms. Practical programming assignments will reinforce theoretical concepts, allowing students to implement data structures from scratch and apply algorithms to real-world problems.

## Learning Objectives

1. **Implement and analyze fundamental data structures** including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs, demonstrating understanding of their properties, operations, and appropriate use cases.

2. **Design and implement efficient algorithms** for sorting, searching, and graph traversal, and analyze their time and space complexity using asymptotic notation.

3. **Apply algorithmic problem-solving techniques** such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms to solve computational problems.

---

### Week 1: Foundation and Complexity Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation

- 
### Week 10: Hash Tables II

- **Topics:**
  - Hash Function: Mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices
  - Collision Resolution: Strategies for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
- **Activities:** Analyzing Database Query Performance Bottlenecks Through Execution Plan Decomposition (95 min)

-

  - Graph representation - adjacency lists vs matrices, their trade-offs in space/time complexity for different operations
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-by-level traversal using queues, applications in shortest unweighted paths

# Data Structures and Algorithms
**Course Code:** CS 202  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 101 (Introduction to Programming)  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithms essential for computer science. Students will explore the design, implementation, and analysis of key data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation skills, covering algorithm analysis using Big O notation to evaluate time and space complexity. Students will implement data structures in a modern programming language and learn to select appropriate structures for specific problem domains. Core algorithms covered include searching, sorting, tree traversals, graph algorithms, and dynamic programming techniques. The course balances mathematical rigor with hands-on programming experience, preparing students for advanced computer science coursework and technical interviews. Weekly programming assignments reinforce theoretical concepts, while larger projects demonstrate real-world applications of data structures in software development. Students will develop critical thinking skills for algorithm design and optimization, learning to trade off between time and space efficiency based on application requirements.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Analyze the time and space complexity of algorithms using Big O notation and select appropriate data structures based on efficiency requirements.  
• Implement fundamental data structures (linked lists, trees, hash tables, graphs) and core algorithms (sorting, searching, graph traversal) in a high-level programming language.  
• Design and optimize algorithms for real-world problems by applying algorithmic techniques such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches.

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction and Algorithm Analysis
**Topics:** Course overview, Big O notation, algorithm efficiency fundamentals  
**Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Reference Chart Creation (45 min)  
**Reading:** Chapter 1-3 (Textbook)

### Week 2: Basic Data Structures - Arrays and Linked Lists
**Topics:** Array operations, dynamic arrays, singly and doubly linked lists  
**Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge (50 min)  
**Assignment:** Implement linked list with basic operations (Due Week 3)

### Week 3: Stacks and Queues
**Topics:** Stack and queue ADTs, implementation using arrays and linked lists  
**Activity:** Deconstructing Algorithm Efficiency: Big O Analysis of Real-World Code Implementations (90 min)  
**Quiz 1:** Algorithm complexity analysis

### Week 4: Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Analysis
**Module Topics:**
- Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
- Collision Resolution - Techniques (chaining, linear probing, quadratic probing) used to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index

**Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Performance Under Different Data Conditions (95 min)

### Week 5: Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Techniques
**Module Topics:**
- Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
- Collision Resolution - Strategies for handling when multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining (linked lists) and open addressing (probing sequences)

**Assignment:** Hash table implementation with collision resolution (Due Week 6)

### Week 6: Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
**Module Topics:**
- Binary Search Tree Property - each node's left subtree contains only values less than the node's value, and right subtree contains only values greater
- Tree Traversal Algorithms - systematic methods for visiting all nodes (inorder for sorted output, preorder for tree copying, postorder for deletion)

### Week 7: Advanced Tree Structures
**Topics:** AVL trees, Red-Black trees, B-trees  
**Activity:** Dissecting a Social Media Algorithm: Analyzing Content Recommendation Systems (85 min)

### Week 8: Midterm Examination Week
**Assessment:** Fundamentals of Programming Logic and Basic Algorithms Exam

### Week 9: Heaps and Priority Queues
**Topics:** Binary heaps, heap operations, heapsort algorithm  
**Assignment:** Priority queue implementation (Due Week 10)

### Week 10: Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
**Module Topics:**
- Graph representation using adjacency lists and adjacency matrices for storing vertex and edge relationships
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) algorithm that explores vertices level by level using a queue data structure

### Week 11: Graph Algorithms: Search, Traversal, and Shortest Path
**Module Topics:**
- Graph representation (adjacency matrix vs adjacency list) - different methods for storing graph data structures with their respective memory and access time implications
- Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, useful for cycle detection and topological sorting

### Week 12: Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
**Module Topics:**
- Dijkstra's Algorithm - greedy approach for finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
- Bellman-Ford Algorithm - dynamic programming solution that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles in directed graphs

**Assignment:** Graph algorithm implementation project (Due Week 14)

### Week 13: Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
**Module Topics:**
- Optimal Substructure: Property where optimal solutions contain optimal solutions to subproblems
- Overlapping Subproblems: Recursive algorithms that solve the same subproblems multiple times

**Activity:** Critical Analysis of Database Normalization Trade-offs in E-commerce System Design (90 min)

### Week 14: Advanced Topics and Applications
**Topics:** Greedy algorithms, divide-and-conquer strategies  
**Assessment:** Data Structures Implementation and Analysis Lab Report due

### Week 15: Course Review and Final Projects
**Assessment:** Scalability Architecture Discussion: From Startup to Enterprise Scale  
**Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz

### Week 16: Final Examination Week
**Final Project Presentations**

# Data Structures and Algorithms
**Course Code:** CS 2420  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Introduction to Programming (CS 1410) and Discrete Mathematics (MATH 2300)  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithms essential for computer science. Students will explore the design, implementation, and analysis of abstract data types including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes algorithmic thinking through the study of searching, sorting, recursion, and graph algorithms. Students will learn to analyze time and space complexity using Big O notation and make informed decisions about selecting appropriate data structures for specific problems. Programming assignments will be completed in Java or Python, reinforcing theoretical concepts through hands-on implementation. Topics include recursive algorithms, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and basic algorithm design paradigms. The course balances theoretical understanding with practical application, preparing students for advanced computer science courses and software development careers. Students will develop problem-solving skills crucial for technical interviews and real-world programming challenges. Laboratory sessions provide opportunities to implement and test data structures and algorithms, fostering deeper understanding of their behavior and performance characteristics.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Implement and analyze fundamental data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs  
• Design and implement efficient algorithms for searching, sorting, and graph traversal while analyzing their time and space complexity using Big O notation  
• Apply algorithmic design paradigms such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches to solve computational problems  
• Evaluate trade-offs between different data structures and algorithms to select optimal solutions for specific programming scenarios  

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Algorithm Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation  
**Key Concepts:**
- Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the limiting behavior of functions, specifically how algorithm runtime grows relative to input size
- Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size, expressed in asymptotic terms

**Activities:**
- Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Memory Matrix (75 minutes)
- Analyzing Algorithm Efficiency: Big O Performance Comparison Through Sorting Algorithms (95 minutes)

### Week 2: Binary Search Trees Fundamentals
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Key Concepts:**
- Binary Search Tree Property: For any node, all values in left subtree are smaller, all values in right subtree are larger
- Tree Traversal Methods: In-order, pre-order, and post-order traversal algorithms for visiting all nodes systematically

**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search and Sort Performance (90 minutes)

### Week 3: Advanced Binary Search Trees
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Applications  
**Key Concepts:**
- BST Property - Each node's value is greater than all values in its left subtree and less than all values in its right subtree
- Tree Traversal Methods - In-order, pre-order, and post-order algorithms for visiting all nodes in a BST

**Activities:**
- Python Data Types Memory Palace - Visual Identification Challenge (45 minutes)

### Week 4: Hash Tables Introduction
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, determining storage location in hash table
- Load Factor - Ratio of stored elements to total table capacity, critical metric affecting performance and collision frequency

### Week 5: Hash Tables Deep Dive
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function: Mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, determining where elements are stored in the hash table
- Collision Resolution: Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods

### Weeks 6-7: Graph Fundamentals and Traversal
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Problems  
**Key Concepts:**
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): Level-by-level graph traversal using queue data structure, optimal for finding shortest unweighted paths
- Depth-First Search (DFS): Deep exploration of graph branches using stack or recursion, essential for topological sorting and cycle detection

### Week 8: **MIDTERM EXAM**

### Weeks 9-10: Advanced Graph Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search  
**Key Concepts:**
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): A graph traversal algorithm that explores vertices level by level, using a queue data structure to visit all neighbors before moving to the next depth level
- Depth-First Search (DFS): A graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, typically implemented using recursion or an explicit stack

### Weeks 11-12: Graph Representations and Applications
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding  
**Key Concepts:**
- Graph representation - Methods for storing graphs in memory including adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and edge lists with their respective trade-offs
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-by-level graph traversal algorithm using queues, optimal for finding shortest unweighted paths and connected components

### Weeks 13-14: Dynamic Programming and Advanced Algorithms
**Topics:** Advanced algorithmic paradigms, optimization problems, and real-world applications

### Week 15: Review and Integration
**Topics:** Comprehensive review, algorithm selection strategies, and preparation for final assessment

### Week 16: **FINAL EXAM PERIOD**

## Assessment Plan

|---|---|---|---|
| **Fundamentals of Programming Logic and Data Types Quiz** | 100 | 15% | Week 3 |
| **Software Design Pattern Implementation and Analysis Presentation** | 100 | 20% | Week 10 |
| **Distributed Systems Architecture Design and Trade-off Analysis** (Discussion) | 100 | 15% | Ongoing (Weeks 5, 8, 12) |
| **Advanced Software Engineering Portfolio: Full-Stack Application Development** | 100 | 25% | Week 15 |

Laboratory sessions are mandatory and provide hands-on experience with course concepts. Students must complete lab exercises during the scheduled time and demonstrate their implementations to the instructor or TA. Make-up labs are available only for excused absences arranged in advance.

# Data Structures and Algorithms
**Course Syllabus - Fall 2024**

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic techniques essential for efficient software development. Students will explore abstract data types including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation of these structures. Students will analyze time and space complexity using Big O notation and learn to select appropriate data structures for specific problems. Key algorithmic paradigms covered include divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and graph traversal methods. Programming assignments will require implementation of data structures from scratch and application to real-world problems such as pathfinding, sorting large datasets, and optimizing search operations. The course balances mathematical rigor with hands-on coding experience, preparing students for advanced computer science courses and technical interviews. Topics include recursion, algorithm correctness proofs, and performance optimization techniques. Students will work in Java or C++ to implement and test their solutions, developing both programming proficiency and analytical problem-solving skills critical for software engineering careers.

---

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Implement and analyze** fundamental data structures including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs, demonstrating understanding of their time and space complexities

• **Design and implement** efficient algorithms using various paradigms such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches  

• **Evaluate algorithm performance** using Big O notation and select appropriate data structures and algorithms for specific computational problems

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Introduction & Algorithm Analysis Foundations
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation - mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - measurement of computational time required by an algorithm relative to input size
- **Activities:**
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (60 minutes)
  - Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Drill (90 minutes)

### Week 2: Fundamental Data Structures Review
**Module:** Basic Data Structures and Their Applications
- Arrays, Dynamic Arrays, Linked Lists
- Stacks and Queues implementation and applications
- **Activities:**
  - Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill (30 minutes)

### Week 3: Binary Search Trees - Part I  
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Binary Search Tree Property: Left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
  - Tree Traversal: Systematic methods (inorder, preorder, postorder) for visiting all nodes in a specific sequence
- **Activities:**
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Time Complexity Evaluation (75 minutes)

### Week 4: Binary Search Trees - Part II
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Advanced Operations and Analysis
- **Key Concepts:**
  - BST Property: For any node, all values in left subtree are smaller, all values in right subtree are larger
  - Tree Traversals: Systematic methods for visiting all nodes (in-order, pre-order, post-order) with specific ordering guarantees
- **Activities:**
  - Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge (45 minutes)

### Week 5: Advanced Tree Structures
- Balanced Trees (AVL Trees, Red-Black Trees)
- Heaps and Priority Queues
- **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz (100 points)

### Week 6: Hash Tables - Part I
**Module:** Hash Tables: Design, Implementation, and Performance Analysis  
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps arbitrary-sized data to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods

### Week 7: Hash Tables - Part II  
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Performance Analysis
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices  
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining (linked lists) and open addressing methods
- **Activities:**
  - Analyzing Algorithmic Complexity and Optimization Trade-offs in Sorting Algorithm Implementations (135 minutes)

### Week 8: Midterm Exam Week
- **Assessment:** Personal Task Manager Application Project Due (100 points)
- Midterm Exam Review

### Week 9: Graph Representation and Basic Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - systematic level-by-level graph exploration using queues, optimal for unweighted shortest paths
  - Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive graph exploration that goes as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for cycle detection and topological sorting
- **Activities:**
  - Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Varying Data Conditions (150 minutes)

### Week 10: Advanced Graph Algorithms - Part I
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach for finding shortest paths from a single source in graphs with non-negative edge weights using priority queues
  - Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles in O(VE) time

### Week 11: Advanced Graph Algorithms - Part II  
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Shortest Path Problem: Finding the minimum-weight path between vertices in a weighted graph, fundamental to routing and navigation
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a source vertex in graphs with non-negative edge weights
- **Activities:**
  - Binary Number System Flashcard Memorization Challenge (25 minutes)

### Week 12: Sorting and Searching Algorithms
- Comparison-based sorting (Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Heap Sort)
- Non-comparison sorting (Radix Sort, Counting Sort)
- **Activities:**
  - Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in Multi-threaded Applications Using Profiler Data (170 minutes)

### Week 13: Dynamic Programming
- Principles of Dynamic Programming
- Classic DP problems and optimization techniques
- **Assessment:** Database Design Trade-offs: Relational vs. NoSQL Implementation Discussion (100 points)

### Week 14: Greedy Algorithms and Advanced Topics
- Greedy algorithm design principles
- Advanced data structures overview
- **Assessment:** Advanced Machine Learning Architecture Design and Implementation Showcase Presentations (100 points)

### Week 15: Course Review and Applications
- Real-world applications of data structures
- Technical interview preparation
- **Assessment:** Introduction to Python Programming: Variables, Data Types, and Basic Operations Lab Report (100 points)

### Week 16: Final Exam Week
- Comprehensive Final Examination

| **Programming Projects** | 100 | 20% | Personal Task Manager Application |  
| **Lab Reports** | 100 | 15% | Introduction to Python Programming Lab Report |
| **Discussions** | 100 | 10% | Database Design Trade-offs Discussion |

# CS 3320: Database Systems
## Course Syllabus - Fall 2024

### COURSE INFORMATION

**Course Title:** Database Systems  
**Course Number:** CS 3320  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 2420 (Data Structures) and CS 2610 (Discrete Mathematics)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

### COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to database systems, focusing on both theoretical foundations and practical applications. Students will explore the fundamental concepts of database design, including entity-relationship modeling, normalization theory, and relational algebra. The course covers database implementation techniques, query processing and optimization, transaction management, and concurrency control. Students will gain hands-on experience with SQL programming, database administration, and modern database technologies including NoSQL systems and distributed databases. Topics include data modeling, schema design, indexing strategies, backup and recovery procedures, and database security. The course emphasizes real-world applications through projects that involve designing and implementing database solutions for various domains. Students will work with popular database management systems such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, and MongoDB. By the end of the course, students will have developed the skills necessary to design efficient database schemas, write complex queries, and understand the trade-offs involved in database system design and implementation.

### LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement relational database schemas using entity-relationship modeling and normalization principles  
• Write complex SQL queries involving joins, subqueries, aggregations, and advanced database operations  
• Analyze database performance issues and apply optimization techniques including indexing and query optimization  
• Understand transaction management, concurrency control, and ACID properties in database systems  
• Compare and contrast relational and NoSQL database systems and select appropriate technologies for specific use cases  

### REQUIRED MATERIALS

**Textbook:** *Database System Concepts* (7th Edition) by Silberschatz, Korth, and Sudarshan  
**Software:** MySQL Workbench, PostgreSQL, MongoDB Community Edition  
**Hardware:** Laptop capable of running database software  

### WEEKLY SCHEDULE

#### Week 1-2: Database Foundations and Query Complexity
**Module:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation - mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - measurement of computational time required by an algorithm relative to input size
- **Topics:** Introduction to databases, query complexity analysis, performance metrics
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Speed Drill (50 minutes)

#### Week 3-4: Database Storage and Indexing
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function: A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (hash codes) used as array indices
  - Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle when multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
- **Topics:** Storage structures, B+ trees, hash indexing
- **Activity:** Python Data Types Memory Match Challenge (45 minutes)

#### Week 5-6: Advanced Indexing and Storage Optimization
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute data uniformly across the hash table
  - Load Factor - Ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical metric affecting performance and collision frequency
- **Topics:** Advanced indexing strategies, storage optimization
- **Activity:** Database Query Performance Analysis Through Execution Plan Comparison (60 minutes)

#### Week 7-8: Tree Structures in Database Systems
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Concepts:**
  - Binary Search Tree Property: Left subtree contains values less than root, right subtree contains values greater than root
  - Tree Traversals: In-order (left-root-right), pre-order (root-left-right), post-order (left-right-root) visiting patterns
- **Topics:** B-trees, B+ trees in database indexing
- **Activity:** Debugging Algorithm Efficiency: Analyzing Sorting Performance Through Code Trace and Complexity Comparison (90 minutes)

#### Week 9-10: Query Optimization and Graph-Based Analysis
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- **Concepts:**
  - Graph representation - Methods for storing graphs in memory including adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists with trade-offs analysis
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-order traversal algorithm using queues, optimal for unweighted shortest paths and connected component detection
- **Topics:** Query execution plans, join algorithms, cost-based optimization
- **Activity:** Analyzing Algorithm Complexity Trade-offs in Real-World Database Query Optimization (110 minutes)

#### Week 11-12: Advanced Query Processing
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions
- **Concepts:**
  - Graph Representation: Adjacency matrices vs adjacency lists, memory usage implications, and performance trade-offs for different graph densities
  - Depth-First Search (DFS): Recursive and iterative implementations, applications in topological sorting, cycle detection, and connected components identification
- **Topics:** Advanced join strategies, parallel query processing
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge (45 minutes)

#### Week 13-14: Database Optimization Strategies
**Module:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
- **Concepts:**
  - Optimal Substructure - A problem exhibits optimal substructure if an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems
  - Overlapping Subproblems - The same subproblems are solved multiple times in a naive recursive approach
- **Topics:** Query optimization using dynamic programming, cost estimation
- **Activity:** Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture (150 minutes)

#### Week 15-16: Distributed Systems and Final Review
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation (Review)
- **Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required as a function of input size, typically expressed in Big O notation
- **Topics:** Distributed databases, NoSQL systems, final project presentations
- **Activity:** Distributed System Architecture Analysis: Decomposing Netflix's Microservices Failure Cascade (170 minutes)

### ASSESSMENT PLAN

| Assessment Type | Title | Points | Weight | Due Date |
|----------------|--------|--------|--------|----------|
| Quiz | Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz | 100 | 15% | Week 4 |
| Project | Library Management System Design and Implementation | 100 | 25% | Week 8 |
| Presentation | Introduction to Programming Concepts Presentation | 100 | 15% | Week 12 |
| Portfolio | Full-Stack Web Application Development Portfolio | 100 | 20% | Week 14 |
| Final Exam | Advanced Distributed Systems Design and Implementation Exam | 100 | 25% | Finals Week |

**Total Points:** 500  
**Grading Scale:**
- A: 90-100% (450-500 points)
- B: 80-89% (400-449 points)
- C: 70-79% (350-399 points)
- D: 60-69% (300-349 points)
- F: Below 60% (<300 points)

### COURSE POLICIES

##### Late Assignment Policy
- Projects and portfolios: 10% deduction per day late
- Quizzes and presentations: No make-ups without prior arrangement or documented emergency
- Final exam: Must be taken at scheduled time unless approved by Academic Affairs

# Data Structures and Algorithms
## CS 2420 - Fall 2024

**Class Time:** [Days/Times]  
**Prerequisites:** CS 1410 (Introduction to Computer Science) or equivalent  
**Credits:** 3  

---

## Course Description

This course provides a comprehensive introduction to fundamental data structures and algorithmic problem-solving techniques essential for computer science. Students will explore abstract data types including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation of these structures. Students will analyze algorithm efficiency using Big O notation and learn to select appropriate data structures for specific problems. Key algorithms covered include sorting (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort), searching (binary search, graph traversal), and basic dynamic programming. Through hands-on programming assignments, students will implement data structures from scratch and solve computational problems of varying complexity. The course balances mathematical rigor with practical coding skills, preparing students for advanced computer science coursework and technical interviews. Laboratory sessions provide guided practice with implementation challenges, while projects encourage creative application of learned concepts. By course completion, students will possess strong foundational knowledge for software development, system design, and algorithmic thinking that serves as a cornerstone for all subsequent computer science studies.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Implement and analyze** the performance of fundamental data structures including linked lists, trees, hash tables, and graphs using appropriate programming languages.

• **Design and implement** efficient algorithms for searching, sorting, and graph traversal problems while analyzing their time and space complexity using Big O notation.

• **Evaluate and select** optimal data structures and algorithms for solving real-world computational problems based on performance requirements and constraints.

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation of Algorithmic Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm runtime as input size approaches infinity
- Asymptotic Analysis - Method for describing algorithm performance characteristics by focusing on growth rates rather than exact runtime

**Activities:**
- Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge (90 minutes)

### Week 2: Tree Structures and Operations
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- Binary Search Tree Property - left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
- Tree Traversal Algorithms - systematic methods for visiting all nodes (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order)

**Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Empirical Testing and Complexity Decomposition (135 minutes)

### Week 3: Hashing Fundamentals
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies
- Hash Function: A mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing elements uniformly across the hash table
- Load Factor: The ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical for predicting performance and determining when to resize

**Activities:**
- Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Drill (60 minutes)

### Week 4: Advanced Hashing Techniques
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
- Hash Function: A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across the hash table
- Load Factor: The ratio of the number of stored elements to the total capacity of the hash table, directly affecting performance and collision probability

**Activities:**
- Algorithmic Complexity Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Variants (110 minutes)

### Week 5: Graph Fundamentals and Traversal
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- Graph representation - adjacency lists vs adjacency matrices, weighted vs unweighted graphs, directed vs undirected graphs
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-order traversal using queues, shortest path in unweighted graphs, connected components

### Week 6: Graph Representations and Search
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- Graph representation - adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists with their respective trade-offs in memory usage and access time
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-order traversal using queues to explore nodes at increasing distances from source

### Week 7: Advanced Graph Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees
- Dijkstra's Algorithm - greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
- Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) - subgraph that connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight, solved by Kruskal's (edge-based) or Prim's (vertex-based) algorithms

### Week 8: **Midterm Exam Week**

### Week 9: Introduction to Dynamic Programming
**Module:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
- Optimal Substructure - property where optimal solutions contain optimal solutions to subproblems
- Overlapping Subproblems - recursive algorithms that repeatedly solve identical subproblems

### Week 10: Advanced Dynamic Programming
**Module:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
- Optimal Substructure: Property where optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, enabling recursive decomposition
- Overlapping Subproblems: Recursive algorithms that solve identical subproblems multiple times, creating opportunities for memoization

### Week 11: Collision Resolution Strategies
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
- Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
- Collision Resolution - Strategies to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing

### Week 12: Project Work Week
- Individual consultations
- Project implementation and debugging
- Peer code reviews

### Week 13: Advanced Topics and Review
- Advanced data structure applications
- Algorithm optimization techniques
- Technical interview preparation

### Week 14: Presentations and Final Review
- Student project presentations
- Comprehensive course review
- Final exam preparation

### Week 15: **Final Exam Week**

# Distributed Consensus Mechanisms and Byzantine Fault Tolerance
**Computer Science Department | Undergraduate Course**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Course Title:** Distributed Consensus Mechanisms and Byzantine Fault Tolerance  
**Course Code:** CS 4XX  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Data Structures and Algorithms, Discrete Mathematics, Probability Theory  
**Duration:** 15-week semester  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course explores the theoretical foundations of achieving agreement in distributed systems where components may fail or behave maliciously. Students will examine classical consensus protocols, Byzantine agreement algorithms, and modern blockchain consensus mechanisms through rigorous mathematical analysis. The curriculum covers impossibility results like the FLP theorem, practical algorithms such as PBFT and Raft, and emerging consensus paradigms including proof-of-stake and hybrid approaches. Emphasis is placed on formal verification techniques, complexity analysis, and theoretical bounds on fault tolerance. Students will analyze trade-offs between safety, liveness, and performance in various network models, from synchronous to partially synchronous environments. The course bridges foundational distributed systems theory with contemporary applications in cryptocurrency, distributed databases, and fault-tolerant computing. Through formal proofs, algorithm analysis, and theoretical exercises, students develop deep understanding of why certain distributed problems are solvable while others are provably impossible, and how real-world systems navigate these theoretical constraints.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master formal models of distributed computation** and analyze consensus algorithms using rigorous mathematical frameworks
2. **Apply theoretical impossibility results** to evaluate the fundamental limits and trade-offs in distributed system design  
3. **Develop expertise in Byzantine fault tolerance mechanisms** and their applications in modern distributed systems

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundations and Prerequisites Review
**Topic:** Algorithm Analysis and Graph Theory Fundamentals
- **Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size
- **Activity:** Algorithmic Complexity Analysis: Big-O Performance Breakdown of Sorting Algorithm Implementations (90 minutes)
- **Reading:** Textbook Ch. 1-2

### Week 2: Graph Algorithms Foundation
**Topic:** Essential Graph Traversal Methods
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS): A graph traversal algorithm that explores nodes level by level, using a queue data structure
  - Depth-First Search (DFS): A graph traversal algorithm that explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (90 minutes)
- **Reading:** Textbook Ch. 3

### Week 3: Shortest Path Algorithms
**Topic:** Path Finding in Distributed Networks
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from single source
  - Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution detecting negative cycles while computing shortest paths

# ETHICAL AI SYSTEMS: FROM BIAS DETECTION TO FAIR ALGORITHM DESIGN
**Course Code:** CS 495 | **Credits:** 3 | **Semester:** Spring 2024

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Meeting:** [Days/Times/Location]  
**Prerequisites:** Data Structures (CS 300), Statistics (STAT 301), Introduction to Machine Learning (CS 405)

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This capstone course challenges students to confront the critical intersection of artificial intelligence and social responsibility. Students will develop, evaluate, and deploy AI systems while addressing real-world ethical challenges including algorithmic bias, fairness metrics, and responsible data governance. The course combines theoretical foundations in machine learning with hands-on experience in bias detection tools, fairness-aware algorithms, and interpretable AI techniques. Working in multidisciplinary teams, students will partner with local organizations, nonprofits, or government agencies to identify and solve authentic problems where AI bias has significant social impact. Projects span domains such as criminal justice risk assessment, hiring algorithms, healthcare diagnostics, and financial lending systems. Students will master cutting-edge techniques including adversarial debiasing, counterfactual fairness, and explainable AI while developing professional skills in stakeholder communication, ethical reasoning, and regulatory compliance. The capstone culminates in a comprehensive portfolio including a deployed AI system, bias audit report, stakeholder presentation, and policy recommendations. Graduates emerge as ethically-minded AI practitioners equipped to lead responsible innovation in an increasingly algorithm-driven society.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Design and implement fairness-aware machine learning algorithms** using techniques such as adversarial debiasing and constraint-based optimization
2. **Conduct comprehensive bias audits** of existing AI systems and develop actionable remediation strategies for real-world stakeholders  
3. **Create interpretable and explainable AI solutions** that balance model performance with transparency requirements for high-stakes applications

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundations of Ethical AI
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Concepts:** Big O Notation - Upper bound representation of algorithm growth rate in worst-case scenarios; Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required as input size increases
- **Activities:** 
  - Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Challenge (45 min)
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis Through Runtime Comparison (95 min)
- **Topics:** Introduction to AI ethics, algorithmic accountability, fairness definitions

### Week 2: Data Structures for Fair AI Systems
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design and Implementation
- **Concepts:** Hash Function - deterministic algorithm mapping arbitrary-sized data to fixed-size values; Collision Resolution - techniques for handling multiple keys hashing to same index
- **Activities:** 
  - Python Data Type Identification and Matching Activity (40 min)
- **Topics:** Efficient data representation, bias in data collection and storage

### Week 3: Tree-Based Models and Interpretability
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Concepts:** Binary Search Property - organizational structure for efficient data access; Tree Traversal Algorithms - systematic node visiting methods
- **Activities:**
  - Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge (45 min)
- **Topics:** Decision trees, interpretable models, SHAP values

### Week 4: Graph-Based Fairness Analysis
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- **Concepts:** Graph representation using adjacency structures; Depth-First Search for systematic exploration
- **Activities:**
  - Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Speed Test (45 min)
- **Topics:** Network analysis, social graphs, representation learning fairness

### Week 5: Advanced Graph Algorithms for Bias Detection
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
- **Concepts:** Dijkstra's Algorithm for shortest path optimization; Bellman-Ford Algorithm for negative cycle detection
- **Activities:**
  - Database Query Performance Analysis (150 min)
- **Topics:** Counterfactual fairness, causal inference, algorithmic auditing

### Weeks 6-8: Mid-Course Project Development
- **Focus:** Team formation, stakeholder partnership establishment, problem identification
- **Activities:** Site visits, stakeholder interviews, preliminary bias assessment
- **Assessment:** Project proposal and initial bias audit

### Weeks 9-12: Advanced Implementation Phase
- **Focus:** Fairness-aware algorithm development, adversarial debiasing implementation
- **Activities:** 
  - Cryptographic Algorithm Security Vulnerability Analysis (150 min)
  - Analyzing Memory Leak Patterns in Multi-threaded Java Applications (3 hours)
- **Topics:** Differential privacy, secure multi-party computation, federated learning

### Weeks 13-14: System Integration and Testing
- **Focus:** Deployment, performance evaluation, comprehensive bias testing
- **Activities:**
  - Distributed System Failure Analysis (150 min)
- **Topics:** Production deployment, monitoring, continuous auditing

### Weeks 15-16: Final Presentations and Policy Recommendations
- **Focus:** Stakeholder presentations, policy briefs, portfolio completion
- **Assessment:** Final presentations and comprehensive portfolios

---

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

### Grade Distribution
| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage |
|----------------|--------|------------|
| Capstone Project Portfolio | 100 | 25% |
| System Architecture Presentation | 100 | 25% |
| Bias Audit Lab Report | 100 | 25% |
| Ethics Discussion Forums | 100 | 15% |
| Algorithm Analysis Quizzes | 100 | 10% |
| **Total** | **500** | **100%** |

### Assessment Details

**1. Capstone Project Portfolio (100 points - 25%)**
- **Type:** Project
- **Description:** Comprehensive portfolio including deployed AI system, bias audit report, stakeholder documentation, and policy recommendations
- **Due:** Week 16
- **Rubric Focus:** Technical implementation (40%), bias mitigation effectiveness (30%), stakeholder communication (20%), documentation quality (10%)

**2. System Architecture Presentation (100 points - 25%)**
- **Type:** Presentation  
- **Description:** Advanced system architecture design and defense of fairness-aware AI solution to stakeholders and technical panel
- **Due:** Week 15
- **Format:** 20-minute presentation + 10-minute Q&A
- **Rubric Focus:** Technical depth (35%), ethical reasoning (25%), presentation quality (25%), stakeholder relevance (15%)

**3. Bias Audit Lab Report (100 points - 25%)**
- **Type:** Lab Report
- **Description:** Distributed system performance analysis implementing and evaluating fairness metrics across multiple demographic groups
- **Due:** Week 12
- **Requirements:** Statistical analysis, visualization, remediation recommendations
- **Rubric Focus:** Methodological rigor (40%), statistical analysis (30%), actionable recommendations (30%)

**4. Ethics Discussion Forums (100 points - 15%)**
- **Type:** Discussion
- **Description:** Weekly discussions on programming paradigms, ethical frameworks, and case study analysis
- **Format:** Initial post (200+ words) + 2 substantive responses to peers
- **Topics:** Procedural vs Object-Oriented approaches to fairness, stakeholder engagement strategies

**5. Algorithm Analysis Quizzes (100 points - 10%)**

# Network Protocol Engineering and Performance Analysis Laboratory
**Course Code:** CSE 4XX  
**Credits:** 4 credit hours  
**Prerequisites:** Computer Networks (CSE 3XX), Operating Systems (CSE 3XX), Data Structures & Algorithms (CSE 2XX)  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

**Lab Coordinator:** [Name]  

## Course Description

This intensive laboratory-driven course challenges students to design, implement, and optimize network protocols from the ground up. Students work in teams to build complete networking stacks, starting with raw socket programming and progressing to custom transport protocols, routing algorithms, and distributed system architectures. The course emphasizes hands-on protocol development using C/C++ and Python, with extensive performance benchmarking across simulated and real network environments.

Weekly coding sprints require students to implement protocol features like congestion control, error correction, and security mechanisms while analyzing performance under various network conditions including high latency, packet loss, and bandwidth constraints. Students deploy their protocols on campus testbeds and cloud infrastructure, conducting rigorous performance comparisons against industry standards like TCP, UDP, and HTTP/3. The intensive nature includes 24-hour protocol hackathons, peer code reviews, and presentations to industry professionals.

Final projects involve designing novel protocols for emerging applications such as IoT mesh networks, edge computing, or real-time gaming systems, with emphasis on scalability, reliability, and efficiency trade-offs.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Design and implement custom network protocols** with advanced features like congestion control, flow control, and error recovery mechanisms  
• **Conduct comprehensive performance analysis** of networking systems using profiling tools, network simulators, and real-world testbed environments  
• **Optimize network protocol performance** through algorithmic improvements, system-level tuning, and architectural design decisions  

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Protocol Fundamentals and Data Structures Foundation
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function: Mathematical function mapping keys to array indices for efficient data storage and retrieval in protocol implementations
- Load Factor: Critical performance metric (α = n/m) affecting hash table efficiency and collision frequency in network data structures

**Lab Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flashcard Drill with Visual Recognition (35 min)
- Protocol header parsing using hash-based lookups

### Week 2: Advanced Hash Table Implementation for Network Data
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Analysis  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function design for uniform data distribution across network routing tables
- Collision Resolution techniques (separate chaining, open addressing) for handling network address conflicts

**Lab Activities:**
- Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge (45 min)
- Implement network address hash tables with collision handling

### Week 3: Routing Algorithm Foundations
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions  
**Key Concepts:**
- Graph Representation using adjacency matrices/lists for network topology modeling
- Depth-First Search (DFS) for network cycle detection and topology analysis

**Lab Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (90 min)
- Implement basic routing table lookup algorithms

### Week 4: Network Topology Analysis and Routing
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding  
**Key Concepts:**
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) for shortest unweighted path finding in network routing
- Depth-First Search (DFS) implementation for network topology exploration

**Lab Activities:**
- Advanced Algorithm Time Complexity Classification Recall Challenge (75 min)
- Protocol routing algorithm implementation and testing

### Week 5: Protocol State Management
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Key Concepts:**
- Binary Search Tree Property for maintaining sorted protocol connection states
- Tree Traversals for efficient protocol state enumeration and management

**Lab Activities:**
- Advanced Concurrency Control Mechanisms Recall Challenge (65 min)
- Implement connection state management using tree structures

### Week 6: Advanced Routing Protocols
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path  
**Key Concepts:**
- Graph Traversal strategies for network discovery protocols
- Dijkstra's Algorithm for optimal routing path calculation in weighted networks

**Lab Activities:**
- Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithm Performance (90 min)
- Implement and benchmark shortest-path routing algorithms

### Week 7: Security in Protocol Design
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Analysis  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Functions for cryptographic applications in secure protocols
- Collision Resolution impact on protocol security and integrity

**Lab Activities:**
- Analyzing Cryptographic Hash Function Vulnerabilities Through Collision Attack Simulation (140 min)
- Implement secure protocol authentication mechanisms

### Week 8: Protocol Performance Optimization
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
**Key Concepts:**
- Hash Function optimization for high-performance protocol implementations
- Load Factor management for maintaining protocol performance under load

**Lab Activities:**
- Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Memory-Constrained Environments (195 min)
- Protocol performance profiling and optimization
