syllabus_content:
# COURSE SYLLABUS

## CS 4850: Building Resilient Distributed Systems: From Theory to Production

**Semester:** Spring 2024  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 3410 (Computer Systems Organization), CS 3110 (Data Structures and Functional Programming)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:10-11:00 AM  

**Teaching Assistants:**  
- [TA Name 1] - [email] - Office Hours: [times]
- [TA Name 2] - [email] - Office Hours: [times]

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This hands-on course explores the design, implementation, and deployment of fault-tolerant distributed systems that can withstand real-world failures. Students will build multiple distributed applications from scratch, learning to handle network partitions, server crashes, and scaling challenges through practical projects. The course emphasizes production-ready solutions, covering consistency models, replication strategies, load balancing, and monitoring systems. Students will work with modern tools like Docker, Kubernetes, message queues, and distributed databases while implementing consensus algorithms, distributed caching systems, and microservices architectures. Through weekly coding assignments and a capstone project deploying a multi-service application to cloud infrastructure, students gain deep understanding of trade-offs between consistency, availability, and partition tolerance.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement distributed systems that gracefully handle various failure modes including network partitions, node crashes, and Byzantine faults

• Apply consensus algorithms, replication strategies, and load balancing techniques to build production-ready scalable applications  

• Develop expertise in containerization, orchestration, and cloud deployment while mastering distributed systems monitoring and debugging methodologies

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1-2: Foundations and System Analysis
**Topics:** Course introduction, distributed systems fundamentals, performance analysis foundations
- **Module:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing upper bounds of algorithm growth rates as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - Measurement of computational steps required by an algorithm relative to input size, expressed in Big O terms
- **Activity:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Dissecting Sorting Performance (110 minutes)
- 
### Week 3-4: Data Structures for Distributed Systems
**Topics:** Core data structures, hash-based distributed storage, consistent hashing
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Analysis
  - Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table buckets
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including open addressing and closed addressing
- **Activity:** Advanced Memory Management Terms and Concepts Recall Challenge (120 minutes)
- 
### Week 5-6: Graph Algorithms and Network Topologies
**Topics:** Network modeling, shortest path algorithms for routing, network partition detection
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - greedy approach for finding shortest paths from single source in non-negative weighted graphs using priority queue
  - Bellman-Ford Algorithm - dynamic programming solution that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles in O(VE) time
- **Activity:** Distributed System Bottleneck Analysis: Microservices Performance Investigation (120 minutes)
- 
### Week 7-8: Tree Structures and Hierarchical Systems
**Topics:** Distributed tree structures, hierarchical naming systems, distributed indexing
- **Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
  - Binary Search Property: Left subtree contains values less than root, right subtree contains values greater than root
  - Tree Traversal Methods: In-order, pre-order, and post-order traversal algorithms for accessing tree nodes systematically
- **Activity:** Database Query Performance Analysis and Optimization (100 minutes)
- 
### Week 9-10: Consensus Algorithms and Fault Tolerance
**Topics:** Paxos, Raft consensus, Byzantine fault tolerance, leader election
- **Activity:** Distributed Systems Consensus Algorithm Memory Challenge (75 minutes)
- **Activity:** Analyzing Security Vulnerabilities in Multi-Threaded Banking System Code (105 minutes)
- - **Project Milestone:** Consensus algorithm implementation due

### Week 11-12: Production Systems and Case Studies
**Topics:** Real-world distributed systems, failure analysis, chaos engineering
- **Activity:** Analyzing Distributed System Fault Tolerance: Netflix Chaos Engineering Case Study Breakdown (3.5 hours)
- 
### Week 13: System Integration and Deployment
**Topics:** Kubernetes orchestration, service meshes, production deployment strategies
- **Activity:** Programming Language Syntax Component Memory Challenge (50 minutes)
- **Activity:** Python Data Types Memory Match Challenge (60 minutes)
- 
### Week 14: Advanced Topics and Review
**Topics:** Emerging trends, system optimization, performance tuning
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Memorization Challenge (55 minutes)
- 
### Week 15: Final Projects and Presentations
**Topics:** Project demonstrations, peer review, course wrap-up
- **Final project presentations**
- **Course evaluation and reflection**

---

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

### Grading Distribution
| Assessment Type | Weight | Points |
|-----------------|--------|--------|
| Quizzes | 15% | 150 |
| Projects | 40% | 400 |
| Presentation | 20% | 200 |
| Final Exam | 25% | 250 |
| **Total** | **100%** | **1000** |

### Assessment Details

**1. Quizzes (150 points total)**
- **Advanced Algorithm Analysis and Design Quiz** (100 points)
- Weekly concept checks and lab assessments (50 points)
- Format: Online, timed assessments focusing on theoretical concepts

**2. Projects (400 points total)**
- **Personal Task Manager Application** (100 points) - Weeks 3-5
  - Build a distributed task management system with fault tolerance
- **Distributed Key-Value Store** (150 points) - Weeks 6-9  
  - Implement consensus algorithms and replication strategies
- **Fault-Tolerant Chat System** (150 points) - Weeks 10-13
  - Create auto-scaling microservices with monitoring

**3. Presentation (200 points)**
- **Advanced Distributed Systems Architecture: Design and Implementation Strategy Presentation** (200 points)
- Final project presentation demonstrating capstone distributed application
- 15-minute presentation + 5-minute Q&A
- Peer evaluation component included

**4. Final Exam (250 points)**
- **Advanced Algorithms Design and Analysis Comprehensive Exam** (250 points)
- Comprehensive exam covering theoretical concepts and practical applications
- Focus on CAP theorem, consensus algorithms, fault tolerance strategies
- Mix of multiple choice, short answer, and design problems

## COURSE POLICIES

### Late Assignment Policy
- Projects: 10% penalty per day late, maximum 3 days
- Presentations: No make-ups without prior arrangement
- Quizzes: Must be completed within designated time windows

### Technology Requirements

- Recommended: "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" by Martin Kleppmann
- All software tools are free/open source or available through university licenses

## Course Description

This survey course explores how artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms are revolutionizing diverse computational domains beyond traditional CS applications. Students examine AI/ML implementations across scientific computing, digital humanities, bioinformatics, financial technology, gaming, and cybersecurity. The course emphasizes understanding algorithmic choices, data preprocessing challenges, and evaluation metrics specific to each domain. Through case studies and hands-on projects, students analyze real-world applications including protein folding prediction, algorithmic trading systems, procedural content generation, anomaly detection in network security, and natural language processing for historical text analysis. The curriculum balances theoretical foundations with practical implementation, covering supervised and unsupervised learning, neural networks, reinforcement learning, and emerging paradigms like federated learning and explainable AI. Students develop critical thinking skills to assess algorithmic bias, ethical implications, and scalability challenges across different domains. By semester's end, students possess a comprehensive understanding of how AI/ML techniques adapt to domain-specific constraints, data characteristics, and success metrics, preparing them to become versatile practitioners capable of applying computational intelligence to novel problem spaces.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Evaluate and compare** AI/ML algorithmic approaches across at least five distinct computational domains

# Collaborative Software Development in Virtual Teams

The course emphasizes remote communication protocols, asynchronous development practices, and cross-cultural team dynamics that mirror modern tech industry practices. # FORMAL VERIFICATION AND CORRECTNESS IN LARGE-SCALE SOFTWARE SYSTEMS
**CS 4XX | Spring 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Meeting:** [Days/Times]  

**Prerequisites:** Data Structures and Algorithms, Discrete Mathematics, Programming Languages  
**Textbook:** *Formal Methods: State of the Art and New Directions* by Dines Bjørner and Martin C. Henson (recommended)

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course explores the mathematical foundations and theoretical frameworks for proving software correctness in complex, distributed systems. Students will study formal specification languages, model checking techniques, and theorem proving methodologies used to verify critical software properties. The curriculum emphasizes the theoretical underpinnings of program verification, including Hoare logic, temporal logic, and invariant analysis. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, students will examine how formal methods can guarantee system reliability, security, and performance in enterprise-level applications. Topics include abstract interpretation, bounded model checking, symbolic execution, and compositional verification techniques. The course addresses the theoretical challenges of scaling verification approaches to real-world software architectures, including microservices, concurrent systems, and safety-critical applications. Students will analyze case studies from aerospace, financial systems, and medical device software where formal verification is mandated. By the end of the course, students will understand the mathematical theory behind automated verification tools and the fundamental limitations of decidability in software verification problems.

---

## COURSE OBJECTIVES

Upon completion of this course, students will be able to:

• Master formal specification languages and mathematical models for expressing software correctness properties  
• Apply theoretical verification techniques including model checking, theorem proving, and abstract interpretation to analyze software systems  
• Develop expertise in compositional verification methodologies for reasoning about large-scale distributed software architectures  

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundational Data Structures for Verification
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
- Binary Search Tree Property: For any node, all values in left subtree are smaller, all values in right subtree are larger
- Tree Traversal Methods: In-order (left, root, right), pre-order (root, left, right), and post-order (left, right, root) traversal algorithms
- **Activity:** Programming Language Syntax Memory Match (50 minutes)

### Week 2: Graph-Based System Modeling
**Module:** Graph Algorithms and Traversal Techniques  
- Graph representation - adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists with trade-offs for different use cases
- Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive and iterative implementations for tree traversal, cycle detection, and connected components

### Week 3: Search Algorithms in State Space Exploration
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search  
- Graph representation using adjacency lists and adjacency matrices - data structures to store vertex relationships and edge connections
- Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-by-level traversal using queues that explores all neighbors before moving to next depth level
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Vocabulary and Notation Recall Challenge (65 minutes)

### Week 4: Algorithmic Complexity in Verification
**Module:** Advanced Sorting Algorithms: Merge Sort and Quick Sort  
- Divide-and-conquer paradigm: Problem-solving approach that recursively breaks problems into smaller subproblems
- Recurrence relations: Mathematical expressions describing recursive algorithm complexity in terms of input size
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Memorization and Recognition Challenge (50 minutes)

### Week 5: Hash-Based State Storage and Lookup
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Analysis  
- Hash Function: A function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
- Load Factor: The ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical for predicting performance
- **Activity:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Dissecting Sorting Performance (130 minutes)

### Week 6: Collision Resolution in State Management
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
- Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing entries uniformly across the hash table
- Load Factor - Ratio of occupied slots to total table size, critical metric affecting hash table performance and resize decisions

### Week 7: Optimization in Verification Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems  
- Dijkstra's Algorithm - greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from single source in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
- Bellman-Ford Algorithm - dynamic programming solution that detects negative cycles while computing shortest paths from single source
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Big O Performance (75 minutes)

### Week 8: Midterm Examination Period
- **Assessment:** Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Practical Exam (100 points)

### Week 9: Performance Analysis in Distributed Systems
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Performance Analysis  
- Hash Function - A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices
- Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing methods
- **Activity:** Python Data Types Memory Card Challenge (45 minutes)

### Week 10: System Architecture Analysis
**Activity:** Distributed System Failure Analysis: Dissecting the 2017 GitLab Database Incident (140 minutes)

### Week 11: Network Protocol Verification
**Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies  
- Hash Function - A deterministic algorithm that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to minimize collisions and distribute keys uniformly
- Load Factor - The ratio of filled slots to total table size (α = n/m), critical for analyzing performance and determining when to resize the table
- **Activity:** TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions and Headers Memorization Challenge (55 minutes)

# COURSE SYLLABUS
## CS 4980: Distributed Systems Orchestration: Building Resilient Network Architectures

**Semester:** Spring 2024  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** CS 3300 (Computer Networks), CS 3400 (Operating Systems), CS 3500 (Database Systems)  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This capstone course challenges students to design, implement, and deploy enterprise-grade distributed systems that can withstand real-world network failures and scale dynamically. Students work in teams to architect complete networked applications spanning multiple cloud regions, implementing advanced concepts like consensus algorithms, service mesh architectures, and chaos engineering. The course culminates in a semester-long project where teams build a fault-tolerant distributed application (such as a distributed database, real-time collaboration platform, or IoT sensor network) while documenting performance under various network conditions including partitions, latency spikes, and node failures. Students gain hands-on experience with container orchestration (Kubernetes), service discovery, load balancing strategies, and network monitoring tools. Weekly design reviews simulate industry practices, requiring teams to justify architectural decisions, demonstrate system resilience through controlled failure injection, and present scalability benchmarks. The final deliverable includes a fully deployed system, comprehensive disaster recovery procedures, and a detailed post-mortem analysis of network-related challenges encountered during development.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement distributed systems that gracefully handle network partitions, node failures, and varying latency conditions  
• Apply industry-standard tools and practices including container orchestration, service mesh deployment, and chaos engineering principles to build resilient networked applications  
• Demonstrate proficiency in network performance analysis, bottleneck identification, and optimization strategies through comprehensive system monitoring and benchmarking  

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundations of Distributed Systems Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation - mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity

- **Activities:**
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Algorithms Through Time Complexity Evaluation (75 min)
  - Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Drill (90 min)
- **Deliverables:** Team formation, project topic selection

### Week 2: Network Routing and Path Optimization
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees

- **Activities:**
  - Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Search Implementations (60 min)
- **Deliverables:** Project proposal draft

### Week 3: Advanced Network Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
- **Concepts:**
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach for finding shortest paths from a single source in graphs with non-negative edge weights using priority queues
  - Bellman-Ford Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution that handles negative edge weights and detects negative cycles in O(VE) time
- **Activities:**
  - Comparative Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Performance Under Varying Data Conditions (150 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz (100 points)

### Week 4: Graph Traversal and System Discovery
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- **Concepts:**
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - systematic level-by-level graph exploration using queues, optimal for unweighted shortest paths
  - Depth-First Search (DFS) - recursive graph exploration that goes as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for cycle detection and topological sorting
- **Activities:**
  - Analyzing Algorithmic Complexity and Optimization Trade-offs in Sorting Algorithm Implementations (135 min)

### Week 5: Distributed Hash Tables and Data Distribution
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Performance Analysis
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across hash table indices
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining (linked lists) and open addressing methods

syllabus_content:
# Digital Forensics and Cybercrime Investigation Fundamentals
**Course Code:** CS 485 | **Credits:** 3 | **Prerequisites:** CS 201 (Data Structures), CS 220 (Computer Systems)

## Course Description

This course introduces students to the fascinating world of digital forensics and cybercrime investigation through hands-on exploration of real-world security incidents. Students will learn to think like digital detectives, uncovering evidence from compromised systems, analyzing malware behavior, and reconstructing cyber attack timelines. The course covers fundamental concepts in computer security while emphasizing practical investigation techniques used by law enforcement and incident response teams. Topics include evidence preservation, file system analysis, network traffic examination, mobile device forensics, and legal considerations in digital investigations. Students will work with industry-standard forensic tools and participate in simulated crime scene investigations using virtual environments. The curriculum balances technical skills with critical thinking, teaching students to identify attack vectors, assess security vulnerabilities, and communicate findings effectively. Through case studies of famous cybercrimes and interactive lab exercises, students gain exposure to various attack methodologies including social engineering, malware deployment, and data exfiltration. This introductory course requires no prior security experience but provides a solid foundation for advanced cybersecurity studies or careers in digital forensics, incident response, or security analysis.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master fundamental digital forensics techniques** including evidence collection, preservation, and analysis using industry-standard tools

• **Apply systematic investigation methodologies** to reconstruct cybercrime scenarios and identify attack vectors in simulated environments  

• **Develop practical expertise** in analyzing file systems, network traffic, and malware while understanding legal and ethical considerations in digital investigations

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation Concepts and Performance Analysis
**Topic:** Introduction to Digital Forensics and Algorithmic Foundations
- **Module:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis and Big O Notation
  - Big O Notation - mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm performance as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - measurement of computational time required by an algorithm relative to input size
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Speed Drill (50 minutes)
- 
### Week 2: Data Storage and Hash Analysis Fundamentals  
**Topic:** Digital Evidence Storage and Hash Function Applications
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval
  - Hash Function: A function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size values (hash codes) used as array indices
  - Collision Resolution: Techniques to handle when multiple keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Memory Palace Creation (45 minutes)
- 
### Week 3: Advanced Hash Techniques for Digital Evidence
**Topic:** Hash-based Evidence Verification and Data Integrity
- **Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies  
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute data uniformly across the hash table
  - Load Factor - Ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical metric affecting performance and collision frequency
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Flash Card Drill with Visual Verification (35 minutes)
- 
### Week 4: File System Analysis and Tree Structures
**Topic:** File System Forensics and Hierarchical Data Analysis
- **Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
  - Binary Search Tree Property: Left subtree contains values less than root, right subtree contains values greater than root
  - Tree Traversals: In-order (left-root-right), pre-order (root-left-right), post-order (left-right-root) visiting patterns
- **Activity:** Python Data Types Memory Match Challenge (45 minutes)
- 
### Week 5: Network Traffic Analysis and Graph Theory
**Topic:** Network Forensics and Connection Analysis
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
  - Graph representation - Methods for storing graphs in memory including adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists with trade-offs analysis
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-order traversal algorithm using queues, optimal for unweighted shortest paths and connected component detection
- **Activity:** Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture (150 minutes)
- 
### Week 6: Advanced Network Investigation Techniques
**Topic:** Deep Packet Analysis and Attack Reconstruction  
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Solutions
  - Graph Representation: Adjacency matrices vs adjacency lists, memory usage implications, and performance trade-offs for different graph densities
  - Depth-First Search (DFS): Recursive and iterative implementations, applications in topological sorting, cycle detection, and connected components identification
- **Activity:** Debugging Algorithm Efficiency: Analyzing Sorting Performance Through Code Trace and Complexity Comparison (90 minutes)
- 
### Week 7: Optimization Techniques in Digital Investigations
**Topic:** Efficient Investigation Methodologies and Case Optimization
- **Module:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
  - Optimal Substructure - A problem exhibits optimal substructure if an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems
  - Overlapping Subproblems - The same subproblems are solved multiple times in a naive recursive approach
- **Activity:** Database Query Performance Analysis Through Execution Plan Comparison (60 minutes)
- 
### Week 8: **Midterm Exam Week**
- **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz
- Review session and practical skills demonstration

### Week 9: System Architecture and Forensic Analysis
**Topic:** Enterprise System Forensics and Architecture Analysis
- **Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation (Review and Advanced Applications)
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity  
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required as a function of input size, typically expressed in Big O notation
- **Activity:** Distributed System Architecture Analysis: Decomposing Netflix's Microservices Failure Cascade (170 minutes)
- 
### Week 10: Performance Analysis in Forensic Investigations
**Topic:** Optimizing Investigation Workflows and Resource Management
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies (Advanced Applications)
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute data uniformly across available slots
  - Load Factor - Ratio of occupied slots to total table size, critical metric affecting performance and determining when to resize
- **Activity:** Analyzing Algorithm Complexity Trade-offs in Real-World Database Query Optimization (110 minutes)
- 
### Week 11-12: **Major Project DevelopmentTopic:** Comprehensive Cybercrime Investigation Simulation
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge (45 minutes)
- **Project Work:** Library Management System Design and Implementation (adapted for forensic evidence management)

### Week 13: **Case Study Analysis and Presentation PreparationTopic:** Real-World Cybercrime Cases and Professional Communication
- Review of famous cybercrime investigations
- **Assessment:** Introduction to Programming Concepts Presentation (adapted for digital forensics concepts)

### Week 14: **Student PresentationsTopic:** Forensic Investigation Case Presentations
- Student presentation of investigation findings
- Peer review and professional feedback

### Week 15: **Portfolio Completion and Course ReviewTopic:** Professional Portfolio Development and Industry Preparation
- **Assessment:** Full-Stack Web Application Development Portfolio (adapted for forensic tool development)
- Course wrap-up and career guidance

### Week 16: **Final Exam**
- **Assessment:** Advanced Distributed Systems Design and Implementation Exam (adapted for comprehensive digital forensics concepts)

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage | Description |
|----------------|--------|------------|-------------|
| **Quizzes & Participation** | 100 | 20% | Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz + weekly participation |
| **Presentations** | 100 | 20% | Introduction to Programming Concepts Presentation (forensics-focused) |
| **Major Project** | 100 | 25% | Library Management System Design and Implementation (evidence management focus) |
| **Portfolio** | 100 | 20% | Full-Stack Web Application Development Portfolio (forensic tools) |
| **Final Exam** | 100 | 15% | Advanced Distributed Systems Design and Implementation Exam |
| **Total** | **500** | **100%** | |

### Late Assignment Policy
- Assignments submitted within 24 hours of deadline: 10% penalty
- Assignments submitted 24-48 hours late: 20% penalty  
- Assignments more than 48 hours late: 50% penalty
- No assignments accepted more than one week late without prior arrangement

### Accommodations
Students with documented disabilities who may need accommodations should schedule an appointment with the instructor as soon as possible. All discussions will remain confidential. Students with disabilities who require accommodations should also contact the Disability Services Office.

### Communication
- Primary communication via course management system
- Email responses within 24-48 hours during business days
- Office hours available for individual consultation
- Course Discord server for peer collaboration (optional)

### Professional Standards
As future cybersecurity professionals, students are expected to:
- Maintain confidentiality of all simulated case materials
- Demonstrate ethical behavior in all forensic activities  
- Communicate findings clearly and professionally
- Show respect for legal and privacy considerations

---

**Important Note:** This course involves simulated cybercrime scenarios for educational purposes only. All activities must be conducted within the provided controlled environment. Any unauthorized use of course techniques on real systems is strictly prohibited and may result in academic discipline and/or legal consequences.

# Course Syllabus
## CS 3345: Algorithmic Problem Solving Through Competitive Programming

**Semester:** Fall 2024  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 2340 (Data Structures and Algorithms), CS 1337 (Computer Science II)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 2:00-2:50 PM  

**Teaching Assistant:** [Name]  
**Lab Sessions:** T/R 2:00-3:15 PM  

---

## Course Description

This comprehensive course bridges theoretical algorithmic concepts with practical implementation skills through the lens of competitive programming challenges. Students will explore advanced data structures, graph algorithms, dynamic programming, and mathematical optimization techniques while developing efficient, contest-ready solutions. The curriculum emphasizes algorithmic thinking, time-space complexity analysis, and code optimization strategies essential for technical interviews and software development careers. Students will tackle progressively challenging problems from platforms like Codeforces, AtCoder, and ICPC archives, learning to recognize problem patterns and select appropriate algorithmic approaches. The course covers string algorithms, number theory applications, geometric algorithms, and advanced topics like segment trees and network flows. Weekly programming contests simulate real competitive environments, fostering quick problem analysis and implementation skills. Students will also study algorithm correctness proofs, worst-case analysis, and debugging strategies for complex algorithmic solutions. By course completion, students will have built a comprehensive toolkit of algorithmic techniques, developed strong coding proficiency in C++ or Java, and gained confidence in solving novel computational problems under time constraints, preparing them for technical careers and advanced algorithms coursework.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master advanced algorithmic techniques** including dynamic programming, graph traversal, string processing, and mathematical algorithms through hands-on competitive programming challenges

• **Apply comprehensive problem-solving methodologies** to analyze complex computational problems, select optimal data structures, and implement efficient solutions with rigorous time-space complexity consideration

• **Develop practical expertise** in algorithmic implementation, code optimization, and debugging strategies while building proficiency in contest programming environments and technical interview preparation

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations and Complexity Analysis
- **Topics:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm runtime as input size approaches infinity
  - Asymptotic Analysis - Method for describing algorithm performance characteristics by focusing on growth rates rather than exact runtime
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Classification Memory Drill (60 minutes)
- 
### Week 2: Hash Tables and Efficient Data Access
- **Topics:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution - Strategies to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Algorithms Through Empirical Testing and Complexity Decomposition (135 minutes)
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #1

### Week 3: Advanced Hash Table Concepts
- **Topics:** Hash Tables and Load Factor Management
  - Hash Function: A mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing elements uniformly across the hash table
  - Load Factor: The ratio of stored elements to table size (α = n/m), critical for predicting performance and determining when to resize
- **Activity:** Advanced Algorithm Complexity Notation Recall Challenge (90 minutes)
- 
### Week 4: Binary Search Trees
- **Topics:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
  - Binary Search Tree Property - left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
  - Tree Traversal Algorithms - systematic methods for visiting all nodes (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order)
- **Activity:** Algorithmic Complexity Analysis of Sorting Algorithm Variants (110 minutes)
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #2

### Week 5: Graph Fundamentals
- **Topics:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
  - Graph representation - adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists with their respective trade-offs in memory usage and access time
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-order traversal using queues to explore nodes at increasing distances from source
- 
### Week 6: Advanced Graph Traversal
- **Topics:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
  - Graph representation - adjacency lists vs adjacency matrices, weighted vs unweighted graphs, directed vs undirected graphs
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - level-order traversal using queues, shortest path in unweighted graphs, connected components
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #3
- **Assessment:Midterm Exam** (100 points)

### Week 7: Shortest Path Algorithms
- **Topics:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - greedy algorithm for finding shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in weighted graphs with non-negative edges
  - Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) - subgraph that connects all vertices with minimum total edge weight, solved by Kruskal's (edge-based) or Prim's (vertex-based) algorithms
- 
### Week 8: Dynamic Programming Foundations
- **Topics:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization
  - Optimal Substructure: Property where optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems, enabling recursive decomposition
  - Overlapping Subproblems: Recursive algorithms that solve identical subproblems multiple times, creating opportunities for memoization
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #4

### Week 9: Advanced Dynamic Programming
- **Topics:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization (Advanced Applications)
  - Optimal Substructure - property where optimal solutions contain optimal solutions to subproblems
  - Overlapping Subproblems - recursive algorithms that repeatedly solve identical subproblems
- **Activity:** Architectural Analysis of Distributed System Performance Bottlenecks in a Multi-Tier E-commerce Application (3 hours)
- 
### Week 10: String Algorithms and Pattern Matching
- **Topics:** String processing algorithms, KMP algorithm, suffix arrays
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #5
- **Assessment:Programming Contest Portfolio Check** (25 points)

### Week 11: Number Theory and Mathematical Algorithms
- **Topics:** Modular arithmetic, prime numbers, combinatorics in competitive programming
- 
### Week 12: Advanced Data Structures
- **Topics:** Segment trees, binary indexed trees, advanced tree structures
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #6

### Week 13: Network Flow and Advanced Graph Algorithms
- **Topics:** Maximum flow algorithms, bipartite matching, advanced graph theory
- **Assessment:Discussion: Software Architecture Trade-offs in Large-Scale Systems** (100 points)

### Week 14: Geometric Algorithms
- **Topics:** Computational geometry, convex hull, line intersection algorithms
- **Contest:** Weekly Programming Contest #7

### Week 15: Contest Strategy and Optimization
- **Topics:** Contest strategies, code optimization, debugging techniques
- **Assessment:Final Programming Contest Portfolio** (100 points)
- 
### Week 16: Finals Week
- **Assessment:Final Comprehensive Exam** (100 points)

| **Discussion Participation** | Software Architecture Trade-offs in Large-Scale Systems | 100 | 10% |

# Computational Intelligence: From Biological Inspiration to Algorithmic Innovation
**CS 3XX | Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

## Course Description

This foundational course explores how nature-inspired computational methods form the backbone of modern artificial intelligence systems. Students will discover how biological processes like neural networks, evolutionary mechanisms, and swarm behaviors translate into powerful algorithmic solutions for complex computational problems. The course bridges theoretical computer science with practical AI applications, covering neural network architectures, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, and fuzzy logic systems. Through hands-on programming projects, students will implement bio-inspired algorithms from scratch, understanding both their mathematical foundations and real-world applications in machine learning, optimization, and pattern recognition.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master Bio-Inspired Algorithm Design**: Design and implement nature-inspired algorithms including neural networks, genetic algorithms, and swarm intelligence methods
2. **Apply Computational Analysis**: Use computational complexity analysis and algorithmic optimization techniques to evaluate and improve nature-inspired AI systems  
3. **Develop Practical AI Expertise**: Translate biological processes into computational models for solving real-world machine learning problems

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1-2: Foundations of Computational Intelligence
**Topics:**
- Introduction to bio-inspired computing
- Mathematical foundations and complexity analysis
- Programming environment setup

**Activity:** Binary Number System Memorization and Recognition Drill (45 minutes)

### Week 3-4: Data Structures for AI Systems
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- Binary Search Property: Left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent
- Tree Traversal: Systematic methods for visiting every node (inorder, preorder, postorder, level-order)

**Activity:** Python Data Type Memory Challenge: Flashcard Classification Drill (35 minutes)

### Week 5-6: Graph-Based Intelligence Models
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
- Breadth-First Search (BFS): Algorithm that explores graph vertices level by level, using a queue data structure to maintain frontier nodes
- Depth-First Search (DFS): Algorithm that explores graph vertices by following paths as deep as possible before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack

**Activity:** Programming Language Syntax Elements Memory Match (50 minutes)

### Week 7-8: Efficient Data Storage and Retrieval
**Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Collision Resolution Strategies
- Hash Functions: Mathematical functions that map keys to array indices, designed to minimize collisions and distribute data uniformly
- Separate Chaining: Collision resolution using linked lists or dynamic arrays at each table position to store multiple key-value pairs

**Activity:** Memory Palace for Python Keywords and Operators (50 minutes)

### Week 9: Midterm Examination Period
- Review and consolidation of foundational concepts
- Midterm project presentations

### Week 10-11: Neural Network Foundations
**Topics:**
- Biological neurons vs. artificial neurons
- Perceptron and multi-layer architectures
- Backpropagation algorithm

**Activity:** Python Data Type Classification Memory Match (40 minutes)

### Week 12-13: Evolutionary Computation
**Topics:**
- Genetic algorithms and evolutionary strategies
- Selection, crossover, and mutation operators
- Fitness landscapes and optimization

**Activity:** Programming Language Syntax Element Identification Challenge (30 minutes)

### Week 14-15: Swarm Intelligence and Fuzzy Systems
**Topics:**
- Particle swarm optimization
- Ant colony optimization
- Fuzzy logic and approximate reasoning

**Activity:** Binary Number Memory Drill with Visual Flashcards (45 minutes)

### Week 16: Final Projects and Course Wrap-up
- Final project presentations
- Integration of bio-inspired methods
- Future directions in computational intelligence

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Points | Percentage | Due Dates |
|----------------|--------|------------|-----------|
| **Quizzes** | 100 | 15% | Weeks 4, 8, 12 |
| **Discussion Participation** | 100 | 15% | Ongoing |
| **Portfolio Projects** | 100 | 20% | Week 9 |
| **Major Project** | 100 | 25% | Week 15 |
| **Final Presentation** | 100 | 25% | Week 16 |
| **Total** | **500** | **100%** | |

### Assessment Details

**Data Structures and Algorithm Analysis Quiz (100 points, 15%)**
- Three quizzes covering fundamental concepts
- Focus on computational complexity and algorithmic thinking
- 33.3 points each

**Introduction to Programming Languages Discussion (100 points, 15%)**
- Weekly discussion posts on bio-inspired computing topics
- Peer responses and engagement with course material
- Critical analysis of research papers and case studies

**Beginner Programming Portfolio: Personal Calculator Project (100 points, 20%)**
- Implementation of bio-inspired algorithms from scratch
- Documentation of design decisions and complexity analysis
- Progressive development throughout first half of semester

**Distributed Database System with ACID Compliance and Performance Optimization (100 points, 25%)**
- Major project implementing a comprehensive bio-inspired AI system
- Integration of multiple computational intelligence techniques
- Performance evaluation and optimization analysis

**Advanced System Architecture Design Presentation (100 points, 25%)**
- Final presentation of major project
- Technical demonstration and Q&A session
- Peer evaluation component

# Probabilistic Reasoning and Uncertainty Quantification in Intelligent Systems

**Department:** Computer Science  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** CS 315 (Data Structures), MATH 340 (Probability and Statistics), MATH 220 (Linear Algebra)  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  

---

## Course Description

This course explores the mathematical foundations of how intelligent systems handle uncertainty and make decisions under incomplete information. Students will delve into the theoretical underpinnings of probabilistic models, Bayesian inference, and uncertainty quantification techniques that power modern AI systems. The curriculum covers advanced topics including probabilistic graphical models, variational inference, Monte Carlo methods, and information-theoretic approaches to learning. 

Emphasis is placed on understanding the mathematical rigor behind uncertainty representation in machine learning algorithms, from naive Bayes classifiers to sophisticated neural network architectures with uncertainty estimation. Students will analyze the theoretical trade-offs between computational efficiency and accuracy in probabilistic reasoning, explore the convergence properties of sampling algorithms, and investigate the philosophical implications of uncertainty in artificial intelligence. 

The course bridges probability theory, statistics, and computer science to provide a comprehensive understanding of how machines can reason about uncertain worlds. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and proof-based assignments, students develop expertise in designing and analyzing probabilistic algorithms that form the backbone of modern AI systems, including autonomous vehicles, medical diagnosis systems, and financial modeling applications.

---

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master** the mathematical foundations of probabilistic inference and develop proficiency in deriving and analyzing Bayesian learning algorithms  
• **Apply** advanced theoretical frameworks including variational methods and MCMC techniques to solve complex uncertainty quantification problems  
• **Develop** expertise in designing probabilistic models for real-world AI applications while understanding their theoretical limitations and convergence properties  

---

### Software
- Python 3.8+ with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, PyTorch
- Jupyter Notebooks
- Access to university computing cluster (provided)

### Hardware
- Laptop capable of running Python development environment

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Probability Theory
**Topics:** Sample spaces, random variables, probability distributions, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 1-2
**Activity:** Probability Review and Mathematical Foundations (45 minutes)

### Week 2: Bayesian Parameter Estimation
**Topics:** Maximum likelihood estimation, Bayesian parameter estimation, conjugate priors
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 3-4
**Activity:** Bayesian Inference Computational Workshop (50 minutes)

### Week 3: Probabilistic Classification
**Topics:** Naive Bayes, logistic regression, discriminative vs. generative models
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 5-6
**Due:** Problem Set 1 (Bayesian Fundamentals)

### Week 4: Linear Regression and Uncertainty
**Topics:** Bayesian linear regression, predictive distributions, model selection
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 7-8
**Activity:** Regression Uncertainty Quantification Lab (45 minutes)

### Week 5: Probabilistic Graphical Models I
**Topics:** Directed graphical models, conditional independence, D-separation
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 9-10
**Assessment:Midterm Exam** (100 points)

### Week 6: Probabilistic Graphical Models II
**Topics:** Undirected graphical models, Markov networks, factor graphs
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 11-12
**Activity:** Graphical Model Construction Workshop (35 minutes)

### Week 7: Exact Inference Algorithms
**Topics:** Variable elimination, message passing, junction tree algorithm
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 13-14
**Due:Lab Report: Probabilistic Model Implementation** (100 points)

### Week 8: Monte Carlo Methods
**Topics:** Rejection sampling, importance sampling, Markov Chain Monte Carlo
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 15-16
**Activity:** MCMC Convergence Analysis Lab (30 minutes)

### Week 9: Advanced MCMC Techniques
**Topics:** Gibbs sampling, Metropolis-Hastings, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 17
**Due:** Problem Set 2 (Inference Algorithms)

### Week 10: Variational Inference
**Topics:** Mean field approximation, variational Bayes, expectation maximization
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 18-19
**Activity:** Variational Methods Implementation (50 minutes)

### Week 11: Information Theory and Learning
**Topics:** Entropy, mutual information, information-theoretic model selection
**Readings:** Murphy Ch. 20
**Assessment:Project Proposal Presentations** (100 points)

### Week 12: Uncertainty in Neural Networks
**Topics:** Bayesian neural networks, dropout as approximation, uncertainty estimation
**Readings:** Selected papers (provided)
**Activity:** Neural Network Uncertainty Workshop (45 minutes)

### Week 13: Advanced Topics in Uncertainty Quantification
**Topics:** Gaussian processes, conformal prediction, calibration
**Readings:** Selected papers (provided)
**Due:** Problem Set 3 (Advanced Methods)

### Week 14: Applications and Case Studies
**Topics:** Medical diagnosis, autonomous systems, financial modeling
**Readings:** Selected case studies
**Activity:** Application Domain Analysis (45 minutes)

### Week 15: Final Project Presentations
**Assessment:Final Project Portfolio and Defense** (100 points)
**Due:Comprehensive Final Exam** (100 points)

---

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Title | Points | Percentage | Due Date |
|----------------|--------|---------|------------|----------|
| Exam | Midterm Exam | 100 | 20% | Week 5 |
| Exam | Comprehensive Final Exam | 100 | 20% | Finals Week |
| Lab Report | Probabilistic Model Implementation | 100 | 20% | Week 7 |
| Presentation | Project Proposal Presentations | 100 | 20% | Week 11 |
| Portfolio | Final Project Portfolio and Defense | 100 | 20% | Week 15 |

**Total Points:** 500  
**Grading Scale:** A (90-100%), B (80-89%), C (70-79%), D (60-69%), F (<60%)

### Assessment Details

**Midterm Exam (100 points):** Covers probability theory foundations, Bayesian inference, and basic probabilistic models. Includes both theoretical derivations and computational problems.

**Comprehensive Final Exam (100 points):** Cumulative exam emphasizing advanced topics including graphical models, inference algorithms, and uncertainty quantification methods. Heavy emphasis on mathematical proofs and algorithm analysis.

**Lab Report - Probabilistic Model Implementation (100 points):** Students implement and analyze a complete probabilistic model from scratch, including theoretical justification, algorithmic implementation, convergence analysis, and experimental validation.

**Project Proposal Presentations (100 points):** 15-minute presentations of final project proposals, including problem formulation, theoretical approach, implementation plan, and expected contributions. Peer feedback component included.

**Final Project Portfolio and Defense (100 points):** Comprehensive portfolio including: (1) novel probabilistic model or algorithm, (2) theoretical analysis with proofs, (3) complete implementation, (4) experimental validation, (5) written report, and (6) oral defense.

---

### Late Assignment Policy
- **0-24 hours late:** 10% penalty
- **24-48 hours late:** 25% penalty
- **48-72 hours late:** 50% penalty
- **More than 72 hours late:** Not accepted without prior arrangement

Exceptions will be made for documented emergencies or health issues.

### Accommodations
Students with documented disabilities should contact the Office of Disability Services to arrange appropriate accommodations. Please inform the instructor of any accommodations needed as early as possible in the semester.

### Grade Disputes
Students wishing to dispute a grade must submit a written explanation within one week of receiving the grade. The instructor will review and respond within one week.

### Course Evaluation
Student feedback is valued and will be collected mid-semester and at course completion. Constructive suggestions for improvement are always welcome.

# CS 4XX: Neural Architecture Search and Automated Model Design
**Course Syllabus - Fall 2024**

## Course Description

This intensive course explores the cutting-edge field of Neural Architecture Search (NAS), where students learn to design and implement algorithms that automatically discover optimal neural network architectures. Students will dive deep into evolutionary algorithms, reinforcement learning-based search methods, and differentiable architecture search techniques. The course combines rigorous theoretical foundations with hands-on implementation of NAS frameworks from scratch. Students will work with resource-constrained optimization problems, multi-objective architecture search, and hardware-aware neural design. Through intensive laboratory sessions, students will build their own NAS systems capable of discovering state-of-the-art architectures for computer vision, natural language processing, and specialized domains. The curriculum emphasizes understanding the mathematical principles behind search spaces, performance prediction, and architecture encoding schemes. Students will critically analyze seminal papers in automated machine learning and contribute to open-source NAS libraries. By course completion, students will have developed several working NAS implementations and conducted original research comparing different search strategies on novel datasets.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master** the design and implementation of neural architecture search algorithms using evolutionary strategies, reinforcement learning, and gradient-based methods
• **Apply** intensive optimization techniques to discover efficient neural architectures under hardware constraints and computational budgets  
• **Develop** practical expertise in automated machine learning pipelines and contribute novel architecture search methodologies to real-world applications

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations and Algorithm Analysis
- **Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Topics:** 
  - Big O Notation - Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size, including best, average, and worst-case analysis
- - **Reading:** Course introduction materials, Chapter 1

### Week 2: Search Space Design Fundamentals
- **Module:** Dynamic Programming: Optimization Through Memoization and Tabulation
- **Topics:**
  - Optimal Substructure - Property where optimal solutions contain optimal solutions to subproblems
  - Overlapping Subproblems - Recursive algorithm revisits the same subproblems multiple times
- - **Reading:** Chapter 2-3

### Week 3: Graph-Based Architecture Representation
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- **Topics:**
  - Graph Representation - Methods for storing graphs including adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and edge lists with their respective trade-offs
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-order traversal algorithm using queues, optimal for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs
- - **Assessment:** Quiz 1 - Algorithm fundamentals

### Week 4: Graph Search in Neural Networks
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
- **Topics:**
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Algorithm that explores graph nodes level by level, visiting all neighbors before moving to the next depth level, optimal for finding shortest unweighted paths
  - Depth-First Search (DFS) - Algorithm that explores graph nodes by going as deep as possible before backtracking, useful for topological sorting and cycle detection
- - **Assessment:** Lab Report 1 - Architecture encoding implementation

### Week 5: Efficient Search Space Management
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Analysis
- **Topics:**
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, used to compute array indices for hash table storage
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques to handle situations where multiple keys hash to the same array index, including chaining and open addressing methods
- - **Reading:** Mid-term paper assignments distributed

### Week 6: Advanced Hash-Based Optimization
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Techniques
- **Topics:**
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Load Factor - Ratio of stored elements to total table size, critical for predicting performance and determining when to resize
- - **Assessment:** Discussion - NAS methodology comparison

### Week 7: Shortest Path Algorithms in NAS
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path and Minimum Spanning Trees
- **Topics:**
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm - Greedy approach for finding shortest paths from a single source vertex using priority queues
  - Floyd-Warshall Algorithm - Dynamic programming solution for computing shortest paths between all pairs of vertices
- - **Assessment:** Midterm Project Checkpoint

### Week 8: **SPRING BREAK**

### Week 9: Advanced Search Strategies
- **Module:** Hash Tables: Implementation and Performance Analysis
- **Topics:**
  - Hash Function - Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution - Strategies for handling cases where multiple keys hash to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing
- - **Reading:** Advanced research papers

### Week 10: Reinforcement Learning for NAS
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies
- **Topics:**
  - Hash Function - Function that maps keys of arbitrary size to fixed-size array indices, ideally distributing keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling situations where multiple keys hash to the same array index, including chaining and open addressing methods
- - **Assessment:** Lab Report 2 - Multi-objective search

### Week 11: Differentiable Architecture Search
- **Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search (Advanced Applications)
- **Topics:** Advanced applications in continuous search spaces
- - **Assessment:** Portfolio Progress Review

### Week 12: Hardware-Aware NAS
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Collision Resolution (Performance Focus)
- **Topics:** Resource-constrained optimization
- - **Reading:** Final project specifications

### Week 13: Progressive and One-Shot Methods
- **Module:** Hash Tables and Collision Resolution Strategies (Advanced Techniques)
- **Topics:** Progressive shrinking and supernet training
- - **Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Quiz

### Week 14: Specialized Domain Applications
- **Module:** Dynamic Programming: Advanced Applications
- **Topics:** NAS for NLP, computer vision, and edge computing
- - **Assessment:** Final Portfolio Due

### Week 15: Research Presentations and Future Directions
- **Topics:** Student research presentations, emerging trends in AutoML
- - **Assessment:** Final Project Presentations

### Week 16: **FINALS WEEK**
- **Assessment:** Comprehensive Final Project Submission

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment Type | Title | Points | Due Date |
|----------------|-------|---------|----------|
| Quiz | Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz | 100 | Week 3 |
| Lab Report | Basic Python Programming Lab Report: Variables, Data Types, and Simple Operations | 100 | Week 4 |
| Discussion | Software Development Methodology Debate: Agile vs. Waterfall Implementation Strategies | 100 | Week 6 |
| Quiz | Advanced Algorithm Quiz | 100 | Week 13 |
| Portfolio | Full-Stack Web Application Development Portfolio | 100 | Week 14 |
| Project | Personal Task Management System with CLI Interface | 100 | Week 16 |

**Total Points:** 600

### Late Assignment Policy
Late assignments will be penalized 10% per day late, up to a maximum of 3 days. After 3 days, assignments will not be accepted unless extraordinary circumstances exist and prior arrangements have been made.

### Collaboration Policy
- **Allowed:** Discussing concepts, debugging strategies, and general approaches
- **Not Allowed:** Sharing code solutions, copying implementations, or submitting identical work
- **Required:** Cite all sources including papers, online resources, and AI assistance

### Technology Requirements
- Reliable internet connection for accessing cloud computing resources
- Laptop capable of running Python development environments
- GitHub account for version control and open-source contributions

### Accommodations
Students with documented disabilities should contact the Office of Disability Services to arrange appropriate accommodations. Please notify the instructor within the first two weeks of class to ensure adequate time for accommodation planning.

### Laboratory Safety
When using shared computing resources, follow all posted guidelines for equipment use and maintain appropriate cybersecurity practices when handling datasets and model implementations.

# Building Digital Solutions: Problem-Solving Through Code
## CS 1301 | Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours

### Course Information
**Class Schedule:** [Days, Times, Location]  
**Prerequisites:** None  

---

## Course Description
This course introduces students to computational thinking and programming through real-world problem-solving scenarios. Students learn to break down complex challenges into manageable components and implement solutions using Python programming language. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on coding experiences where students develop applications addressing everyday problems such as personal finance calculators, data organization tools, and interactive games. Rather than focusing solely on syntax and theory, this course bridges the gap between abstract programming concepts and practical applications. Students work individually and in teams to design, implement, test, and refine their solutions while learning fundamental programming constructs including variables, control structures, functions, and basic data structures. The course incorporates elements of user interface design, basic debugging techniques, and version control practices. By the end of the semester, students will have built a portfolio of functional programs and gained confidence in approaching new programming challenges.

## Learning Objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
• Design and implement Python programs to solve real-world problems using fundamental programming constructs  
• Apply computational thinking principles to break down complex problems into algorithmic solutions  
• Develop debugging skills and testing strategies to create reliable, well-documented code  
• Collaborate effectively on programming projects using version control and code review practices  
• Create user-friendly applications that demonstrate understanding of basic software development principles  

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Introduction to Programming and Problem-Solving
**Topics:** Course overview, computational thinking, Python basics, IDE setup  
**Activities:** Binary Number System Memory Card Match (45 min)  
**Readings:** Course materials Ch. 1-2  

### Week 2: Variables, Data Types, and Input/Output
**Topics:** Python syntax, variables, strings, numbers, user input  
**Activities:** Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Drill (45 min)  

### Week 3: Control Structures - Conditional Statements
**Topics:** If/elif/else statements, boolean logic, comparison operators  
**Activities:** Binary Number System Flashcard Memorization Challenge (50 min)  
**Project:** Decision-making calculator  

### Week 4: Control Structures - Loops
**Topics:** While loops, for loops, loop design patterns  
**Assessment:** Introduction to Programming Concepts Presentation (100 pts)  

### Week 5: Functions and Modular Programming
**Topics:** Function definition, parameters, return values, scope  
**Activities:** TCP/IP Protocol Stack Layer Functions Memorization Challenge (75 min)  
**Project:** Function library development  

### Week 6: Lists and Basic Data Structures
**Topics:** List operations, indexing, list methods, string manipulation  
**Assessment:** Introduction to Programming Fundamentals Exam (100 pts)  

### Week 7: File Operations and Data Persistence
**Topics:** Reading/writing files, CSV processing, data validation  
**Project:** Personal finance tracker application  

### Week 8: Error Handling and Debugging
**Topics:** Exception handling, debugging strategies, testing methodologies  

### Week 9: Dictionaries and Advanced Data Structures
**Topics:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Implementation and Collision Resolution  
**Concepts:**  
- Hash Function: Mathematical function that maps keys to array indices, designed to distribute keys uniformly across the hash table  
- Collision Resolution: Strategies to handle multiple keys mapping to the same index, including separate chaining and open addressing methods  
**Activities:** Security Vulnerability Analysis of Multi-Tier Web Application Architecture (2 hours)  

### Week 10: Algorithm Analysis and Efficiency
**Topics:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation  
**Concepts:**  
- Big O Notation: Mathematical notation describing the upper bound of algorithm growth rate as input size approaches infinity  
- Time Complexity: Measure of computational time required by an algorithm as a function of input size  
**Activities:** Algorithm Complexity Analysis: Big O Notation Comparison Lab (90 min)  
**Assessment:** Advanced Algorithm Design and Complexity Analysis Quiz (100 pts)  

### Week 11: Binary Search Trees
**Topics:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis  
**Concepts:**  
- Binary Search Tree Property: Left subtree contains values less than parent, right subtree contains values greater than parent  
- Tree Traversal Algorithms: Systematic methods for visiting all nodes (in-order, pre-order, post-order, level-order)  
**Activities:** Algorithmic Complexity Analysis: Big-O Performance Breakdown of Sorting Algorithm Implementations (90 min)  

### Week 12: Graph Algorithms - Basic Traversal
**Topics:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search

# COMPUTATIONAL PROBLEM SOLVING THROUGH ALGORITHMIC DESIGN
**CS 2350 | Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Schedule:** [Days, Times, Location]  
**Prerequisites:** CS 1400 (Introduction to Programming) and MATH 1210 (Calculus I)

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This foundational course explores the art and science of designing efficient algorithms to solve computational problems across diverse domains. Students learn to think algorithmically by analyzing problem structures, developing step-by-step solutions, and evaluating their computational complexity. The course covers fundamental algorithmic paradigms including divide-and-conquer, greedy approaches, dynamic programming, and backtracking through hands-on problem-solving sessions. 

Emphasis is placed on understanding how to break down complex problems into manageable subproblems and selecting appropriate algorithmic strategies. Students work with real-world scenarios from data processing, optimization, searching, and sorting to develop intuition for algorithmic thinking. The course bridges theoretical computer science concepts with practical implementation skills, teaching students to analyze time and space complexity while building confidence in creating original algorithmic solutions. 

Through collaborative projects and individual challenges, students develop the critical thinking skills necessary for advanced computer science coursework and software development careers. By the end of the semester, students will have internalized the fundamental principles of algorithmic design and gained experience applying these principles to novel computational challenges.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master core algorithmic design paradigms** and apply them to solve complex computational problems systematically
• **Develop proficiency in analyzing and comparing algorithm efficiency** using Big-O notation and complexity analysis  
• **Demonstrate the ability to design, implement, and optimize** original algorithms for real-world problem scenarios

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### Week 1: Foundation of Algorithmic Analysis
**Module:** Algorithm Analysis and Big O Notation
- **Concepts:**
  - Big O Notation - Upper bound representation of algorithm growth rate in worst-case scenarios
  - Time Complexity - Measure of computational time required as input size increases
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Time Complexity Decomposition (150 minutes)

### Week 2: Data Structure Fundamentals
**Module:** Binary Search Trees: Implementation and Analysis
- **Concepts:**
  - Binary Search Property: Each node's left subtree contains only values less than the node's value, and right subtree contains only values greater
  - Tree Traversal Algorithms: Systematic methods (in-order, pre-order, post-order) for visiting every node in a tree exactly once
- **Activity:** Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Recall Challenge (75 minutes)

### Week 3-4: Hash Table Design and Implementation
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design and Implementation
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function: A deterministic algorithm that maps arbitrary-sized data to fixed-size values, designed to distribute keys uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution: Techniques (chaining, open addressing, linear probing, quadratic probing) used to handle cases where multiple keys hash to the same table index
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Flashcard Memory Challenge (40 minutes)

### Week 5-6: Graph Representation and Basic Traversal
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search
- **Concepts:**
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS): Level-by-level graph traversal using a queue data structure, guaranteeing shortest path in unweighted graphs
  - Depth-First Search (DFS): Deep exploration traversal using a stack (recursive or iterative), useful for topological sorting and detecting cycles
- **Activity:** Memory Palace: Advanced Data Structure and Algorithm Complexity Recall Challenge (75 minutes)

### Week 7-8: Advanced Graph Algorithms
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path Finding
- **Concepts:**
  - Graph representation - Methods for storing graphs in memory including adjacency lists and adjacency matrices, with trade-offs in space and access time
  - Breadth-First Search (BFS) - Level-by-level graph exploration using queues, optimal for finding shortest unweighted paths and minimum spanning trees
- **Activity:** Analyzing Database Query Performance: Execution Plan Investigation (75 minutes)

### Week 9-10: Shortest Path Optimization
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Shortest Path Problems
- **Concepts:**
  - Dijkstra's Algorithm: Greedy approach using priority queues to find shortest paths from a single source in non-negative weighted graphs
  - Bellman-Ford Algorithm: Dynamic programming technique that detects negative cycles while computing shortest paths from a single source
- **Activity:** Algorithm Efficiency Analysis: Comparing Sorting Methods Through Time Complexity Decomposition (150 minutes)

### Week 11-12: Advanced Hash Table Optimization
**Module:** Hash Tables and Hash Functions: Design, Implementation, and Collision Resolution
- **Concepts:**
  - Hash Function - A mathematical function that maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, ideally distributing inputs uniformly across the hash table
  - Collision Resolution - Techniques for handling cases when different keys hash to the same index, including chaining and open addressing methods
- **Activity:** Binary Number System Flashcard Drill and Recognition Challenge (55 minutes)

### Week 13-14: Comprehensive Graph Algorithm Applications
**Module:** Graph Algorithms: Traversal and Shortest Path
- **Concepts:**
  - Graph representation using adjacency lists and adjacency matrices - different methods to store graph structure in memory
  - Depth-First Search (DFS) - systematic exploration of graph nodes by going as deep as possible before backtracking
- **Activity:** Security Vulnerability Analysis in Real-World Web Application Code (120 minutes)

### Week 15: Final Projects and Presentations
- Final project presentations
- Course review and synthesis
- **Activity:** Distributed System Failure Analysis: Decomposing the 2017 Amazon S3 Outage (150 minutes)

### Week 16: Finals Week
- Final examinations and project submissions

---

## ASSESSMENT PLAN

| Assessment | Type | Points | Due Date | Weight |
|------------|------|--------|----------|---------|
| Programming Fundamentals Quiz | Quiz | 100 | Week 3 | 20% |
| Distributed Hash Table Implementation | Project | 100 | Week 8 | 25% |
| Algorithm Design Pattern Analysis | Presentation | 100 | Week 12 | 20% |
| Distributed Systems Discussion | Discussion | 100 | Week 14 | 10% |
| Advanced Algorithmic Solutions Portfolio | Portfolio | 100 | Week 16 | 25% |

**Total Points:** 500  
**Grading Scale:** A (90-100%), B (80-89%), C (70-79%), D (60-69%), F (<60%)

### Assessment Descriptions

**Programming Fundamentals Quiz (Week 3):** Comprehensive assessment covering variables, data types, basic operations, and foundational algorithmic thinking concepts.

**Distributed Hash Table Implementation (Week 8):** Students design and implement a distributed hash table with fault tolerance mechanisms, demonstrating mastery of hash functions and collision resolution strategies.

**Algorithm Design Pattern Analysis Presentation (Week 12):** Students present analysis of software design patterns, their implementation, and their application to algorithmic problem-solving scenarios.

**Distributed Systems Discussion (Week 14):** Collaborative discussion forum analyzing the architecture design of a global content delivery network, incorporating learned algorithmic principles.

**Advanced Algorithmic Solutions Portfolio (Week 16):** Comprehensive portfolio showcasing full-stack application development with microservices architecture, demonstrating integration of all course concepts.

---

## COURSE POLICIES

### Late Assignment Policy
- Assignments submitted up to 24 hours late: 10% penalty
- Assignments submitted 24-48 hours late: 25% penalty
- Assignments submitted more than 48 hours late: 50% penalty
- No assignments accepted more than one week late without prior arrangement

- **Software:** Python 3.8+ or Java 11+, preferred IDE
- **Hardware:** Laptop capable of running development environments
- **Platform:** University learning management system account

### Extra Credit Policy
Limited extra credit opportunities may be offered at instructor discretion. Extra credit cannot substitute for major assignment completion but may improve borderline grades.

# Building Software That Matters: From Code to Community Impact

**Course Code:** CS 250  
**Credits:** 3  
**Semester:** Spring 2024  

---

## Course Description

This course introduces students to software engineering through the lens of creating meaningful applications that address real-world problems. Students learn fundamental programming concepts, software design principles, and collaborative development practices while building projects that serve actual community needs. The curriculum emphasizes human-centered design, where students interview stakeholders, gather requirements, and iterate on solutions based on user feedback. Core topics include version control with Git, agile development methodologies, testing strategies, code documentation, and deployment practices. Students work in small teams to develop web or mobile applications for local nonprofits, campus organizations, or social causes. The course bridges the gap between theoretical computer science concepts and practical software development, showing how technical skills can create positive social impact. By semester's end, students will have contributed to open-source projects, presented their work to community partners, and developed a portfolio demonstrating both technical competency and social responsibility.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Design and implement software solutions** for authentic community problems using fundamental programming concepts and software engineering principles
2. **Collaborate effectively** in development teams using industry-standard tools like Git, code reviews, and agile methodologies  
3. **Evaluate software projects** through the lens of social impact, user experience, and ethical considerations in technology design
