# Decision Trees to Deep Learning: Building Your First Intelligent Systems

## Course Description

This hands-on course demystifies machine learning by guiding students through the complete journey of building intelligent systems from scratch. Students begin with interpretable models like decision trees and logistic regression, then progressively advance to neural networks and deep learning architectures. Each week focuses on implementing one core algorithm while solving real-world problems across domains like healthcare, finance, and social media. The course emphasizes practical coding skills using Python libraries (scikit-learn, TensorFlow, pandas) alongside fundamental mathematical concepts. Students work on three major projects: predicting customer behavior, classifying medical images, and building a recommendation system. By semester's end, students will have constructed a portfolio of working machine learning applications and gained intuitive understanding of when and why different algorithms succeed or fail.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

• **Implement and Compare Algorithms:** Students will implement and compare supervised learning algorithms including decision trees, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks

• **Develop ML Pipelines:** Students will develop end-to-end machine learning pipelines encompassing data preprocessing, feature engineering, model training, validation, and deployment

• **Evaluate and Interpret Models:** Students will evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics and techniques, identifying overfitting, bias, and ethical considerations in algorithmic decision-making

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Course Foundation and Data Exploration
- **Topics:** Course overview, ML landscape, Python environment setup
- **Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) with Python: Uncovering Data Stories
  - Data Profiling: Systematic examination of dataset structure, completeness, and quality
  - Statistical Summarization: Computing and interpreting descriptive statistics
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real-World Datasets: Customer Purchase Behavior Analysis (45 min)
- **Due:** Environment setup verification

### Week 2: Understanding Your Data
- **Topics:** Data quality assessment, visualization best practices
- **Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization
  - Data Profiling: Systematic examination of dataset structure and quality assessment
  - Univariate Analysis: Statistical and visual exploration of individual variables
- **Lab Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Choices for Customer Survey Analysis (50 min)
- **Due:** Discussion post on data quality importance

### Week 3: Preparing Data for Machine Learning
- **Topics:** Feature transformation, handling categorical variables
- **Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
  - Feature transformation: Mathematical operations like scaling and polynomial features
  - Categorical encoding: Converting categorical variables using one-hot encoding
- **Lab Activity:** Evaluating the Effectiveness of Data Cleaning Strategies on Dataset Quality (120 min)
- **Due:** EDA report on provided dataset

### Week 4: Feature Selection and Optimization
- **Topics:** Identifying relevant features, scaling techniques
- **Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning
  - Feature Selection: Methods to identify and retain most relevant features
  - Feature Scaling: Standardization, min-max scaling, and robust scaling techniques
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Data Distribution Patterns Through Statistical Visualization Analysis (60 min)
- **Due:** Feature engineering assignment

### Week 5: Decision Trees - Your First ML Algorithm
- **Topics:** Decision tree algorithm, entropy, information gain, pruning
- **Lab Activity:** Building decision trees from scratch, scikit-learn implementation
- **Due:** Quiz 1 - Data preparation and EDA concepts

### Week 6: Ensemble Methods - Random Forests
- **Topics:** Bootstrap aggregating, random forests, feature importance
- **Lab Activity:** Comparing single trees vs. forest performance
- **Major Project 1 Assigned:** Customer Behavior Prediction Pipeline

### Week 7: Linear Models - Logistic Regression
- **Topics:** Linear regression review, logistic regression, regularization
- **Lab Activity:** Implementing gradient descent for logistic regression
- **Due:** Decision tree vs. random forest comparison report

### Week 8: Model Evaluation and Validation
- **Topics:** Cross-validation, performance metrics, bias-variance tradeoff
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Decomposition Analysis (80 min)
- **Due:** Major Project 1 - Customer Behavior Prediction Pipeline

### Week 9: Support Vector Machines
- **Topics:** Linear SVM, kernel trick, non-linear classification
- **Lab Activity:** Visualizing decision boundaries with different kernels
- **Assessment:** End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline: Business Case Presentation

### Week 10: Introduction to Neural Networks
- **Topics:** Perceptron, multi-layer networks, backpropagation
- **Lab Activity:** Building neural networks with TensorFlow/Keras
- **Major Project 2 Assigned:** Medical Image Classification

### Week 11: Deep Learning Architectures
- **Topics:** Convolutional neural networks, image classification
- **Lab Activity:** Critical Assessment of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Prediction Systems (180 min)
- **Due:** Neural network implementation assignment

### Week 12: Advanced Neural Networks
- **Topics:** Transfer learning, pre-trained models, fine-tuning
- **Lab Activity:** Using pre-trained CNNs for medical image analysis
- **Due:** Major Project 2 - Medical Image Classification

### Week 13: Recommendation Systems
- **Topics:** Collaborative filtering, content-based filtering, matrix factorization
- **Lab Activity:** Building recommendation engines with different approaches
- **Major Project 3 Assigned:** Recommendation System

### Week 14: Model Deployment and Ethics
- **Topics:** Model deployment strategies, ethical considerations, bias detection
- **Lab Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Customer Churn Prediction (180 min)
- **Due:** Ethics in ML reflection paper

### Week 15: Advanced Topics and Review
- **Topics:** Unsupervised learning preview, clustering, dimensionality reduction
- **Lab Activity:** Portfolio preparation and peer code reviews
- **Due:** Major Project 3 - Recommendation System

### Week 16: Final Presentations and Portfolio Review
- **Final Project Presentations**
- **Portfolio Submission**
- **Course Reflection and Feedback**

# PREDICTIVE ANALYTICS FOR BUSINESS DECISION MAKING: FROM RAW DATA TO STRATEGIC MODELS

**Course Code:** DS 3350  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Introduction to Statistics, Programming Fundamentals (Python), Database Management  
**Duration:** 15-week semester  
**Meeting Time:** Tuesday/Thursday 2:00-3:30 PM  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This hands-on course bridges the gap between data science theory and real-world business applications by focusing on building, validating, and deploying predictive models that drive strategic decision-making. Students work with authentic datasets from various industries including retail, finance, healthcare, and technology to solve pressing business challenges such as customer churn prediction, demand forecasting, risk assessment, and revenue optimization. 

The course emphasizes the complete modeling lifecycle: from exploratory data analysis and feature engineering to model selection, validation, and interpretation for non-technical stakeholders. Students learn to navigate common modeling pitfalls, handle imbalanced datasets, incorporate domain expertise, and communicate model insights effectively to business leaders. Through project-based learning, students develop expertise in supervised learning techniques including regression, classification, ensemble methods, and time series forecasting while gaining practical experience with model deployment considerations, A/B testing for model evaluation, and ethical implications of predictive analytics in business contexts.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Design and implement end-to-end predictive modeling workflows** for authentic business problems across multiple industries
2. **Master advanced feature engineering techniques, model validation strategies, and ensemble methods** to build robust predictive systems
3. **Develop expertise in translating complex model outputs** into actionable business insights and recommendations for executive audiences

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

- **Textbook:** "Hands-On Machine Learning" by Aurélien Géron (3rd Edition)
- **Software:** Python 3.8+, Jupyter Notebook, scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, seaborn
- **Platform:** Course materials available on Canvas
- **Hardware:** Laptop capable of running Python and Jupyter notebooks

---

**Topics:**
- Data Profiling: Systematic examination of data structure, quality, and characteristics
- Univariate Analysis: Statistical and visual exploration of individual variables
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Correlation Patterns in Real-World Dataset Scenarios (75 min)
- **Reading:** Chapter 1-2, Géron

### **Week 2: Foundation - Exploratory Data Analysis IIModule:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Statistical Visualization  
**Topics:**
- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis: Investigation of relationships between variables
- Advanced visualization techniques for business insights
- **Lab Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Quality: Bar Chart vs. Pie Chart Effectiveness (35 min)
- **Reading:** Chapter 3, Géron

### **Week 3: Data Preparation - Feature Engineering FundamentalsModule:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning  
**Topics:**
- Feature scaling and normalization techniques (StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, RobustScaler)
- Categorical encoding methods (one-hot, label, target, frequency encoding)
- **Lab Activity:** Evaluating Data Cleaning Approaches for Customer Survey Analysis (90 min)
- **Reading:** Chapter 4-5, Géron

### **Week 4: Data Preparation - Advanced Feature EngineeringModule:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Predictive Modeling  
**Topics:**
- Feature Engineering Pipeline: Systematic transformation processes
- Data Leakage Prevention: Maintaining model validity
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Advanced Feature Engineering Techniques in High-Dimensional Customer Churn Prediction (110 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Optimization Quiz **(Due: 100 points)**

### **Week 5: Business Applications - Customer AnalyticsFocus:** Customer churn prediction and segmentation  
**Topics:**
- Business context and problem framing
- Industry-specific feature engineering
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (55 min)
- **Project Launch:** Customer Segmentation Analysis Project

### **Week 6: Statistical FoundationsTopics:**
- Correlation vs. causation in business contexts
- Statistical inference for business decisions
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Churn Analysis (75 min)
- **Reading:** Chapter 6-7, Géron

### **Week 7: Model Building I - Supervised LearningTopics:**
- Linear and logistic regression for business applications
- Decision trees and interpretation
- Cross-validation strategies
- **Assessment:** Customer Segmentation Analysis Project **(Due: 100 points)**

### **Week 8: Model Building II - Advanced AlgorithmsTopics:**
- Ensemble methods (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting)
- Support Vector Machines
- Handling imbalanced datasets
- **Reading:** Chapter 8-9, Géron

### **Week 9: MIDTERM WEEKAssessment:** Advanced Predictive Modeling and Analysis Comprehensive Exam **(100 points)**

### **Week 10: Model Evaluation and ValidationTopics:**
- Business-relevant evaluation metrics
- A/B testing for model evaluation
- Validation strategies for time series data
- **Lab Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models (3.5 hours - split session)
- **Project Launch:** End-to-End Customer Churn Prediction Portfolio Project

### **Week 11: Advanced Topics - Dimensionality and ComplexityTopics:**
- Dimensionality reduction techniques
- Feature selection methods
- Model complexity and interpretability trade-offs
- **Lab Activity:** Interpreting Dimensionality Reduction Trade-offs (90 min)

### **Week 12: Model Interpretation and CommunicationTopics:**
- SHAP values and LIME for model explanation
- Communicating results to non-technical stakeholders
- Creating executive dashboards
- **Reading:** Chapter 10-11, Géron

### **Week 13: Deployment and Production ConsiderationsTopics:**
- Model deployment strategies
- Monitoring and maintenance
- Ethical considerations in predictive analytics
- **Lab Activity:** Evaluating Machine Learning Model Selection and Deployment Strategies (3 hours)

### **Week 14: Industry Applications and Case StudiesTopics:**
- Time series forecasting for demand planning
- Risk assessment in financial services
- Healthcare predictive analytics
- **Assessment:** End-to-End Customer Churn Prediction Portfolio Project **(Due: 100 points)**

### **Week 15: Final Presentations and Course Wrap-upAssessment:** End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline: Business Impact Analysis and Technical Implementation **(Presentations: 100 points)**
- Student presentations of portfolio projects
- Peer evaluations and feedback
- Course reflection and next steps

context.course_title: Ensemble Methods and Model Architecture Design for Complex Data Systems
context.course_description: This advanced course explores sophisticated ensemble modeling techniques and the strategic design of model architectures for complex, real-world data systems. Students will master the art of combining multiple learning algorithms to create robust predictive systems that outperform individual models. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on implementation of advanced ensemble methods including stacking, blending, and dynamic ensemble selection, while addressing critical challenges such as model diversity optimization, computational efficiency, and ensemble interpretability. Students will work with heterogeneous data sources, design custom ensemble architectures for specific domain problems, and learn to balance bias-variance tradeoffs in multi-model systems. The course integrates theoretical foundations with practical applications across domains including finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems. Advanced topics include ensemble pruning strategies, online ensemble learning, and ensemble methods for streaming data. Students will complete a capstone project involving the design and implementation of a novel ensemble architecture for a complex prediction task, demonstrating mastery of advanced modeling principles and their application to challenging real-world scenarios.
learning_objectives: Students will master advanced ensemble methods including stacking, boosting, and dynamic selection techniques for complex modeling scenarios

# Course Syllabus: Ensemble Methods and Model Architecture Design for Complex Data Systems

## Course Description

This advanced course explores sophisticated ensemble modeling techniques and the strategic design of model architectures for complex, real-world data systems. Students will master the art of combining multiple learning algorithms to create robust predictive systems that outperform individual models. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on implementation of advanced ensemble methods including stacking, blending, and dynamic ensemble selection, while addressing critical challenges such as model diversity optimization, computational efficiency, and ensemble interpretability. Students will work with heterogeneous data sources, design custom ensemble architectures for specific domain problems, and learn to balance bias-variance tradeoffs in multi-model systems. The course integrates theoretical foundations with practical applications across domains including finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems. Advanced topics include ensemble pruning strategies, online ensemble learning, and ensemble methods for streaming data. Students will complete a capstone project involving the design and implementation of a novel ensemble architecture for a complex prediction task, demonstrating mastery of advanced modeling principles and their application to challenging real-world scenarios.

## Learning Objectives

Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master Advanced Ensemble Methods:** Students will master advanced ensemble methods including stacking, boosting, and dynamic selection techniques for complex modeling scenarios
2. **Design Custom Model Architectures:** Students will design and implement custom model architectures that optimize performance across diverse data types and problem domains  
3. **Develop Ensemble Optimization Expertise:** Students will develop expertise in ensemble interpretability, model diversity metrics, and computational optimization strategies for large-scale systems

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation Review and Data Preparation
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization with Python
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Descriptive Statistics - measures of central tendency, variability, and distribution shape used to summarize dataset characteristics
  - Data Profiling - systematic examination of data quality, completeness, consistency, and structure to understand dataset limitations
- **Activities:** 
  - Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Business Decision-Making (45 min)
- **Readings:** Chapter 1-2 of textbook

### Week 2: Advanced Feature Engineering Foundations  
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature Engineering: The process of creating new features from existing data through mathematical transformations, combinations, and domain-specific knowledge to improve model performance
  - Feature Selection: Statistical and algorithmic methods for identifying the most relevant subset of features, including filter, wrapper, and embedded approaches to reduce dimensionality
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Feature Importance in Random Forest Models for Customer Churn Prediction (60 min)
- **Readings:** Chapter 3 of textbook, supplementary articles on feature engineering

### Week 3: Multivariate Analysis and Relationship Exploration
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Visualization Techniques  
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Univariate Analysis - Statistical summary and distribution examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and shape
  - Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis - Investigation of relationships between two or more variables using correlation analysis, crosstabulation, and conditional distributions
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Customer Behavior Data (85 min)
- **Assessment:** Fundamentals of Data Science: Exploratory Data Analysis Exam (100 points)

### Week 4: Advanced Feature Preprocessing Techniques
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- **Concepts Covered:**
  - Feature scaling and normalization - standardizing numerical features using min-max scaling, z-score normalization, and robust scaling techniques
  - Categorical encoding methods - converting categorical variables to numerical format using one-hot encoding, target encoding, and ordinal encoding
- **Activities:**
  - Evaluating the Quality of Data Visualizations for Sales Performance Analysis (70 min)
- **Readings:** Advanced preprocessing techniques literature

### Week 5: Introduction to Ensemble Methods
**Topics:**
- Theoretical foundations of ensemble learning
- Bias-variance decomposition in ensemble contexts
- Diversity measures and ensemble performance correlation
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance (75 min)
- **Readings:** Chapter 4-5 of textbook

### Week 6: Bagging and Random Forest Methods
**Topics:**
- Bootstrap aggregating principles and implementation
- Random Forest architecture and hyperparameter tuning
- Out-of-bag error estimation and variable importance
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Model Performance Metrics Through Cross-Validation Results Analysis (70 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Machine Learning Pipeline Design and Implementation Quiz (100 points)

### Week 7: Boosting Algorithms and Implementations
**Topics:**
- AdaBoost, Gradient Boosting, XGBoost architectures
- Sequential learning and error correction mechanisms
- Regularization strategies in boosting
- **Activities:**
  - Interpreting Feature Importance in Gradient Boosting Models Using SHAP Values (105 min)
- **Readings:** Chapter 6-7 of textbook

### Week 8: Stacking and Meta-Learning Strategies
**Topics:**
- Multi-level ensemble architectures
- Meta-learner selection and training strategies
- Cross-validation strategies for stacking
- **Assessment:** Customer Churn Prediction Analysis Lab Report (100 points)

### Week 9: Dynamic Ensemble Selection and Blending
**Topics:**
- Competence-based ensemble member selection
- Blending techniques and weight optimization
- Local vs. global ensemble selection strategies
- **Readings:** Advanced ensemble selection papers

### Week 10: Ensemble Optimization and Pruning
**Topics:**
- Computational efficiency optimization
- Ensemble pruning algorithms and strategies
- Trade-offs between ensemble size and performance
- **Activities:**
  - Critical Evaluation of Competing Machine Learning Models for Healthcare Prediction (180 min)

### Week 11: Interpretability in Ensemble Models
**Topics:**
- SHAP values for ensemble interpretation
- LIME applications in multi-model systems
- Ensemble-specific interpretability challenges
- **Assessment:** Ethical AI and Algorithmic Bias: Case Study Analysis and Mitigation Strategy Discussion (100 points)

### Week 12: Online Learning and Streaming Ensembles
**Topics:**
- Adaptive ensemble methods for streaming data
- Concept drift detection and ensemble adaptation
- Memory management in online ensemble systems
- **Readings:** Online learning ensemble papers

### Week 13: Domain-Specific Ensemble Applications
**Topics:**
- Ensemble methods in finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems
- Domain-specific architectural considerations
- Performance benchmarking across domains
- **Activities:**

### Week 14: Advanced Topics and Emerging Techniques
**Topics:**
- Deep ensemble methods
- Neural architecture search for ensembles
- Ensemble methods in deep learning contexts

### Week 15: Capstone Project Presentations
**Topics:**

# Predictive Analytics Laboratory: From Raw Data to Deployable Models

## Course Description

This intensive laboratory course bridges the gap between theoretical machine learning concepts and real-world predictive analytics implementation. Students work exclusively with messy, unstructured datasets from industry partners to build, validate, and deploy machine learning models that solve authentic business problems. The course emphasizes the complete ML pipeline - from data acquisition and preprocessing through feature engineering, model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and production deployment. 

Weekly lab sessions involve hands-on work with cloud platforms, automated ML pipelines, and model monitoring systems. Students collaborate in teams to tackle different domains including healthcare diagnostics, financial risk assessment, marketing optimization, and supply chain forecasting. Each team must deliver a fully functional, deployed model with accompanying API endpoints and monitoring dashboards. The course culminates in a 'Demo Day' where teams present their solutions to industry stakeholders.

Unlike traditional courses that use clean academic datasets, this laboratory focuses exclusively on the challenges of production machine learning - handling missing data, concept drift, model bias, scalability issues, and ethical considerations in automated decision-making systems.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement end-to-end machine learning pipelines using real-world, unstructured datasets from industry partners  
• Deploy production-ready predictive models with API endpoints, monitoring systems, and automated retraining capabilities on cloud platforms  
• Evaluate and mitigate bias, fairness, and ethical concerns in automated decision-making systems across different industry domains  
• Optimize model performance through advanced feature engineering, ensemble methods, and hyperparameter tuning techniques  
• Present deployed machine learning solutions to industry stakeholders and defend technical and business decisions  

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation and Data Understanding
**Topics:** Course introduction, industry partner presentations, team formation  
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization  
- Descriptive Statistics: Measures of central tendency, variability, and distribution shape including mean, median, mode, standard deviation, quartiles, and skewness
- Data Quality Assessment: Techniques for identifying and handling missing values, outliers, duplicates, and inconsistencies in real-world datasets

**Lab Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Housing Market Analysis (90 minutes)

### Week 2: Data Exploration and Quality Assessment
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization  
- Univariate Analysis - Statistical and visual examination of individual variables including measures of central tendency, dispersion, and distribution shape
- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis - Investigation of relationships between two or more variables using correlation analysis, contingency tables, and multi-dimensional visualizations

**Lab Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (75 minutes)

### Week 3: Feature Engineering Foundations
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning  
- Feature scaling and normalization - standardizing numerical features to similar ranges using techniques like StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, and RobustScaler
- Categorical encoding methods - converting categorical variables to numerical format using one-hot encoding, target encoding, and embedding techniques

**Assessment Due:** Data Science Fundamentals Quiz: Exploring Data Types and Basic Analysis (100 points)

### Week 4: Advanced Feature Engineering
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning  
- Feature Engineering: The process of creating new features from existing data through mathematical transformations, domain knowledge, and statistical techniques
- Feature Selection: Methods for identifying the most relevant subset of features including univariate selection, recursive feature elimination, and regularization-based approaches

**Lab Activity:** Interpreting Customer Segmentation Results from K-Means Clustering Analysis (60 minutes)

### Week 5: Feature Selection and Dimensionality Reduction
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning  
- Feature transformation: Mathematical operations (scaling, normalization, binning) applied to raw variables to improve model performance and ensure algorithm compatibility
- Dimensionality reduction: Techniques like PCA and t-SNE that reduce feature space while preserving essential information to combat curse of dimensionality

### Week 6: Model Building and Validation
**Topics:** Model selection, cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning  
**Lab Activity:** Interpreting Bias-Variance Tradeoff Through Cross-Validation Decomposition Analysis (90 minutes)

**Assessment Due:** Ethics and Bias in Machine Learning: A Critical Analysis Discussion (100 points)

### Week 7: Ensemble Methods and Advanced Modeling
**Topics:** Random forests, gradient boosting, ensemble techniques  
**Lab Activity:** Interpreting Bias-Variance Decomposition in Ensemble Model Performance (90 minutes)

### Week 8: Mid-Semester Project Check-in
**Assessment Due:** End-to-End Customer Churn Prediction and Business Impact Analysis - Progress Report (50 points)

### Week 9: Cloud Deployment and MLOps
**Topics:** AWS/GCP deployment, Docker containers, CI/CD pipelines  
**Lab Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Deployment Strategies for Real-World Business Impact (160 minutes)

### Week 10: Model Monitoring and Maintenance
**Topics:** Concept drift detection, automated retraining, A/B testing

### Week 11: API Development and Integration
**Topics:** RESTful APIs, Flask/FastAPI, database integration  
**Assessment Due:** End-to-End Customer Churn Prediction and Business Impact Analysis - Final Project (100 points)

### Week 12: Bias, Fairness, and Ethics in Production ML
**Topics:** Algorithmic bias detection, fairness metrics, ethical frameworks  
**Lab Activity:** Critical Evaluation of Machine Learning Model Performance in Healthcare Fraud Detection (210 minutes)

### Week 13: Dashboard Creation and Visualization
**Topics:** Interactive dashboards, business intelligence integration  
**Lab Activity:** Evaluating Data Visualization Effectiveness for Sales Dashboard Design (50 minutes)

### Week 14: Final Project Integration and Testing
**Topics:** System integration, performance optimization, final testing  
**Assessment Due:** End-to-End Machine Learning Pipeline Portfolio Project (100 points)

### Week 15: Demo Day Preparation
**Topics:** Presentation preparation, stakeholder communication, business case development

### Week 16: Demo Day and Course Wrap-up
**Assessment Due:** Real-World Data Science Project: From Raw Data to Business Insights - Final Presentation (100 points)  
**Event:** Industry Stakeholder Demo Day

## Assessment Plan

| Assessment | Type | Points | Due Date | Weight |
|------------|------|--------|----------|--------|
| Data Science Fundamentals Quiz | Quiz | 100 | Week 3 | 15% |
| Ethics and Bias Discussion | Discussion | 100 | Week 6 | 15% |
| Customer Churn Analysis Project | Project | 100 | Week 11 | 25% |
| ML Pipeline Portfolio | Portfolio | 100 | Week 14 | 25% |
| Final Presentation (Demo Day) | Presentation | 100 | Week 16 | 20% |
| **Total** | | **500** | | **100%** |

### Late Assignment Policy
- 0-24 hours late: -10%
- 24-48 hours late: -25%
- 48-72 hours late: -50%
- More than 72 hours late: 0 points (without prior arrangement)

Extensions may be granted for documented emergencies or health issues with advance notice.

### Team Work Policy
Most projects will be completed in teams of 3-4 students. All team members are expected to contribute equally. Peer evaluations will be conducted, and individual grades may be adjusted based on contribution levels. Team conflicts should be reported to the instructor immediately.

### Industry Partnership Guidelines
- All student work with industry partners is subject to signed NDAs
- Data security protocols must be followed strictly
- Professional communication standards apply to all industry interactions
- Students may not share proprietary data outside the course context

# Visual Storytelling with Data: From Raw Numbers to Compelling Narratives

**Course Code:** DS 210  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Introduction to Statistics, Basic Programming (Python recommended)  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## Course Description

This foundational course bridges the gap between raw data analysis and effective communication by teaching students how to transform complex datasets into clear, compelling visual stories. Students will explore the psychology of visual perception, learn to identify patterns and outliers through exploratory data visualization, and master the art of creating audience-appropriate data narratives. The course emphasizes hands-on experience with industry-standard visualization tools while developing critical thinking skills to evaluate when, why, and how different visualization techniques should be employed. Through real-world case studies spanning business, science, journalism, and public policy, students will learn to navigate ethical considerations in data presentation, avoid common visualization pitfalls, and create interactive dashboards that drive decision-making. By semester's end, students will possess both the technical skills to implement sophisticated visualizations and the design sensibility to ensure their data stories are both accurate and engaging.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Design and implement effective data visualizations using principles of visual perception and cognitive psychology  
• Critically evaluate visualization choices and identify misleading or inappropriate graphical representations  
• Create interactive dashboards and data stories that effectively communicate insights to diverse audiences  
• Apply exploratory data analysis techniques through visualization to discover patterns, trends, and anomalies in real datasets  
• Demonstrate proficiency in multiple visualization tools and programming libraries while understanding their appropriate use cases  

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Introduction to Visual Storytelling
**Module:** Course Introduction and Foundations

- The role of visualization in data science
- Psychology of visual perception
- History and evolution of data visualization

### Week 5: Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis

**Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (90 minutes)

### Week 6: Correlation vs. Causation in Data Visualization

### Week 7: Data Quality and Visualization Ethics

# Digital Gold Rush: Extractive Analytics Across Industries and Domains

**Course Code:** DATA 3XX  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Introduction to Data Science, Statistics for Data Science, Programming in Python  
**Semester:** Fall/Spring 2024  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

## Course Description

This survey course explores the diverse landscape of data mining applications across multiple industries, treating data as a valuable resource to be extracted, refined, and monetized. Students will examine how different sectors—from healthcare and finance to social media and manufacturing—approach the mining of insights from their unique data assets. The course covers both traditional mining techniques (association rules, clustering, classification) and emerging extraction methodologies (text mining, graph mining, stream mining) while emphasizing the economic and strategic value of mined insights. Through case studies and hands-on projects, students will learn to identify mining opportunities, select appropriate extraction techniques, and evaluate the quality of mined knowledge. The curriculum balances technical mining methods with business applications, ethical considerations, and industry-specific challenges. Students will develop a practitioner's perspective on how data mining creates competitive advantage across diverse domains, understanding both the technical pipeline from raw data to actionable insights and the strategic decision-making that determines mining success. The course culminates in a comparative analysis project where students evaluate mining approaches across different industries.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• Compare and contrast data mining approaches across at least five different industry sectors  
• Apply multiple mining techniques (clustering, classification, association rules, text mining) to extract insights from diverse datasets  
• Evaluate the business value and ethical implications of mining strategies in different organizational contexts  
• Design industry-appropriate mining pipelines that account for domain-specific data characteristics and constraints  
• Critically assess the quality and actionability of mined insights across different application domains  

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundation and Industry Overview
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis and Data Visualization with Python
- Descriptive Statistics: measures of central tendency, variability, and distribution shape
- Data Profiling: systematic examination of dataset structure and quality assessment
- **Activity:** Interpreting Statistical Distributions in Real Estate Data (65 min)

### Week 2: Data Quality and Preparation
**Module:** Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) and Data Visualization Fundamentals  
- Univariate Analysis: examining individual variables through statistical measures and visualizations
- Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis: exploring variable relationships and dependencies
- **Activity:** Interpreting Feature Correlation Patterns in Customer Churn Analysis (60 min)

### Week 3: Feature Engineering Foundations
**Module:** Feature Engineering and Selection for Machine Learning
- Feature Transformation: mathematical operations to improve predictive power
- Categorical Encoding: converting categorical variables to numerical representations
- **Activity:** Interpreting Feature Importance Rankings in Machine Learning Models (95 min)

### Week 4: Advanced Feature Engineering
**Module:** Feature Engineering for Machine Learning: Creating Predictive Variables
- Feature scaling and normalization techniques for algorithm preparation
- Advanced categorical encoding methods including target and hash encoding
- **Assessment:** Customer Churn Analysis: Feature Engineering and Model Evaluation Quiz (100 points)

### Week 5: Healthcare Industry Mining
- Electronic Health Records (EHR) mining challenges and opportunities
- Clinical decision support systems and predictive modeling
- HIPAA compliance and privacy-preserving mining techniques
- **Activity:** Interpreting Correlation vs. Causation in Real-World Healthcare Datasets (90 min)

### Week 6: Financial Services Analytics
- Fraud detection and risk assessment models
- Algorithmic trading and market analysis
- Credit scoring and loan default prediction
- Regulatory compliance in financial data mining

### Week 7: Retail and E-Commerce Mining
- Customer segmentation and recommendation systems
- Market basket analysis and association rules
- Supply chain optimization and demand forecasting

# SURVIVAL ANALYSIS AND RELIABILITY THEORY
## Statistical Methods for Time-to-Event Data

**Course Number:** MATH 4XX  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** MATH 3610 (Mathematical Statistics), MATH 2270 (Linear Algebra), STAT 3000 (Statistical Computing)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  
**Semester:** [Term Year]

---

## INSTRUCTOR INFORMATION

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION
This advanced undergraduate course explores the statistical analysis of time-to-event data, where the primary outcome is the time until an event occurs. Students will master survival functions, hazard rates, and censoring mechanisms while developing expertise in parametric and non-parametric survival models. The course covers Kaplan-Meier estimation, Cox proportional hazards regression, accelerated failure time models, and competing risks analysis. Emphasis is placed on real-world applications across diverse fields including biomedical research, engineering reliability, customer lifetime value analysis, and actuarial science. Students will work with complex datasets involving right-censored, left-truncated, and interval-censored observations. Advanced topics include frailty models for correlated survival times, joint modeling of longitudinal and survival data, and Bayesian survival analysis. The course integrates theoretical foundations with practical implementation using statistical software, preparing students for graduate studies or careers in data science, biostatistics, quality control, or risk analysis.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master fundamental concepts** of survival analysis including survival functions, hazard functions, and various censoring mechanisms in time-to-event data

2. **Apply non-parametric methods** such as Kaplan-Meier estimation and log-rank tests, alongside semi-parametric approaches like Cox proportional hazards regression

3. **Develop expertise** in implementing survival analysis techniques using statistical software to solve real-world problems in medicine, engineering, and business analytics

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS
- **Textbook:** Klein, J.P. & Moeschberger, M.L. (2003). *Survival Analysis: Techniques for Censored and Truncated Data*, 2nd Edition. Springer.

# CONVERGENCE AND CONTINUITY: A CAPSTONE JOURNEY THROUGH REAL ANALYSIS

**Course Number:** MATH 4XX  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** Calculus III, Introduction to Proofs, Linear Algebra  
**Semester:** Fall 2024  

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This capstone course synthesizes fundamental concepts in real analysis through rigorous exploration of limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration. Students will master epsilon-delta proofs, investigate pathological functions that challenge intuition, and analyze the convergence properties of sequences and series. The course emphasizes deep theoretical understanding while connecting abstract concepts to applications in physics, economics, and computer science. Students will complete an independent research project examining a specialized topic such as fractal dimensions, measure theory, or functional analysis. Through collaborative problem-solving sessions and peer presentations, students will develop mathematical maturity and communication skills essential for graduate study or careers requiring analytical thinking. The curriculum bridges pure mathematical theory with computational methods, incorporating software tools for visualization and numerical analysis. Students will construct counterexamples to false conjectures, prove original theorems, and critically analyze mathematical literature. This capstone experience culminates in a comprehensive portfolio demonstrating mastery of proof techniques, analytical reasoning, and the ability to communicate complex mathematical ideas to diverse audiences.

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master rigorous proof techniques** including epsilon-delta arguments and construct counterexamples to demonstrate deep understanding of real analysis concepts

• **Synthesize theoretical knowledge** through an independent research project, demonstrating ability to analyze mathematical literature and communicate original findings

• **Develop mathematical maturity** by connecting abstract analytical concepts to real-world applications and computational methods

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

- **Textbook:** Rudin, W. *Principles of Mathematical Analysis*, 3rd Edition

# CALCULUS THROUGH MATHEMATICAL MODELING AND APPLICATIONS
**Course Syllabus - Fall 2024**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Course Title:** Calculus Through Mathematical Modeling and Applications  
**Course Code:** MATH 251  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** College Algebra or equivalent (MATH 140 or placement exam)  
**Classroom:** Mathematics Building,   

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This foundational course explores calculus concepts through real-world mathematical modeling, emphasizing how differential and integral calculus serve as powerful tools for understanding dynamic systems. Students will discover calculus principles by investigating practical problems from physics, economics, biology, and engineering. The course covers limits, derivatives, and integrals not as abstract concepts, but as natural solutions to concrete modeling challenges. Topics include population dynamics using differential equations, optimization problems in business contexts, rates of change in scientific phenomena, and accumulation processes in various fields. Students will develop computational skills while building intuitive understanding of why calculus works and when to apply specific techniques. The modeling approach helps students see calculus as a living language for describing change and accumulation in the natural and social sciences.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master fundamental calculus concepts** including limits, derivatives, and integrals through modeling real-world phenomena
• **Apply differential and integral calculus** to construct and analyze mathematical models in diverse scientific and social contexts  
• **Develop practical expertise** in using calculus as a problem-solving tool while building strong computational and analytical skills

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1: Foundations - Linear Functions and Real-World Relationships**
- **Module:** Linear Functions: Modeling Real-World Relationships
- **Topics:** Slope as rate of change, y-intercept as initial value
- **Activity:** Budget Planning for a Class Pizza Party (60 min)

### **Week 2: Systems and Applications**
- **Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems
- **Topics:** System definitions, solution methods (graphing, substitution, elimination)
- **Activity:** Pizza Party Fraction Calculator (35 min)

### **Week 3: Advanced Systems Methods**
- **Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Real-World Applications
- **Topics:** Augmented matrices, Gaussian elimination
- 
### **Week 4: Quadratic Models I**
- **Module:** Quadratic Functions and Their Real-World Applications
- **Topics:** Standard form, vertex form fundamentals
- **Activity:** Design Your Dream Playground (100 min)

### **Week 5: Quadratic Models II**
- **Module:** Quadratic Functions: Modeling Real-World Phenomena
- **Topics:** Vertex form applications, discriminant analysis
- **Assessment:** Basic Math Concepts Presentation (Due)

### **Week 6: Advanced Quadratic Applications**
- **Module:** Quadratic Functions: Graphing, Transformations, and Real-World Applications
- **Topics:** Comprehensive quadratic analysis and transformations
- **Activity:** Design Your Dream Theme Park (75 min)

### **Week 7: Exponential and Logarithmic Foundations**
- **Module:** Exponential and Logarithmic Functions: Properties, Applications, and Problem Solving
- **Topics:** Exponential growth/decay, logarithmic inverses
- **Assessment:** Basic Arithmetic and Problem-Solving Skills Assessment (Midterm Exam)

### **Week 8: Introduction to Limits**
- **Topics:** Intuitive approach to limits through modeling continuous change
- **Applications:** Instantaneous rates in population models
- 
### **Week 9: Limits and Continuity**
- **Topics:** Formal limit definitions, continuity in real-world contexts
- **Applications:** Modeling discontinuous phenomena
- **Assessment:** Advanced Mathematical Reasoning Forum (Discussion begins)

### **Week 10: Introduction to Derivatives**
- **Topics:** Derivatives as rates of change, geometric interpretation
- **Applications:** Velocity, population growth rates
- **Activity:** Optimizing Water Distribution Networks (110 min)

### **Week 11: Derivative Rules and Applications**
- **Topics:** Power rule, product rule, chain rule through modeling
- **Applications:** Related rates in engineering contexts
- 
### **Week 12: Optimization I**
- **Topics:** Critical points, first and second derivative tests
- **Applications:** Business optimization problems
- **Activity:** Optimizing Multi-Variable Production Functions (70 min)

### **Week 13: Optimization II**
- **Topics:** Applied optimization, constrained optimization introduction
- **Activity:** Optimization Engineering Challenge: Solar Panel Array (120 min)
- **Assessment:** Statistical Analysis Lab Report (Due)

### **Week 14: Introduction to Integration**
- **Topics:** Antiderivatives, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
- **Applications:** Accumulation in physical and social systems
- **Activity:** Design Community Water Park Project (Begin - 5 hours total)

### **Week 15: Integration Applications**
- **Topics:** Definite integrals, area under curves, applications
- **Applications:** Total change, displacement, accumulation problems
- **Activity:** Complete Water Park Project

### **Week 16: Advanced Modeling Project**
- **Topics:** Comprehensive modeling using all calculus tools
- **Activity:** Urban Traffic Flow Optimization Model (270 min)
- **Assessment:** Advanced Multivariable Calculus Quiz (Final Week)

---

# MATH 4950: Differential Equations and Dynamic Systems
## Mathematical Modeling of Real-World Phenomena

**Semester:** Fall 2024  
**Credits:** 3  
**Prerequisites:** Calculus III (Multivariable Calculus), Linear Algebra, Differential Equations  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM  

---

## Course Description

This capstone course synthesizes advanced calculus concepts through the lens of differential equations and dynamic systems theory to model complex real-world phenomena. Students will employ multivariable calculus, vector calculus, and advanced integration techniques to formulate, analyze, and solve systems of differential equations arising in physics, biology, economics, and engineering. The course emphasizes the geometric interpretation of solutions, phase plane analysis, and stability theory while utilizing computational tools for visualization and numerical methods. Students will work on semester-long research projects, applying Laplace transforms, Fourier analysis, and partial differential equations to investigate problems such as population dynamics, heat diffusion, fluid flow, or epidemic spread. The capstone nature involves independent research, literature review, mathematical modeling from first principles, rigorous analysis using calculus-based methods, and presentation of findings. This course bridges theoretical mathematics with practical applications, requiring students to demonstrate mastery of calculus concepts while developing critical thinking skills for mathematical research and problem-solving in interdisciplinary contexts.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master advanced calculus techniques** including multivariable calculus, vector fields, and infinite series to solve complex differential equation systems
2. **Apply capstone research methodologies** to independently formulate, analyze, and solve mathematical models of real-world dynamic systems
3. **Develop expertise in stability analysis**, phase plane methods, and computational approaches using calculus-based mathematical modeling

## Weekly Schedule

- Gaussian elimination and row echelon form

- Separation of variables and integrating factors

### **Week 5-6: Nonlinear Systems and Phase Plane AnalysisModule:** Linear Systems and Matrix Solutions
- Nonlinear differential equations
- Phase portraits and equilibrium points
- Linearization techniques
- Stability analysis of critical points

### **Week 7-8: Second-Order Systems and OscillationsModule:** Quadratic Functions: Modeling Real-World Phenomena
- Second-order linear differential equations
- Characteristic equations and solution methods
- Damped and forced oscillations
- Energy methods and conservation laws

### **Week 9: Midterm Examination Period**

- **Midterm Exam:** Quadratic Functions and Real-World Applications Exam

### **Week 10-11: Laplace Transforms and Fourier AnalysisModule:** Linear Functions and Their Real-World Applications
- Laplace transform methods
- Solving differential equations with discontinuous forcing
- Introduction to Fourier series
- Applications to periodic phenomena

### **Week 12-13: Partial Differential EquationsModule:** Quadratic Functions: Modeling Real-World Phenomena (Advanced)
- Heat equation and diffusion processes
- Wave equation and vibrating systems
- Separation of variables method
- Boundary value problems

### **Week 14: Computational Methods and Numerical SolutionsModule:** Linear Functions and Their Applications
- Euler's method and Runge-Kutta methods
- Numerical stability and error analysis
- Computer simulations of dynamic systems
- Chaos and strange attractors

### **Week 15: Research Project Presentations**
- Student presentations of semester research projects
- Peer review and discussion
- Integration of course concepts

### **Week 16: Final Examination Period**
- Comprehensive final examination
- Course reflection and synthesis

# COMPUTATIONAL STATISTICS FOR HIGH-DIMENSIONAL DATA ANALYSIS
**Course Code:** MATH 4XX | **Credits:** 4 | **Semester:** Fall/Spring 2024

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Meeting:** [Days/Times]  
**Lab Sessions:** [Day/Time] - [Computer Lab Location]

### Prerequisites
- MATH 3XX: Advanced Linear Algebra
- STAT 3XX: Mathematical Statistics  
- Programming experience in R or Python
- Multivariable Calculus

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This intensive course explores advanced statistical methods designed for analyzing complex, high-dimensional datasets commonly encountered in modern data science, genomics, and machine learning applications. Students will dive deep into computational approaches that traditional statistical methods cannot handle, including curse of dimensionality problems, sparse regression techniques, and non-parametric methods for big data. 

The course emphasizes hands-on implementation of algorithms from scratch, theoretical understanding of convergence properties, and real-world applications using R and Python. Weekly intensive lab sessions require students to work with datasets containing thousands of variables and millions of observations. Topics include regularization methods (LASSO, Ridge, Elastic Net), dimensionality reduction techniques (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP), bootstrap methods for high-dimensional inference, and modern clustering algorithms. 

Students will complete three major projects involving genomic data analysis, financial time series with thousands of assets, and image classification using statistical learning approaches. The course culminates in an original research project where students must develop and validate a novel statistical method for a high-dimensional problem of their choosing, requiring both theoretical justification and empirical validation through simulation studies.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

• **Master advanced regularization techniques** and understand their theoretical properties in high-dimensional settings
• **Implement computational algorithms** for dimensionality reduction and assess their performance on real-world datasets  
• **Develop expertise in bootstrap and resampling methods** for statistical inference when traditional asymptotic theory fails
• **Design and execute comprehensive simulation studies** to validate statistical methods and compare algorithmic performance
• **Analyze complex datasets** from genomics, finance, and computer vision using appropriate statistical frameworks

---

## WEEKLY SCHEDULE

### **Week 1-2: Mathematical Foundations**
*Building the theoretical groundwork for high-dimensional analysis*

**Week 1: Linear Systems and Matrix Operations**
- System of Linear Equations: Collections of equations solved simultaneously in high-dimensional spaces
- Augmented Matrix: Matrix formulations for large-scale linear systems
- 
**Week 2: Advanced Matrix Theory for Statistics**  
- Row Echelon Form (REF) and Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF): Standardized formats revealing solution structure
- Singular Value Decomposition and eigendecomposition in high dimensions
- 
### **Week 3-4: The Curse of Dimensionality**
*Understanding fundamental challenges in high-dimensional statistics*

**Week 3: High-Dimensional Geometry**
- Distance metrics and their behavior in high dimensions
- Concentration of measure phenomena
- 
**Week 4: Classical Statistics Breakdown**
- Why traditional methods fail in high dimensions
- Sample complexity and overfitting
- 
### **Week 5-7: Regularization Methods**
*Sparse regression techniques for high-dimensional data*

**Week 5: Ridge Regression and Theory**
- L2 regularization theory and implementation
- Bias-variance tradeoff in high dimensions
- - **PROJECT 1 ASSIGNED:** Genomic Data Analysis

**Week 6: LASSO Regression**
- L1 regularization and sparsity
- Coordinate descent algorithms
- 
**Week 7: Elastic Net and Extensions**
- Combined L1/L2 penalties
- Group LASSO and fused LASSO
- 
### **Week 8-10: Dimensionality Reduction**
*Computational approaches to reduce data complexity*

**Week 8: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)**
- Theory and computation for high-dimensional PCA
- Robust PCA methods
- - **PROJECT 1 DUEWeek 9: Non-linear Dimensionality Reduction**
- t-SNE algorithm and implementation
- UMAP theory and practice
- - **PROJECT 2 ASSIGNED:** Financial Time Series Analysis

**Week 10: Random Projections and Sketching**
- Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma
- Fast random projection methods
- 
### **Week 11-12: Bootstrap and Resampling Methods**
*Statistical inference in high-dimensional settings*

**Week 11: Bootstrap Theory**
- Bootstrap consistency in high dimensions
- Wild bootstrap and multiplier bootstrap
- 
**Week 12: Resampling for Model Selection**
- Cross-validation in high dimensions
- Stability selection methods
- - **PROJECT 2 DUE**

### **Week 13-14: Clustering and Classification**
*Modern algorithms for unsupervised and supervised learning*

**Week 13: High-Dimensional Clustering**
- K-means modifications for high dimensions
- Spectral clustering algorithms
- - **PROJECT 3 ASSIGNED:** Image Classification

**Week 14: Statistical Classification Methods**
- Nearest neighbor methods in high dimensions
- Support Vector Machines theory
- 
### **Week 15-16: Research Project and Presentations**
*Original research in high-dimensional statistics*

**Week 15: Research Project Development**
- Novel method development
- Simulation study design
- - **PROJECT 3 DUE**
- **FINAL PROJECT ASSIGNEDWeek 16: Final Presentations**
- Student research presentations
- Peer review and discussion
- Course wrap-up and advanced topics preview

# MATH 4850: Algebraic Structures in Cryptographic Systems and Error-Correcting Codes

**Semester:** Spring 2024  
**Credits:** 4  
**Prerequisites:** Abstract Algebra (MATH 3310), Linear Algebra (MATH 2340), Number Theory (MATH 3320)  
**Meeting Time:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM, Lab: T 2:00-3:50 PM  

---

## Course Description

This advanced course explores the deep algebraic foundations underlying modern cryptography and error-correction technologies. Students will investigate how abstract algebraic structures—including finite fields, polynomial rings, elliptic curves, and lattices—serve as the mathematical backbone for securing digital communications and ensuring data integrity. The course bridges pure algebraic theory with real-world applications, examining how Galois fields enable AES encryption, how elliptic curve groups power modern public-key cryptography, and how Reed-Solomon codes protect data in everything from QR codes to satellite communications.

Students will construct and analyze cryptographic protocols, implement error-correcting algorithms, and prove security properties using advanced algebraic techniques. Topics include the algebraic structure of block ciphers, the discrete logarithm problem in various groups, lattice-based cryptography for post-quantum security, and the connection between coding theory and algebraic geometry. Through hands-on projects, students will build functional cryptographic systems and explore cutting-edge research in algebraic cryptanalysis.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master the application of finite fields, polynomial rings, and elliptic curves** to construct and analyze cryptographic protocols
2. **Apply advanced group theory and ring theory** to implement and break various encryption schemes and error-correcting codes  
3. **Develop expertise in using algebraic geometry and lattice theory** to design next-generation cryptographic systems

---

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1: Foundations of Linear Algebraic Systems in Cryptography
- **Topics:** Linear systems in cryptanalysis, matrix methods for breaking classical ciphers
- **Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems with Multiple Variables
- **Key Concepts:** 
  - System of linear equations as applied to frequency analysis
  - Solution types in cryptographic contexts (unique keys, multiple keys, no solution)

### Week 2: Matrix Methods in Cryptographic Analysis
- **Topics:** Advanced matrix operations for Hill ciphers and linear cryptanalysis
- **Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Real-World Applications
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Augmented matrices in cryptographic key recovery
  - Row operations for systematic cryptanalysis

### Week 3: Linear Transformations and Block Ciphers
- **Topics:** Matrix representation of cryptographic transformations
- **Module:** Linear Systems and Matrix Operations
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Matrix representation of encryption operations
  - Systematic solution methods for linear cryptanalysis

### Week 4-5: Gaussian Elimination in Cryptographic Attacks
- **Topics:** Structured approaches to breaking linear ciphers
- **Modules:** Advanced matrix methods and inverse operations
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Gaussian elimination for key recovery
  - Matrix inverse methods in decryption
- **Lab Activity:** Optimizing Hospital Staffing Using Linear Programming (adapted for cryptographic resource allocation)

### Week 6: Finite Fields - Foundations
- **Topics:** Construction and properties of Galois fields
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Field axioms and finite field arithmetic
  - Irreducible polynomials and field extensions

### Week 7: Finite Fields in AES Encryption
- **Topics:** GF(2^8) operations in Advanced Encryption Standard
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Polynomial representation in GF(2^8)
  - S-box construction using multiplicative inverses

### Week 8: Reed-Solomon Codes and Error Correction
- **Topics:** Algebraic construction of error-correcting codes
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Polynomial evaluation codes
  - Syndrome decoding algorithms
- **Lab Activity:** Design and Construct a Multi-Variable Optimization Model for Real-World Resource Allocation (adapted for error correction parameters)

### Week 9: Group Theory in Public-Key Cryptography
- **Topics:** Discrete logarithm problem in cyclic groups
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Group operations and subgroup structure
  - Computational complexity of discrete logarithms

### Week 10: Elliptic Curve Cryptography - Algebraic Foundations
- **Topics:** Elliptic curves over finite fields
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Point addition formulas and group law
  - Elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem

### Week 11: Advanced ECC and Cryptographic Protocols
- **Topics:** ECDH, ECDSA, and elliptic curve implementations
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Protocol security based on elliptic curve groups
  - Curve selection and security parameters

### Week 12: Polynomial Rings and Stream Ciphers
- **Topics:** Linear feedback shift registers and algebraic attacks
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Polynomial rings over finite fields
  - Berlekamp-Massey algorithm
- **Lab Activity:** Engineering Bridge Design Using Quadratic Optimization (adapted for cryptographic parameter optimization)

### Week 13: Lattice-Based Cryptography
- **Topics:** Post-quantum cryptographic systems
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Lattice problems (SVP, CVP, LWE)
  - NTRU and Ring-LWE cryptosystems

### Week 14: Algebraic Attacks and Cryptanalysis
- **Topics:** Gröbner bases and equation solving in cryptanalysis
- **Key Concepts:**
  - Polynomial system solving
  - Algebraic immunity

### Week 15: Advanced Topics and Current Research
- **Topics:** Isogeny-based cryptography, multivariate cryptography
- **Student Presentations:** Research project presentations

### Week 16: Final Projects and Comprehensive Review
- **Final project presentations**
- **Course synthesis and future directions**

---

## Assessment Plan

### Grade Distribution
- **Homework Assignments (8 @ 50 points each):** 400 points (40%)
- **Midterm Examinations (2 @ 100 points each):** 200 points (20%)
- **Research Project:** 200 points (20%)
- **Lab Reports (5 @ 20 points each):** 100 points (10%)
- **Final Examination:** 100 points (10%)

**Total Points:** 1000

1. **Personal Budget Planning Project** (100 points) - *Adapted as "Cryptographic Parameter Selection Project"*

2. **Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation** (100 points)

3. **Advanced Problem Solving Quizzes** (100 points each)

   - Focus on implementation and analysis skills

4. **Mathematical Problem-Solving Discussions** (100 points total)

   - Peer review and mathematical communication emphasis

5. **Mathematical Patterns Lab Reports** (100 points total, 20 points each)

# PROBABILISTIC MODELING IN RISK ASSESSMENT AND DECISION SCIENCES
**MATH 3850 | Fall 2024 | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## COURSE INFORMATION

**Class Meetings:** MWF 10:00-10:50 AM, [Room Number]  
**Prerequisites:** MATH 2410 (Probability and Statistics), MATH 2350 (Linear Algebra)

---

## COURSE DESCRIPTION

This course explores the application of probability theory to real-world risk assessment and decision-making scenarios across industries including finance, insurance, healthcare, and engineering. Students will learn to construct and analyze probabilistic models for uncertain events, utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, Bayesian inference, and stochastic processes to quantify risk and optimize decision strategies. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on experience with statistical software and case studies drawn from actuarial science, portfolio management, quality control, and epidemiological modeling. Key topics include probability distributions for modeling failure times and claim amounts, value-at-risk calculations, decision trees under uncertainty, Markov chains for system reliability, and Bayesian updating for dynamic risk assessment. Students will work on semester-long projects involving real datasets from partner organizations, developing comprehensive risk models and presenting actionable recommendations to stakeholders. The course bridges theoretical probability concepts with practical implementation, preparing students for careers in quantitative risk management, actuarial consulting, or data-driven decision making roles where uncertainty quantification is critical.

---

## LEARNING OBJECTIVES

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Construct and validate probabilistic models** for complex real-world risk scenarios using appropriate probability distributions and stochastic processes
2. **Apply Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian methods** to quantify uncertainty and update risk assessments with new information
3. **Develop expertise in translating probabilistic analysis results** into actionable business recommendations and risk management strategies

---

## REQUIRED MATERIALS

# MATH 3350: Cryptographic Foundations and Network Security Mathematics

## Course Description

This course explores the mathematical foundations underlying modern cryptography and network security systems. Students will delve into number theory, modular arithmetic, graph theory, and combinatorial structures that form the backbone of encryption algorithms, digital signatures, and secure communication protocols. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on implementation of cryptographic schemes including RSA, elliptic curve cryptography, and blockchain mechanisms. The course bridges theoretical concepts with industry practices, examining how mathematical structures ensure data integrity, authentication, and privacy in digital systems.

# Statistical Reasoning in Modern Data Sciences
**Mathematics 3XXX | Fall/Spring 20XX | 3 Credit Hours**

---

## Course Description

This survey course explores the fundamental statistical principles that underpin contemporary data analysis across diverse fields including business analytics, biomedical research, social sciences, and machine learning. Students will examine how statistical reasoning evolved from classical hypothesis testing to modern computational approaches, investigating real-world applications through case studies from genomics, economics, environmental science, and digital marketing. 

The course emphasizes understanding when and why different statistical methods are appropriate, rather than computational mechanics. Topics include exploratory data analysis, probability distributions, statistical inference, regression modeling, experimental design, and an introduction to Bayesian methods and machine learning algorithms. Students will critically evaluate statistical claims in scientific literature and media, developing skills to identify misleading uses of statistics. 

Hands-on projects using software tools like R or Python will demonstrate how statistical concepts apply to authentic datasets. By surveying both traditional and emerging statistical paradigms, students gain appreciation for statistics as a powerful lens for understanding uncertainty and making data-driven decisions in an increasingly quantitative world.

# Bayesian Decision Theory and Risk Modeling in Financial Mathematics
**Course Syllabus - Fall 2024**

## Course Description

This advanced undergraduate course explores the intersection of Bayesian statistics, decision theory, and financial risk assessment. Students will develop expertise in constructing prior distributions, implementing Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, and applying Bayesian inference to real-world financial scenarios. The curriculum emphasizes hands-on analysis of portfolio optimization, credit risk modeling, and derivative pricing under uncertainty. Through computational projects using R and Python, students will master advanced statistical techniques including hierarchical modeling, empirical Bayes methods, and sequential decision-making processes. The course integrates modern statistical learning with classical financial mathematics, preparing students to tackle complex problems in quantitative finance, actuarial science, and risk management.

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this course, students will be able to:

1. **Master Bayesian statistical inference techniques** and apply them to financial risk assessment and portfolio optimization problems
2. **Develop proficiency in computational statistics methods** including MCMC, variational inference, and bootstrap techniques for complex financial modeling
3. **Construct and validate sophisticated risk models** using real financial data while understanding regulatory frameworks and industry best practices

## Weekly Schedule

### Week 1-2: Mathematical Foundations
**Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Methods and Applications
- **Concepts:**
  - Augmented Matrix: Rectangular array combining coefficient matrix with constants vector to represent linear systems
  - Row Echelon Form: Systematic arrangement enabling back-substitution for financial modeling applications
- **Applications:** Portfolio constraint matrices, risk factor models

### Week 3-4: Advanced Linear Systems
**Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems Using Matrix Methods
- **Concepts:**
  - Gaussian elimination: Systematic method using elementary row operations for solving financial optimization problems
  - System solutions in portfolio theory: Understanding consistent, inconsistent, and dependent solutions
- **Applications:** Multi-asset portfolio optimization, arbitrage detection

### Week 5-6: Functional Analysis for Finance
**Module:** Quadratic Functions: Graphing, Transformations, and Real-World Applications
- **Concepts:**
  - Standard form (ax² + bx + c): Risk-return relationships in portfolio theory
  - Vertex form (a(x-h)² + k): Optimization of utility functions and efficient frontiers
- **Applications:** Mean-variance optimization, quadratic utility functions

### Week 7-8: Linear Risk Models
**Module:** Linear Functions and Their Real-World Applications
- **Concepts:**
  - Slope as rate of change: Beta coefficients and systematic risk measures
  - Y-intercept as initial value: Alpha generation and risk-free components
- **Applications:** Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), factor models

### Week 9-10: Advanced Calculus Applications
**Module:** Limits and Continuity of Functions
- **Concepts:**
  - One-sided limits: Modeling asymmetric risk distributions and tail behavior
  - Epsilon-delta definition: Formal foundation for convergence in stochastic processes
- **Applications:** Value-at-Risk calculations, extreme value theory

### Week 11-12: Bayesian Inference Foundations
**Module:** Systems of Linear Equations: Solving Real-World Problems
- **Concepts:**
  - Bayesian updating systems: Multiple equations representing prior beliefs and data
  - Solution methods: Computational approaches to posterior inference
- **Applications:** Credit risk updating, dynamic portfolio rebalancing

### Week 13-14: Advanced Optimization
**Module:** Quadratic Functions: Graphing, Transformations, and Real-World Applications
- **Concepts:**
  - Vertex form transformations: Optimizing risk-adjusted returns
  - Axis of symmetry: Understanding risk-return trade-offs
- **Applications:** Modern Portfolio Theory, Black-Litterman model

### Week 15-16: Integration and Review
**Module:** Linear Functions and Their Applications
- **Concepts:**
  - Rate of change applications: Dynamic hedging ratios
  - Initial value problems: Setting up Bayesian priors
- **Final project presentations and comprehensive review**

## Assessment Plan

### Major Assessments (85% of total grade)

**1. Advanced Mathematical Research Presentation (20% - 100 points)**
- **Type:** Presentation
- **Topic:** Real-world applications of Bayesian methods in financial risk modeling
- **Due:** Week 14
- **Requirements:** 20-minute presentation with mathematical derivations and empirical analysis

**2. Mathematical Problem-Solving Portfolio (25% - 100 points)**
- **Type:** Portfolio
- **Content:** Collection of solved problems demonstrating mastery of Bayesian inference, MCMC methods, and risk modeling
- **Due:** Week 15
- **Components:** 5 major problem sets with computational implementations

**3. Advanced Numerical Analysis Lab Report (20% - 100 points)**
- **Type:** Lab Report
- **Topic:** Comparative study of MCMC algorithms for financial applications
- **Due:** Week 12
- **Requirements:** Full statistical analysis with R/Python code and interpretation

**4. Advanced Calculus and Linear Algebra Integration Exam (20% - 100 points)**
- **Type:** Exam
